Define the BN sublattice-staggering parametrization and topology label used in the illustrative device model: set $U_B = -U_N = \lambda U_0$, where $U_0$ measures the strength of the staggered potential and $\lambda=\pm 1$ defines the BN fragment topology (i.e., whether the $B$- vs $N$-site potential sign is one way or inverted); for illustrative transport calculations the authors choose $U_0=t$ and fix $t=2.6\ \mathrm{eV}$.

Specify the device geometry and numerical details used with this tight-binding model: the two-terminal geometry has semi-infinite zigzag (ZZ) graphene nanoroad leads acting as source and drain, a central scattering region containing a snake-shaped or straight graphene nanoroad embedded in BN with $96\times 60$ lattice sites, and a nanoroad width fixed at 32 carbon atoms; the BN/graphene interface staggering is encoded by the $U_B$/$U_N$ pattern with $\lambda=\pm1$ controlling the relative topology of left and right BN shoulders.

Report the principal numerical transport signatures reproduced by this illustrative tight-binding device model: (a) for same-topology BN shoulders and straight ZZ nanoroads the conductance per spin is quantized to $G = 2n\,(e^{2}/h)$ with a small insulating gap near charge neutrality due to finite-size edge effects; (b) for opposite-topology BN shoulders and straight ZZ nanoroads the conductance quantization rule changes to $G = (2n-1)\,(e^{2}/h)$ reflecting the addition of a single topologically supported kink channel; and (c) for curved reversed-topology nanoroads (snake-shaped geometries with mixed ZZ and AC edge fragments) the conductance near charge neutrality remains on a robust plateau associated with the kink-derived channel with only minor fluctuations and negligible backscattering — these features are observed in the conductance versus Fermi-energy plots the authors present.

motivating_questions.content: Realistic device-level transport predictions require a compact lattice Hamiltonian and computationally tractable evaluation of Green's functions and lead self-energies for finite central regions with semi-infinite graphene leads. Prior to this work there was no explicitly-stated, demonstrably-capable tight-binding device-level model in the literature that both encodes BN sublattice staggering as a topology parameter and shows that the model reproduces the expected topologically assisted conductance behavior in straight and curved nanoroad geometries. Without such an operational model, it would be difficult to explore how device geometry and topology combine to produce the observed transport plateaus.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A practical atomistic tight-binding computational scheme is developed that simulates an effectively infinite graphene half-plane to the output side of a QPC while using only a finite computational box. The scheme attaches semi-infinite in-plane leads along the upper and lower horizontal edges on the output side of the QPC to carry away current into an in-plane continuum, and additionally attaches semi-infinite vertical leads at the two right-hand corners of the finite box that act as current sinks to suppress artificial corner backscattering. The leads preserve the graphene atomic structure by duplicating elementary cells and using nearest-neighbor hoppings equal to the graphene intra-layer hoppings. This open-boundary configuration eliminates edge-induced standing waves and subband-quantization artefacts from the conductance maps and enables convergence of SGM simulations that represent an infinite graphene sheet outside the QPC while retaining atomistic detail inside the finite box.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Open-boundary computational method to simulate infinite graphene half-plane for atomistic tight-binding SGM

conclusion.content: A practical atomistic tight-binding computational scheme is developed that simulates an effectively infinite graphene half-plane on the output side of a quantum point contact (QPC) while using only a finite computational box. The scheme attaches semi-infinite in-plane leads along the upper and lower horizontal edges on the output side of the QPC to carry away current into an in-plane continuum, and additionally attaches semi-infinite vertical leads at the two right-hand corners of the finite box that act as current sinks to suppress artificial corner backscattering. The leads preserve the graphene atomic structure by duplicating elementary cells and using nearest-neighbor hoppings equal to the graphene intra-layer hoppings ($t_{ij} = -3.12$ eV). This open-boundary configuration eliminates edge-induced standing waves and subband-quantization artefacts from the conductance maps and enables convergence of scanning gate microscopy (SGM) simulations that represent an infinite graphene sheet outside the QPC while retaining atomistic detail inside the finite box.

For the atomistic tight-binding simulation of a graphene quantum point contact (QPC) etched in an armchair nanoribbon of width 509 atoms (~62 nm) with semicircular constrictions of radius 28 nm and narrowest width 6 nm, the open-boundary configuration consisting of (i) semi-infinite in-plane leads along the full length of the upper and lower horizontal edges on the output side of the QPC, which duplicate the graphene elementary cells and use the same nearest-neighbor intra-layer hopping $t_{ij} = -3.12$ eV, and (ii) additional semi-infinite vertical leads attached at the two right-hand corners of the computational box that act as current sinks, absorbs all outgoing current without producing measurable spurious reflection from the boundaries or corners.

premises.content: For the etched graphene QPC without singly-connected edge atoms at EF = 0.312 eV, the conductance map with closed boundary conditions (finite nanoribbon of width 509 atoms) shows complex, non-regular fluctuations due to many transverse subbands, while the map with open boundary conditions (semi-infinite in-plane leads and corner current sinks) shows a clean, periodic λF/2 interference pattern far from the QPC (Fig. 5). The two maps share the same QPC-centered halos, confirming that the open BCs do not alter the near-constriction physics and remove the multi-mode contamination.

steps.reasoning:
Define the atomistic tight-binding model used as the starting microscopic description: the Hamiltonian is
$H=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\left(t_{ij}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}+h.c.\right)+\sum_{i}V(\mathbf{r}_{i})c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i}$,
where the sum $\langle i,j\rangle$ runs over nearest-neighbor pairs of atomic sites, $t_{ij}$ denotes the hopping matrix element between sites $i$ and $j$, $c_{i}^{\dagger}$ ($c_{i}$) is the creation (annihilation) operator for the $p_{z}$ orbital at site $i$, and $V(\mathbf{r}_{i})$ is the external potential at the atomic position $\mathbf{r}_{i}$.
[41]

State the computational objective and constraint: simulate scattering and scanning-gate microscopy (SGM) for a graphene quantum point contact (QPC) while representing an effectively infinite graphene half-plane to the right (output) side of the QPC, but using only a finite rectangular computational box so that atomistic tight-binding resolution is retained inside the box.

Introduce the primary open-boundary strategy to represent an infinite graphene half-plane: attach two semi-infinite in-plane leads along the upper and lower horizontal edges on the output (right) side of the finite computational box so that outgoing current can propagate into an in-plane continuum rather than being reflected by the finite box edges; these two leads are semi-infinite in the $y$ direction and extend along the full upper and lower edge on the output side.
Fig. 1(c)

Describe the atomic construction of the horizontal in-plane leads so that they preserve the graphene lattice and couple seamlessly to the finite box: the leads are built by duplicating an elementary cell of graphene along the lead direction to enforce periodic semi-infinite extension, the duplicated elementary cell provides the periodic continuation, and the hoppings inside the leads are taken equal to the nearest-neighbor intra-layer graphene hoppings $t_{ij} = -3.12\ \mathrm{eV}$ (i.e., the same intra-layer tight-binding parameter used inside the finite box) so that the leads preserve the graphene atomic structure and dispersion.
Fig. 3
[41]

Identify and describe a remaining artificial scattering source created by the finite-box geometry after attaching the horizontal in-plane leads: the right-hand corners of the finite rectangular box (the corner regions between the horizontal in-plane leads and the finite-box right edge) act as scattering centers that can reflect current back into the computational region and produce artificial corner backscattering and interference.
Fig. 1(c)

Introduce the corner-sink remedy: attach two additional semi-infinite vertical leads at the two right-hand corners of the finite box (one at the upper-right corner and one at the lower-right corner) that are semi-infinite in the out-of-plane ($z$) direction and act as current sinks; these vertical leads absorb the current that would otherwise scatter at the corners and return to the computational region, thereby suppressing corner-induced artificial backscattering.
Fig. 1(c)

Describe the atomic construction of the vertical corner leads and the choice of hopping elements: the vertical corner leads are attached at the corner atoms in an atomistically consistent way, and, consistent with the atomistic tight-binding approach used everywhere else in the simulation, the hopping elements for these leads are chosen equal to the nearest-neighbor intra-layer graphene hoppings so that the leads remain compatible with the graphene lattice and tight-binding parametrization.
Fig. 3

Explain how the combined boundary configuration (horizontal in-plane leads on the output side plus vertical corner sink leads) functions to emulate an effectively infinite graphene half-plane: the horizontal leads remove reflection from the finite upper and lower edges by allowing outgoing modes to continue into semi-infinite graphene strips (thus preventing subband-quantization-induced multiple Fermi wavelengths in the output region), while the vertical corner sink leads remove artificial corner reflections; together these open boundary conditions allow outgoing waves to leave the finite box without producing standing waves tied to the simulation box boundaries.
Fig. 1(c)

State the consequence for SGM simulations: with the described open-boundary lead configuration the computed conductance maps are free of edge-induced standing waves and subband-quantization artefacts (i.e., the maps show a single characteristic Fermi-wavelength oscillation in the output region rather than a superposition of subband-dependent wavelengths), enabling convergent atomistic tight-binding SGM simulations that represent an infinite graphene sheet outside the QPC while retaining atomistic detail inside the finite computational box.
Fig. 5(b)

motivating_questions.content: In atomistic tight-binding calculations of SGM for graphene QPCs, a finite simulation domain with closed boundary conditions produces spurious reflections from the domain edges and especially from the box corners; these reflections create artificial interference patterns and generate multiple transverse subband-dependent Fermi wavelengths, which obscure the scattering signal originating from the tip–QPC interaction. Prior approaches either required impractically large simulation domains or accepted contamination of the SGM maps by finite-size artefacts. A computational method that (a) preserves atomistic detail near the QPC, (b) enforces current absorption at distant boundaries without introducing additional unphysical scattering, and (c) is efficient enough for tight-binding calculations of realistic samples was missing. Without such a method one could not produce conductance maps that isolate tip-induced backscattering and thereby could not test whether the Klein tunneling physics would suppress or allow observable standing-wave fringes in graphene QPCs.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
The nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) framework is formulated for layered device geometries by folding the semi-infinite leads into the finite device region via lead self-energies. The core matrix equations defined over the device layers are
$$
A(E)G(E)=I,\quad A(E)=EI-H-\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)-\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E),
$$
$$
A(E)G^{n}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E),
$$
$$
A(E)G^{p}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E),
$$
with definitions:
- $G(E)$: retarded Green's function over device layers 1..$n$,
- $G^{n}(E)$: electron correlation function (occupied-state density kernel),
- $G^{p}(E)$: hole (unoccupied-state) correlation function,
- $H$: device Hamiltonian in layered block-tridiagonal form,
- $\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$: lead self-energies nonzero only on device boundary layers (1 and $n$), obtained from surface Green's functions of semi-infinite leads,
- $\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)$: self-energy due to electron–phonon interactions (in general nonlocal but in the presented layered approximation taken diagonal per layer),
- $\Sigma^{\text{in(out)}}(E)=\Sigma_{\text{lead}}^{\text{in(out)}}(E)+\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}^{\text{in(out)}}(E)$ are the total in/out scattering self-energies.
These relations include explicit identifications of $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)=-2\operatorname{Im}[\Sigma_{L,R}(E)]$ and the lead in-scattering forms $\Sigma_{L}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{L}(E)f_{L}(E)$ and $\Sigma_{R}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{R}(E)f_{R}(E)$, thereby providing a compact, device-oriented NEGF system suitable for numerical solution on layered (quasi-1D in transport) discretizations.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Compact NEGF formulation for layered device models with folded lead self-energies

conclusion.content:
The nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) equations for a device discretized into layers 1..n are written over the finite device region after folding the semi-infinite leads into energy-dependent lead self-energies, yielding the linear systems
      $$
      A(E)G(E)=I,\qquad A(E)=E I - H - \Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)-\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E),
      $$
      $$
      A(E)G^{n}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E),
      $$
      $$
      A(E)G^{p}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E).
      $$
      In these expressions: $G(E)$ is the retarded Green's function defined on the device-layer degrees of freedom labeled $1,\dots,n$; $G^{n}(E)$ is the electron correlation (occupied-state density) matrix; $G^{p}(E)$ is the hole (unoccupied-state) correlation matrix; $H$ is the device Hamiltonian arranged in block-tridiagonal form with block rows and columns indexed by layer; $\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$ is the sum of lead self-energies that are nonzero only on the device boundary layer blocks (layer 1 and layer $n$) and represent the effect of semi-infinite leads; $\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)$ is the self-energy due to electron–phonon interactions (in the layered approximation treated as a block-diagonal operator with nonzero blocks on each device layer); and the total in/out scattering self-energies are $\Sigma^{\text{in(out)}}(E)=\Sigma_{\text{lead}}^{\text{in(out)}}(E)+\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}^{\text{in(out)}}(E)$.  The lead broadening matrices are defined by $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)=-2\operatorname{Im}[\Sigma_{L,R}(E)]$, and the lead in-scattering blocks take the form $\Sigma_{L}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{L}(E)f_{L}(E)$ and $\Sigma_{R}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{R}(E)f_{R}(E)$ where $f_{L,R}(E)$ are the lead Fermi functions; these relations allow a compact, device-only NEGF system suitable for numerical solution on layered (quasi-1D transport) discretizations.

The dominant residual risks are computational/model bridges: (P1) the assumption that semi-infinite leads can be reduced to localized surface self-energies in realistic nonperiodic or strongly scattering leads, and (P2) the tractability of energy-dependent phonon self-energies and lead+phonon coupled surface Green's functions. H1 converts the infinite-dimensional problem into a clearly defined finite object, but P1/P2 limit the claim's practical scope: the formulation is correct, but numerical suitability in all realistic lead/device scenarios is not guaranteed without further algorithmic advances.", "structural_edges": [{"target": "paper:811903549792321536::conclusion_2", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:811903549792321536::conclusion_3", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:811903549792321536::conclusion_4", "type": "supports"}]}

premises.content:
For a layered device discretization connected to semi-infinite leads that are locally periodic (constant per-lead block Hamiltonian and constant inter-layer coupling within each lead), the influence of a given semi-infinite lead on the finite device region is represented by a lead self-energy block computed from the surface Green's function of that semi-infinite lead: specifically, if $T_{D-L}$ denotes the matrix coupling device layer 1 (the device edge) to the first lead layer and $g_{L}^{\text{surf}}(E)$ denotes the surface Green's function of the semi-infinite left lead (the block of the lead Green's function corresponding to the lead edge layer), then the left-lead self-energy block that appears on the device-layer row/column 1 is
      $$
      \Sigma_{L}(E)=T_{D-L}\,g_{L}^{\text{surf}}(E)\,T_{L-D},
      $$
      and analogously for the right lead at the device layer $n$.  Here $g_{L}^{\text{surf}}(E)$ is obtained as the inverse of the semi-infinite-lead block operator restricted to the lead (i.e., it satisfies $A_{LL}^\prime g_{L}^{\text{surf}}=I$ in the lead subspace), and $\Sigma_{L}(E)$ is therefore a compact operator supported only on the device boundary-layer degrees of freedom.
      Eq. (115); Eq. (118)

That construction is exact for leads that are periodic, homogeneous, or handled by a controllable surface-Green's\u2011function solver; when leads are inhomogeneous, have comparable mode count to the device, or have spatially varying scattering, the surface-Green's\u2011function approximation can be inaccurate or expensive to obtain. The paper itself flags this difficulty (Sec. V-B, VI and the Open Questions) but nevertheless presents the compact formulation as the central device-oriented object.", "failure_mode": "If the surface-Green's\u2011function representation of a lead is inaccurate in the sense that the real device\u2013lead coupling cannot be reduced to a boundary self-energy that is localized on the first/last device layers (for example because the \"lead\" region is only weakly periodic, includes strong inelastic processes, or shares many modes with the device), then the compact A(E)G(E)=I device equations (and therefore any numerical NEGF solver built around them) will misrepresent boundary scattering and mode mixing. Concretely, predicted boundary Gamma matrices, in\u2011scattering terms, and therefore G, G^n and current expressions will be quantitatively biased: transmission T(E) and local densities near the contact will be wrong, and device-level predictions (currents and potential profiles used in Conclusions 1,4,5\u20139) can shift by amounts comparable to the reported effects. The mechanism is that an incorrect Sigma_lead changes A(E) and all downstream Green's functions; the scope of damage is large \u2014 numerical solutions claimed to be \"device-only\" would no longer be reliable unless the lead treatment is revised or the device region is expanded to include more of the nonperiodic lead."}
premises.title: Lead self-energy equals coupling matrices times lead surface Green's function

premises.content:
The device-only NEGF formulation remains numerically tractable for layered discretizations because (i) the phonon self-energy is represented as a block-diagonal operator with nonzero block on each device layer (in the layered approximation the phonon self-energy is taken diagonal per layer), and (ii) the surface Green's functions of periodic semi-infinite leads required to form the lead self-energies can be obtained either by solving the matrix quadratic surface-Green's equation
      $$
      \big[A_l' - T_l^\dagger g_{L}^{\text{surf}}(E) T_l\big]\,g_{L}^{\text{surf}}(E)=I,
      $$
      iteratively via
      $$
      \big[A_l' - T_l^\dagger g_{L}^{\text{surf},(m-1)}(E) T_l\big]\,g_{L}^{\text{surf},(m)}(E)=I,
      $$
      or by transforming the lead blocks to a transverse-mode basis in which the blocks are diagonal and solving the scalar quadratic equations for each mode; once the diagonal per-layer phonon self-energy and the lead surface Green's functions are available, the combined operator
      $A(E)=E I - H - \Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E) - \Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$
      has block-tridiagonal structure and can be solved by the layer-recursive algorithms described for layered systems.
      Fig. 12

The paper acknowledges iterative inner loops and computational burden (Sec. V, VI, Appendix III) but does not provide complexity bounds or convergence controls for coupled phonon + lead computations in realistic (non-ideal) leads; the assumption that the presented layered approximation and diagonal-in-layer phonon model makes the problem tractable is therefore an uncertain bridge.", "failure_mode": "If computing energy-dependent, possibly nonlocal phonon self-energies and the corresponding surface Green's functions cannot be made tractable (either because the number of energy points required, the coupling across energies, or the nonlocal off-diagonal scattering terms blow up memory/time), then the claim that the compact layered-device NEGF is \"suitable for numerical solution\" narrows: it will remain formally exact but infeasible for realistic devices except under further approximations (e.g., diagonal phonon, Born approximation, neglect of real parts). Consequently many of the paper's practical demonstrations (self-consistent device solutions and device-level predictions) would be limited to smaller, idealized devices or would require additional uncontrolled approximations, reducing the generality of Conclusion 1."}
premises.title: Device-only NEGF tractable because phonon self-energy localized and surface Green's functions computable

premises.content: Starting from the infinite-dimensional Green's equation over device plus semi-infinite leads including phonon self-energy A'G=I, the authors apply exact block-matrix elimination (Dyson partitioning) to fold the leads into finite-dimensional boundary self-energies and obtain a device-only operator A(E)=EI-H-Sigma_Phonon(E)-Sigma_lead(E) satisfying A(E)G(E)=I defined over device layers 1..n.

steps.reasoning: Start from a nearest-neighbor tight-binding description of a layered device in which each layer $q$ contains $N_q$ orbitals (grid points) and layers couple only to nearest neighbors; the single-particle Hamiltonian restricted to the device-and-leads region is a block-tridiagonal matrix whose diagonal blocks are the per-layer Hamiltonians $H_q$ and whose off-diagonal blocks are interlayer couplings $T_{q,q\pm1}$. Define the energy variable $E$ (electron energy measured from an arbitrary reference), the identity matrix $I$ over the device-layer degrees of freedom, and the (retarded) Green's function $G(E)$ to satisfy $[EI-H]G(E)=I$ when no other processes are present.

Partition the system conceptually into three regions: left semi-infinite lead (L), finite device region (D) comprising layers $1,\dots,n$, and right semi-infinite lead (R). Define $H_D$ as the Hamiltonian restricted to device layers 1..$n$, and let the semi-infinite lead blocks couple to the device only at device boundary layers $1$ and $n$ via coupling matrices $T_{DL}$ and $T_{DR}$. Note: the indexing of layers and the block-tridiagonal structure are explicit in the layered discretization.

Eliminate (fold) the semi-infinite leads into the finite device region by expressing the effect of each lead as an energy-dependent self-energy acting only on the corresponding boundary device layer: define the lead self-energy matrices $\Sigma_L(E)$ and $\Sigma_R(E)$ with nonzero blocks only at device-layer indices $(1,1)$ and $(n,n)$ respectively, where $\Sigma_{L} = T_{D L}\,g_{L}(E)\,T_{L D}$ and $\Sigma_{R} = T_{D R}\,g_{R}(E)\,T_{R D}$ and $g_{L}(E)$ and $g_{R}(E)$ are the surface Green's functions of the isolated semi-infinite leads evaluated at their edge layers. These relations follow from elimination of the lead degrees of freedom in the block partitioned linear system for the full Green's function.

Define the total phonon (and other interaction) self-energy over device layers as $\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)$, which may be nonzero on all device layers; when interactions are ignored in the leads their effect is retained in the device through $\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}$ restricted to device layers. The full device Dyson equation (retarded) including lead and phonon self-energies becomes $A(E)G(E)=I$ with
$A(E)=EI-H-\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)-\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$,
where $\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$ is the block-diagonal matrix whose only nonzero blocks are $\Sigma_{L}(E)$ at layer 1 and $\Sigma_{R}(E)$ at layer $n$.

Introduce the electron correlation (occupied-state) function $G^{n}(E)$ and the hole (unoccupied-state) correlation function $G^{p}(E)$ and define their governing linear equations on the device layers by folding lead and phonon in/out scattering into the right-hand sides. Explicitly state the device-layer equations
$A(E)G^{n}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E)$ and
$A(E)G^{p}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E)$,
where $G^{\dagger}(E)$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate (advanced) Green's function and $\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)$ and $\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)$ are the total in- and out-scattering self-energy matrices defined over device layers.

Define the total in/out self-energies as sums of lead and phonon contributions: for in-scattering $\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)=\Sigma_{\text{lead}}^{\text{in}}(E)+\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}^{\text{in}}(E)$ and for out-scattering $\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)=\Sigma_{\text{lead}}^{\text{out}}(E)+\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}^{\text{out}}(E)$, where the lead in/out terms are nonzero only on device layers $1$ and $n$ and the phonon terms are in general nonzero across device layers (the paper later specifies forms for the phonon contributions under the Born approximation).

Make explicit the identification between lead self-energies and lead-driven scattering rates: define the coupling-strength matrices $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)$ by $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)=-2\operatorname{Im}[\Sigma_{L,R}(E)]$ (where $\operatorname{Im}[\cdot]$ denotes the matrix imaginary part) and express the lead in-scattering matrices as $\Sigma_L^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_L(E) f_L(E)$ and $\Sigma_R^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_R(E) f_R(E)$ where $f_{L,R}(E)$ are the lead occupation (Fermi) functions; similarly express lead out-scattering as $\Sigma_L^{\text{out}}(E)=\Gamma_L(E)[1-f_L(E)]$ and $\Sigma_R^{\text{out}}(E)=\Gamma_R(E)[1-f_R(E)]$.

Collect the above definitions into the compact, device-oriented NEGF system suitable for layered discretizations: the retarded Dyson equation $A(E)G(E)=I$ with $A(E)=EI-H-\Sigma_{\text{Phonon}}(E)-\Sigma_{\text{lead}}(E)$ together with the correlation equations $A(E)G^{n}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{in}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E)$ and $A(E)G^{p}(E)=\Sigma^{\text{out}}(E)G^{\dagger}(E)$ and with the identifications $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)=-2\operatorname{Im}[\Sigma_{L,R}(E)]$, $\Sigma_{L}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{L}(E) f_{L}(E)$, and $\Sigma_{R}^{\text{in}}(E)=\Gamma_{R}(E) f_{R}(E)$ provides the compact finite-dimensional device-level NEGF formulation claimed. This set of matrix relations is sufficient to compute device Green's functions, densities, and currents once numerical methods for solving the layered linear systems and for evaluating phonon self-energies are specified. [16]

motivating_questions.content: Physical context: realistic nanoscale transistors and layered nanostructures (nanowires, nanotubes, double-gate MOSFET cross-sections) require quantum mechanical modeling of transport including open boundaries and interactions. Prior state: quantum transport had been formulated in several equivalent many-body and scattering frameworks, but the full many-body NEGF equations are infinite-dimensional when leads are treated explicitly, and practical device simulation needs device-only equations. Limitations: without a compact device-only NEGF representation that folds lead effects into self-energies, numerical implementations would require handling semi-infinite matrices or ad hoc boundary treatments; this complicates inclusion of scattering and self-consistent electrostatics. Consequences: absence of a standardized device-level NEGF formalism prevented the straightforward development of simulation codes that couple quantum transport, scattering self-energies, and Poisson electrostatics for layered device geometries; it impeded quantitatively consistent predictions of densities, currents, and transmission in device-relevant cross sections. The presented compact layered-device NEGF equations directly address this gap by casting the transport problem into finite-dimensional matrix equations with physically defined lead and phonon self-energies, enabling self-consistent simulation workflows.

A computational method is formulated that (a) constructs the complete scattering-state wave function of a layered device with noncollinear magnetization by matching the solution in a finite scattering region to Bloch eigenmodes of the semi-infinite crystalline leads (using Bloch-factor matrices $F(\\pm)$ defined from the eigenmode matrices $\\mathbf{W}(\\pm)$ and their eigenvalues), (b) uses TB-LMTO potentials obtained self-consistently (TB-LMTO-SGF with CPA for disorder) and the rigid-rotation approximation to represent noncollinear local spin quantization axes via unitary rotations $U_{\\mathbf{R}}(\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}},\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}})$, and (c) evaluates spin-transfer torque as the imbalance of spin currents computed from the obtained TB basis amplitudes via the spin-current operator and the linear-response expression
$$
T_{\\mathbf{R}}=\\left(\\frac{\\hbar}{2}\\right)\\frac{e}{h}\\frac{1}{N_{\\|}}\\sum_{s,\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\langle\\hat{\\mathbf{T}}_{\\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\rangle V_b,
$$
where $\\langle\\hat{\\mathbf{T}}_{\\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\rangle$ is the difference of incoming and outgoing spin-current expectation values for site $\\mathbf{R}$ at Fermi energy, $N_{\\|}$ is the number of lateral $\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}$ points, and $eV_b=\\mu_L-\\mu_R$. The method explicitly formulates embedding potentials from the leads (e.g. $S_{0,-1}F_L^{-1}(-)$) so that the finite scattering-region equations of motion yield the full, normalized scattering wave function used to compute transmission, reflection, particle currents, spin currents and site-resolved STT in the same TB-LMTO basis.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: First-principles wave-function matching method for STT in noncollinear layered systems

conclusion.content:

      T_{\mathbf{R}}=\left(\frac{\hbar}{2}\right)\frac{e}{h}\frac{1}{N_{\|}}\sum_{s,\mathbf{k}_{\|}}\langle\hat{\mathbf{T}}_{\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\mathbf{k}_{\|})\rangle V_b,

steps.reasoning:
Define the device geometry and basis: a layered device consists of a finite scattering region S (principal layers indexed $1\\le I\\le N$) sandwiched by semi-infinite crystalline leads denoted L (left) and R (right); there is perfect lattice periodicity in the lateral $X$-$Z$ plane and transport is along the $Y$ axis. The localized orbital tight-binding linearized muffin-tin orbital (TB-LMTO) basis $|\\mathbf{R}L\\zeta\\rangle$ is used, where $\\mathbf{R}$ is a site index, $L\\equiv(l,m)$ with $l,m$ orbital quantum numbers, and $\\zeta=\\uparrow(\\downarrow)$ denotes the spin eigenstate parallel (antiparallel) to a local spin-quantization axis. 
[19]
Fig. 1

Write the short-range TB-LMTO Hamiltonian (first-order in $E-E_F$) in the global coordinate system with rigid-rotation treatment of local spin quantization axes: the Hamiltonian matrix elements are
$$
\\mathbf{H}_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\alpha}=U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\overline{\\mathcal{C}}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}U_{\\mathbf{R}'}^{\\dagger}\\delta_{\\mathbf{R}'L'\\mathbf{R}L}
+\\left[U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\left(\\overline{\\Delta}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}\\right)^{\\frac{1}{2}}U_{\\mathbf{R}}^{\\dagger}S_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\alpha}
U_{\\mathbf{R}'}\\left(\\overline{\\Delta}_{\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\alpha}\\right)^{\\frac{1}{2}}U_{\\mathbf{R}'}^{\\dagger}\\right],
$$
where $\\overline{\\mathcal{C}}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}$ and $\\overline{\\Delta}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}$ are $2\\times2$ potential-parameter matrices diagonal in the local coordinate system, $S_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\alpha}$ are screened structure-constant matrices block-diagonal in spin space, and $U_{\\mathbf{R}}(\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}},\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}})$ is the unitary rotation matrix that rigidly rotates the local spin quantization axis at site $\\mathbf{R}$ with angles $\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}},\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}$ given explicitly by
$$
U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\left(\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}},\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}\\right)=\\left[\\begin{array}{cc}
\\cos\\frac{\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}e^{-i\\frac{\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}} & -\\sin\\frac{\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}e^{-i\\frac{\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}} \\\\
\\sin\\frac{\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}e^{i\\frac{\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}} & \\cos\\frac{\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}e^{i\\frac{\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}}}{2}}
\\end{array}\\right].
$$
This implements the rigid-rotation approximation for noncollinear magnetization representation in the TB-LMTO framework.

State the KKR (tail-cancellation) equation for noncollinear systems that yields the equation of motion in the TB-LMTO representation at energy $E$ (set to the Fermi energy $E_F$ for transport):
$$
\\sum_{\\mathbf{R}',L'}\\left(-U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\overline{P}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}(E)U_{\\mathbf{R}}^{\\dagger}\\delta_{\\mathbf{R}\\mathbf{R}'}\\delta_{LL'}-S_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\alpha}\\right)C_{\\mathbf{R}'L'}=0,
$$
where $\\mathbf{C}_{\\mathbf{R}L}=U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\left(\\overline{\\Delta}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}\\right)^{\\frac{1}{2}}U_{\\mathbf{R}}^{\\dagger}\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}$ relates the KKR amplitudes $\\mathbf{C}_{\\mathbf{R}L}$ to the TB-LMTO amplitudes $\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}$, and $\\overline{P}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}(E)$ is the screened potential-function matrix diagonal in the local coordinate system. This provides the layerwise equations of motion used to construct scattering solutions.

Exploit the two-dimensional translational symmetry in the lateral plane to label states by lateral crystal momentum $\\mathbf{k}_{\\parallel}$ in the 2D Brillouin zone and write the layer EOM in mixed real/reciprocal representation as a tridiagonal recurrence over principal layers $I$:
$$
- S_{I,I-1}^{\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\mathbf{C}_{I-1}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}) +\\left(U_I\\overline{P}_{I,I}(E_F)U_I^{\\dagger}-S_{I,I}^{\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\right)\\mathbf{C}_I(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}) - S_{I,I+1}^{\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\mathbf{C}_{I+1}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}) = 0,
$$
where $\\mathbf{C}_I(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})$ is the $2M$-dimensional layer amplitude vector (with $M=(l_{\\max}+1)^2 h$ and $h$ atoms per principal layer). This sets up a finite-range tight-binding-like EOM ready for matching to lead Bloch states.

Construct Bloch eigenmodes (propagating and evanescent) of the semi-infinite crystalline leads by solving the lead EOM with Bloch ansatz $\\overline{\\mathbf{C}}_n=\\lambda^n\\overline{\\mathbf{C}}_0$ in the local coordinate system, obtaining eigenvectors $\\overline{\\mathbf{w}}_{\\mu}^{\\uparrow(\\downarrow)}(\\pm)$ and eigenvalues $\\lambda_{\\mu}(\\pm)$ sorted into right-going $(+)$ and left-going $(-)$ sets for majority ($\\uparrow$) and minority ($\\downarrow$) spin local quantization. Form the eigenmode matrix in the global coordinate system
$$
\\mathbf{W}(\\pm)=U_0\\overline{\\mathbf{W}}(\\pm)\\equiv U_0[\\overline{\\mathbf{w}}_{1}^{\\uparrow}(\\pm),\\ldots,\\overline{\\mathbf{w}}_{M}^{\\uparrow}(\\pm),
\\overline{\\mathbf{w}}_{1}^{\\downarrow}(\\pm),\\ldots,\\overline{\\mathbf{w}}_{M}^{\\downarrow}(\\pm)].
$$
This provides the basis for expressing lead embedding.
[17]

Define the Bloch-factor matrices $F(\\pm)$ from the eigenmode matrices $\\mathbf{W}(\\pm)$ and their eigenvalues collected into diagonal matrices $\\boldsymbol{\\Lambda}(\\pm)$ via
$$
F(\\pm)\\equiv\\mathbf{W}(\\pm)\\boldsymbol{\\Lambda}(\\pm)\\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\\pm),
$$
where $\\boldsymbol{\\Lambda}(\\pm)$ has diagonal elements $[\\lambda_{1}^{\\uparrow}(\\pm),\\ldots,\\lambda_{M}^{\\uparrow}(\\pm),\\lambda_{1}^{\\downarrow}(\\pm),\\ldots,\\lambda_{M}^{\\downarrow}(\\pm)]$. The Bloch-factor matrices $F(\\pm)$ satisfy the Bloch relation $\\mathbf{C}_I(\\pm)=F(\\pm)^{I-J}\\mathbf{C}_J(\\pm)$ which relates layer amplitudes within the leads. This gives a compact way to propagate mode amplitudes into and out of the scattering region.
[22]

Formulate open-boundary scattering-region equations by incorporating lead embedding potentials into the finite set of EOM for layers $I=0\\ldots N+1$. For an electron incident from the left lead, write the $I=0$ equation of motion with the left-lead embedding potential explicitly as
$$
\\left(U_0\\bar{P}_{0,0}U_0^{\\dagger}-\\tilde{S}_{0,0}\\right)\\mathbf{C}_0 - S_{0,1}\\mathbf{C}_1
= S_{0,-1}\\left[F_L^{-1}(+)-F_L^{-1}(-)\\right]\\mathbf{C}_0(+),
$$
where $\\tilde{S}_{0,0}=S_{0,0}+S_{0,-1}F_L^{-1}(-)$ and $S_{0,-1}F_L^{-1}(-)$ is the left-lead embedding potential; similarly, for the right lead $\\tilde{S}_{N+1,N+1}=S_{N+1,N+1}+S_{N+1,N+2}F_R(+)$ provides the right-lead embedding potential $S_{N+1,N+2}F_R(+)$. These embedding potentials reduce the infinite-lead problem to a finite linear system for the scattering-region amplitudes $\\{\\mathbf{C}_I\\}$ and yield the complete, normalized scattering-state wave function in the TB-LMTO amplitudes $\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}$ upon back-transformation.
Fig. 1

Obtain the full scattering-state wave function of the device by solving the finite linear system formed in the previous step for each incident lead mode labelled by spin and lateral $\\mathbf{k}_{\\parallel}$; the solved layer amplitude vectors $\\mathbf{C}_I(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})$ are converted to TB-LMTO amplitudes $\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})$ via the inverse relation $\\mathbf{C}_{\\mathbf{R}L}=U_{\\mathbf{R}}\\left(\\overline{\\Delta}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\alpha}\\right)^{\\frac{1}{2}}U_{\\mathbf{R}}^{\\dagger}\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}$, yielding a site- and orbital-resolved, properly normalized scattering wave function for use in transport and torque calculations. This completes the wave-function matching (WFM) construction for noncollinear layered systems.
[17]

Define the spin-current operator between sites $\\mathbf{R}$ and $\\mathbf{R}'$ for a given lateral $\\mathbf{k}_{\\parallel}$ as the projection of the tensor operator $\\hat{\\mathcal{J}}=\\frac{1}{2}[\\hat{\\sigma}\\otimes\\hat{\\mathbf{V}}+\\hat{\\mathbf{V}}\\otimes\\hat{\\sigma}]$ (where $\\hat{\\sigma}$ is the $2\\times2$ Pauli spin matrix and $\\hat{\\mathbf{V}}$ is the velocity operator) along the direction $\\mathbf{x}_{\\mathbf{R},\\mathbf{R}'}$; the explicit tight-binding matrix form used in expectation values for a specific state $|\\Psi\\rangle$ is
$$
\\left\\langle\\hat{\\mathcal{J}}_{\\mathbf{R}',\\mathbf{R}}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\right\\rangle
=\\sum_{LL'}\\frac{1}{2i\\hbar}\\left[\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\dagger}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\hat{\\sigma}\\mathbf{H}_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}'L'}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})
+\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}L}^{\\dagger}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\mathbf{H}_{\\mathbf{R}L,\\mathbf{R}'L'}^{\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\hat{\\sigma}\\mathbf{a}_{\\mathbf{R}'L'}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})-h.c.\\right],
$$
which permits evaluation of spin currents from the obtained TB-LMTO amplitudes.

Define the site-resolved spin-transfer torque (STT) at site $\\mathbf{R}$ for an incoming spin channel label $s$ (where $s$ denotes whether the incoming state is parallel or antiparallel to the local spin quantization axis of the injecting lead) and lateral momentum $\\mathbf{k}_{\\parallel}$ as the difference between the sum of incoming spin currents into site $\\mathbf{R}$ from adjacent planes and the sum of outgoing spin currents from site $\\mathbf{R}$ to adjacent planes:
$$
\\left\\langle\\hat{\\mathbf{T}}_{\\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\right\\rangle
=\\sum_{\\mathbf{R}'\\in I-1,I}\\left\\langle\\hat{\\mathcal{J}}_{\\mathbf{R}',\\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\right\\rangle
-\\sum_{\\mathbf{R}'\\in I,I+1}\\left\\langle\\hat{\\mathcal{J}}_{\\mathbf{R},\\mathbf{R}'}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\right\\rangle,
$$
where $I$ is the principal-layer index of site $\\mathbf{R}$. This definition equals (up to a sign) the exchange torque on the injected spin and is the quantity to be averaged over incident channels.
[11]

Express the linear-response, site-resolved STT under a small bias $V_b$ and zero temperature by summing channel contributions over injection spin $s$ and lateral momenta $\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}$ in the 2D Brillouin zone:
$$
\\mathbf{T}_{\\mathbf{R}}=\\left(\\frac{\\hbar}{2}\\right)\\frac{e}{h}\\frac{1}{N_{\\|}}\\sum_{s,\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}}\\left\\langle\\hat{\\mathbf{T}}_{\\mathbf{R}}^{s}(\\mathbf{k}_{\\|})\\right\\rangle V_b,
$$
where $eV_b=\\mu_L-\\mu_R$ is the electrochemical potential difference between the left and right leads, and $N_{\\|}$ is the number of sampled lateral $\\mathbf{k}_{\\|}$ points. This provides the explicit linear-response expression used to compute STT from the scattering wave functions and spin-current operator in the TB-LMTO basis.

Summarize the computational ingredients and implementations: self-consistent potentials for device and leads are generated with the TB-LMTO surface Green's function (TB-LMTO-SGF) method, combined with the coherent potential approximation (CPA) to treat substitutional disorder in layer(s); the rigid-potential rotation $U_{\\mathbf{R}}(\\theta_{\\mathbf{R}},\\varphi_{\\mathbf{R}})$ implements noncollinear magnetization; Bloch eigenmodes and Bloch-factor matrices $F(\\pm)$ provide embedding potentials such as $S_{0,-1}F_L^{-1}(-)$ used in the finite scattering-region EOM; solving these EOM yields the full normalized scattering wave function used to compute transmission, reflection, particle currents, spin currents and site-resolved STT all in the same TB-LMTO basis.
[19]
[17]

motivating_questions.content: In modeling current-induced torques in layered magnetic devices, practitioners needed a calculation that sits on the same ab initio electronic-structure footing used to obtain self-consistent atomic potentials, yet produces explicit scattering wave functions (not just transmission probabilities) so that local spin currents and torques can be evaluated site-by-site. Prior approaches either mixed quantum interface scattering with semiclassical bulk treatments, used empirical tight-binding parameters, or employed NEGF in localized-orbital bases without presenting the full scattering wave function in the TB-LMTO representation tied to first-principles potentials; none combined (i) self-consistent TB-LMTO potentials (with CPA for disorder) with (ii) a wave-function–matching solution of the open-boundary scattering problem that yields layer-resolved, basis-consistent spin-current operators. Without this, it was not possible to compute ab initio spatial profiles of STT, separate propagating and evanescent contributions locally, or treat substitutional interfacial disorder on the same footing as the underlying electronic structure.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: The qualitative switching behavior does not require an exact microscopic lead lattice model: although the presented calculations used armchair leads attached to zigzag edges with an odd number of transverse atoms, qualitatively similar cross-conductance patterns are reproducible using square-lattice leads provided the local potential in the leads is chosen appropriately to model contacts. At the same time, finite-size symmetry (for example, odd versus even number of atoms across a lead) and the specific choice of zigzag-contact geometry materially affect quantitative results in the small computational domains studied, indicating that the contact-edge termination and transverse atom-count can be important design parameters.

steps.reasoning: State the computational-lead modeling choices and a symmetry detail used in the primary calculations: the authors used armchair leads attached to zigzag edges with an odd number of transverse atoms (i.e., the number of atoms across each lead in the transverse direction is odd), and the computational domains are relatively small so finite-size symmetry effects are noticeable.

Report the claim about qualitative robustness to lead model: the authors assert that the qualitative switching behaviour (the gate-controlled rerouting of current among terminals) does not require an exact microscopic lead lattice model; specifically, qualitatively similar cross-conductance patterns are reproducible using square-lattice leads provided that the local potential in the square-lattice leads is chosen appropriately to model the contacts, meaning that the phenomenon is not an artifact of the specific armchair-lead microscopic model.
[17]

Report the authors' observation about the quantitative sensitivity to finite-size symmetry and zigzag-contact details: due to the small size of the computational domain, finite-size symmetry (for example, whether the transverse atom count across a lead is odd versus even) and the specific choice of zigzag-contact geometry materially affect quantitative results (e.g., exact cross-conductance magnitudes), indicating that contact-edge termination and transverse atom-count can be important design parameters in small devices.

Synthesize these statements into the conclusion that while qualitative switching behaviour is robust to the precise microscopic lead lattice model (so long as leads model contacts appropriately), quantitative results in the small computational domains studied depend on finite-size symmetry such as odd versus even transverse atom counts and the zigzag-contact geometry; therefore the lead modelling choice is not critical for the qualitative effect but can be important for quantitative design.

motivating_questions.content: Numerical studies commonly model leads and contacts with simplified boundary conditions; designers need to know whether predicted routing and switching phenomena are artifacts of a particular contact model or robust features of graphene devices. Prior to this work it was unclear whether the switching effects required finely tuned lead lattice matching or were generic. Lacking this knowledge, predictions could not reliably inform contact engineering in experimental realizations.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
The scattering problem for a multi-terminal tight-binding spin-orbit coupled device is cast as a coupled linear system for the device internal wave-function vector $\psi_{s}$ (length $2N$, spin-resolved amplitudes on $N$ lattice sites) and the lead outgoing-amplitude vector $\phi$ (length $2M$, all transverse modes on all leads), in the pair of matrix equations
$$
\mathbf{A}\,\psi_{s}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\,\phi,\qquad
\mathbf{C}\,\phi=\mathbf{d}+\mathbf{D}\,\psi_{s},
$$
where $\mathbf{A}=E-H_{sys}$, $\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D}$ encode hopping between device and leads and intra-lead propagation, and $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{d}$ encode the chosen incident mode. Eliminating $\phi$ yields the closed-form device solution
$$
\psi_{s}=G^{R}\,\mathbf{g},\qquad G^{R}=(\mathbf{A}-\Sigma^{R})^{-1},\quad \mathbf{g}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d},
$$
with the lead self-energy matrix $\Sigma^{R}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{D}$. The scattering amplitudes are given explicitly by
$$
\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}
=-\delta_{p p'}\delta_{m m'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}
+t_{p'}^{-1}t_{p' s}\sum_{y_p,y_{p'}}\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_{p'})\,G^{R}(n_{y_{p'}}\sigma',n_{y_p}\sigma)\,[2 i t_{p s}\sin(k_m^{p})\chi_{m}^{p}(y_p)],
$$
where $t_{ps}$ is device–lead hopping, $\chi_m^{p}(y)$ are transverse lead modes, and $k_m^{p}$ the longitudinal wavevectors. This formulation gives an explicit, single-particle prescription to compute any local observable (via ensemble averaging of these scattering wave functions) in a multi-terminal LB geometry.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Explicit linear scattering-wave formulation and closed-form solution for multi-terminal tight-binding SO systems

conclusion.content:
The scattering problem for a multi-terminal tight-binding spin-orbit coupled device is cast as a coupled linear system for the device internal wave-function vector $\psi_{s}$ (length $2N$, spin-resolved amplitudes on $N$ lattice sites) and the lead outgoing-amplitude vector $\phi$ (length $2M$, all transverse modes on all leads), in the pair of matrix equations
      $$
      \mathbf{A}\,\psi_{s}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\,\phi,\qquad
      \mathbf{C}\,\phi=\mathbf{d}+\mathbf{D}\,\psi_{s},
      $$
      where $\mathbf{A}=E-H_{sys}$ (with $H_{sys}$ the tight-binding Hamiltonian of the spin-orbit coupled device on the $N$-site lattice), $\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D}$ encode hopping between device and leads and intra-lead propagation, and $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{d}$ encode the chosen incident mode. Eliminating $\phi$ yields the closed-form device solution
      $$
      \psi_{s}=G^{R}\,\mathbf{g},\qquad G^{R}=(\mathbf{A}-\Sigma^{R})^{-1},\quad \mathbf{g}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d},
      $$
      with the lead self-energy matrix $\Sigma^{R}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{D}$. The scattering amplitudes are given explicitly by
      $$
      \phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}
      =-\delta_{p p'}\delta_{m m'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}
      +t_{p'}^{-1}t_{p' s}\sum_{y_p,y_{p'}}\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_{p'})\,G^{R}(n_{y_{p'}}\sigma',n_{y_p}\sigma)\,[2 i t_{p s}\sin(k_m^{p})\chi_{m}^{p}(y_p)],
      $$
      where $t_{ps}$ is the hopping amplitude between lead $p$ and the device, $t_{p}$ is the nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude within lead $p$, $\chi_m^{p}(y)$ are the transverse mode wavefunctions of lead $p$, $k_m^{p}$ are the longitudinal wavevectors (real for propagating modes, complex for evanescent modes), and $n_{y_p}$ denotes the device boundary site adjacent to lead $p$ at transverse position $y$. This formulation gives an explicit, single-particle prescription to compute any local observable (via ensemble averaging of these scattering wave functions) in a multi-terminal Landauer-Büttiker geometry.

steps.reasoning:
Define the total tight-binding Hamiltonian of the coupled lead+device system as $\mathcal{H}=H_{leads}+H_{sys}+H_{int}$, where $H_{leads}$ is the tight-binding Hamiltonian of the half-infinite ideal leads, $H_{sys}$ is the device (spin-orbit, SO) system Hamiltonian, and $H_{int}$ describes the nearest-neighbor hopping coupling between each lead and the device; the tunable lead–device hopping parameter is denoted $t_{ps}$ with lead index $p$ and device boundary site index labels as defined below.
[1]

Model each lead $p$ in a discrete nearest-neighbor representation with longitudinal coordinate $x_p=1,\ldots,\infty$ and transverse coordinate $y_p=1,\ldots,N_p$; denote the device lattice site coordinates as $(x_s,y_s)$ and denote the device boundary site adjacent to lead $p$ first-row site $(1,y_p)$ by $n_{p y_p}$.
Fig. 1

Introduce an incident scattering channel in lead $p$ specified by transverse mode index $m$ and spin index $\sigma$, whose incident wave in lead $p$ is $e^{-i k_m^p x_p}\,\chi_{m\sigma}^p(y_p)$, where $k_m^p$ is the longitudinal wavevector of mode $m$ in lead $p$ (determined below) and $\chi_m^p(y)$ is the transverse-mode wavefunction of mode $m$ in lead $p$; adopt $z$ as the spin-quantization axis so spin index values are $\uparrow,\downarrow$.

Write the general form of the full scattering eigenstate in an arbitrary lead $p'$ as the sum of the incident wave (present only when $p'=p$ and spin matches) plus outgoing scattered waves:
$ \psi_{\sigma' l}^{p m \sigma}(x_{p'},y_{p'})=\delta_{p p'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'} e^{-i k_m^p x_p}\chi_{m\sigma}^p(y_p)+\sum_{m'\in p'}\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}\,e^{i k_{m'}^{p'} x_{p'}}\chi_{m' \sigma'}^{p'}(y_{p'})$,
where $\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}$ are the unknown outgoing scattering amplitudes for conversion of incoming channel $(p,m,\sigma)$ to outgoing channel $(p',m',\sigma')$, and the longitudinal wavevectors $k_{m'}^{p'}$ are determined below.

Define the longitudinal wavevectors $k_{m'}^{p'}$ of transverse mode $m'$ in lead $p'$ from the tight-binding lead dispersion: for mode on-site transverse energy $\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}$ and lead hopping $t_{p'}$, set
$k_{m'}^{p'}=\cos^{-1}\!\big(\frac{E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}}{-2t_{p'}}\big)$ when $|E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}|\le 2t_{p'}$ (propagating mode), and the analytic continuations
$k_{m'}^{p'}=i\cosh^{-1}\!\big(\frac{E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}}{2t_{p'}}\big)+\pi$ for $E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}>2t_{p'}$ and
$k_{m'}^{p'}=i\cosh^{-1}\!\big(\frac{E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}}{-2t_{p'}}\big)$ for $E-\varepsilon_{m'}^{p'}<-2t_{p'}$ (evanescent modes).

Collect the unknown device internal wave-function amplitudes into a column vector $\psi_s$ of length $2N$ (where $N$ is the number of device lattice sites and the factor $2$ accounts for two spin components per site), so that $\psi_s$ lists $\psi_{\sigma'}^{p m \sigma}(x_s,y_s)$ for all device sites and spins for the given incident channel; collect all outgoing-mode amplitudes $\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}$ into a column vector $\phi$ of length $2M$ (where $M=\sum_p N_p$ is total number of transverse sites on all leads).

Impose the discrete Schrödinger equation on every device site and on the first-row sites of each lead (those coupled to the device). For device internal sites the equation is $E\psi_{\sigma'}^{pm\sigma}(y_s')=\sum_{y_s''\sigma''}H_{sys}(y_s'\sigma',y_s''\sigma'')\psi_{\sigma''}^{pm\sigma}(y_s'')-\sum_{p',y} t_{p' s}\delta_{y_s',n_{p'y}}\psi_{\sigma'}^{pm\sigma}(1,y_{p'})$, and for first-row lead sites $E\psi_{\sigma'}^{pm\sigma}(1,y_{p'}')=\sum_{y''}H_{leads}(1,y_{p'}';1,y_{p'}')\psi_{\sigma'}^{pm\sigma}(1,y_{p'}')-\sum_{y_s} t_{p' s}\delta_{y_s,n_{p'y'}'}\psi_{\sigma'}^{pm\sigma}(y_s)$, where $H_{sys}$ and $H_{leads}$ are the tight-binding device and lead Hamiltonian matrix elements and $t_{p's}$ couples first-row lead sites to adjacent device boundary sites.

Substitute the lead wavefunction expansion from the outgoing/incident-mode representation into the first-row lead-site Schrödinger equations and, after collecting terms and rearranging, obtain a coupled linear matrix system for the unknown vectors $\psi_s$ and $\phi$ of the form
$\mathbf{A}\,\psi_s=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\,\phi$ and $\mathbf{C}\,\phi=\mathbf{d}+\mathbf{D}\,\psi_s$,
where $\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D}$ are matrices of dimensions $2N\times 2N$, $2N\times 2M$, $2M\times 2M$, $2M\times 2N$ respectively, determined by $H_{sys}$, $H_{leads}$ and the interfacial hoppings; $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{d}$ are source vectors determined by the chosen incident mode.

Write the explicit matrix-element expressions: $\mathbf{A}=E-H_{sys}$; for device boundary site index $n_{p'' y}$ and a lead mode labeled by $(p',m',\sigma')$,
$\mathbf{B}(n_{p'' y}\sigma'',p' m' \sigma')=-\delta_{p'',p'}\delta_{\sigma'',\sigma'}\,t_{p' s}\,\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_{p''})\,e^{i k_{m'}^{p'}}$,
$\mathbf{D}(p' m' \sigma', n_{p'' y}\sigma'')=-\delta_{p'',p'}\delta_{\sigma'',\sigma'}\,t_{p' s}\,\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_{p''})$,
$\mathbf{C}(p' m' \sigma', p'' m'' \sigma'')=-\delta_{p'',p'}\delta_{\sigma'',\sigma'}\delta_{m'' m'}\,t_{p'}$,
$\mathbf{b}(n_{p' y}\sigma')=-\delta_{p p'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}\,t_{p s}\,\chi_m^p(y_{p'})\,e^{-i k_m^p}$,
$\mathbf{d}(p' m' \sigma')=\delta_{p p'}\delta_{m m'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}\,t_p$,
and all other elements are zero; here $t_p$ is the nearest-neighbor lead hopping for lead $p$ and $\chi_m^p(y)$ are transverse-mode amplitudes.

Note that the matrix $\mathbf{C}$ is diagonal in the lead-mode basis and therefore invertible; define the retarded lead self-energy matrix acting on the device boundary sites as $\Sigma^{R}\equiv\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{D}$, whose nonzero elements on device boundary sites $n_{y_1 p'}$ and $n_{y_2 p'}$ are
$\Sigma^{R}(n_{y_1 p'},\sigma';n_{y_2 p'},\sigma')=-\sum_{m'}\frac{t_{p' s}^{2}}{t_{p'}}\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_1)\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_2)\,e^{i k_{m'}^{p'}}$,
and all other elements are zero.

Eliminate $\phi$ using $\phi=\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d}+\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{D}\psi_s$ (from the second matrix equation) to obtain the closed-form device solution by substituting into the first equation and solving for $\psi_s$:
$\psi_s=(\mathbf{A}-\Sigma^{R})^{-1}(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d})\equiv G^{R}\,\mathbf{g}$,
where the device retarded Green's function is $G^{R}=(\mathbf{A}-\Sigma^{R})^{-1}$, and the effective incident boundary vector is $\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d}$.

Compute the nonzero elements of the effective incident vector $\mathbf{g}$ explicitly; for a boundary site $n_{y_{p'}}$ adjacent to lead $p'$,
$\mathbf{g}(n_{y_{p'}}\sigma')=2 i\,\delta_{p p'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}\,t_{p s}\,\sin\!\left(k_m^{p}\right)\,\chi_m^p(y)$,
which arises from combining the incident-wave source $\mathbf{b}$ and lead-propagation contribution $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d}$.

Obtain the explicit scattering amplitudes by expanding $\phi=\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{d}+\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{D}G^{R}\mathbf{g}$ to yield, for outgoing channel $(p',m',\sigma')$ from incoming $(p,m,\sigma)$,
$\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}=-\delta_{p p'}\delta_{m m'}\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}+t_{p'}^{-1}t_{p' s}\sum_{y_p,y_{p'}}\chi_{m'}^{p'}(y_{p'})\,G^{R}(n_{y_{p'}}\sigma',n_{y_p}\sigma)\,[2 i t_{p s}\sin(k_m^{p})\chi_{m}^{p}(y_p)]$,
with symbol meanings as above; this expression is the closed-form single-particle scattering amplitude in the multi-terminal tight-binding SO system.

Conclude that given the explicit scattering-wave device solution $\psi_s=G^{R}\mathbf{g}$ and scattering amplitudes $\phi_{p' m' \sigma'}^{p m \sigma}$, any local single-particle observable (an operator expressed in the device site/spin basis) can be computed in the Landauer–Büttiker ensemble-averaging spirit by summing contributions from all incident channels with their respective mode densities and velocities, thus providing a concrete prescription to compute local observables in a multi-terminal LB geometry.
[1]

motivating_questions.content: In studies of phase-coherent transport through spin-orbit coupled mesoscopic devices, practitioners needed an explicit, computationally practical representation of the single-particle scattering wave function in the device region in order to obtain local observables (e.g., site-resolved spin density, local link currents) and to relate them to incident modes on the leads. Previously, the field relied chiefly on scattering matrices or Green's-function formulas that yield terminal conductances but do not provide the device wave function explicitly, and on Landauer–Keldysh approaches that are not manifestly single-particle and are less transparent. This gap prevented clear, direct calculations of local, non-equilibrium quantities in the LB single-particle framework and obscured the role of boundary couplings and evanescent contributions. The explicit linear-algebraic formulation above addresses this deficit by providing device-size linear equations, a closed-form retarded Green's function $G^{R}$ including lead self-energy, and an explicit formula for the scattering amplitudes, thereby enabling direct computation of spatially resolved observables and facilitating rigorous manipulations needed for later analytical proofs.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A computational workflow was implemented that combines: (i) a tight-binding central device Hamiltonian H_D=E_0\sum_i c_i^\dagger c_i - t\sum_{<i,j>} c_i^\dagger c_j + \hat{H}_R with the Rashba term \hat{H}_R = i t_R \sum_{<i,j>} c_i^\dagger ( \mathbf{s}\times\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij} )\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{z}}\, c_j + h.c., (ii) calculation of semi‑infinite graphene lead surface Green's functions via the Lopez‑Sancho iterative scheme producing lead self‑energies \Sigma_i^R = V_{DL}^i g_L^i V_{LD}^i, (iii) nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) evaluation of device Green's functions G^{R/A}=(E-H_D-\sum_i\Sigma_i^{R/A}-\Sigma_{im}^{R/A}-\Sigma_{vib}^{R/A})^{-1} and G^{\lessgtr}=G^{R}[\sum_i\Sigma_i^{\lessgtr}+\Sigma_{im}^{\lessgtr}+\Sigma_{vib}^{\lessgtr}]G^{A}, and (iv) diagrammatic self‑consistent Born approximation (SCBA) for disorder and electron‑vibron scattering giving self‑energies \Sigma_{im}(x,y,t,t')=\gamma(x-y)G(x-y,t,t')\delta(t-t') for impurities and Hartree/Fock SCBA expressions for vibrons, e.g. \Sigma_{SCBA}^{F,r}(\omega)=i\hbar\sum_\lambda\int\frac{d\omega'}{2\pi} M^\lambda [D_0^{r}(\lambda,\omega-\omega')G^{<}(\omega')+... ] M^\lambda. The Meir–Wingreen current formula J_i=\frac{1}{\hbar}\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\mathrm{Tr}[\Sigma_i^{<}G^{>}-\Sigma_i^{>}G^{<}] was used to obtain non‑equilibrium currents. This integrated scheme was applied to a finite graphene ring central device (114 carbon atoms) coupled to semi‑infinite armchair graphene nanoribbon leads.

conclusion.content: The computational workflow for a graphene nanoring device of 114 carbon atoms connected to semi-infinite armchair graphene nanoribbon leads combines: (i) a tight-binding central device Hamiltonian with on-site energy \(E_0\): \(H_D = E_0 \sum_i c_i^\dagger c_i - t \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} c_i^\dagger c_j + \hat{H}_R\), where \(t \approx 2.7 \text{ eV}\) is the nearest-neighbor hopping and the Rashba term is \(\hat{H}_R = i t_R \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} c_i^\dagger (\mathbf{s} \times \hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij})\cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}\, c_j + \text{h.c.}\) with \(t_R\) the Rashba coupling strength, \(\mathbf{s}\) the vector of Pauli matrices, \(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij}\) the unit vector from site \(i\) to \(j\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) the unit vector perpendicular to the graphene plane; (ii) surface Green's functions of the semi-infinite leads computed by the Lopez-Sancho iterative scheme, yielding lead self-energies \(\Sigma_i^R = V_{DL}^i g_L^i V_{LD}^i\), where \(g_L^i = (E + i\eta - H_L^i)^{-1}\) is the Green's function of the isolated lead, \(V_{LD}^i\) (\(V_{DL}^i\)) is the hopping from lead to device (device to lead); (iii) nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) evaluation of the device retarded/advanced Green's functions \(G^{R/A} = (E - H_D - \sum_i \Sigma_i^{R/A} - \Sigma_{im}^{R/A} - \Sigma_{vib}^{R/A})^{-1}\) and the lesser/greater Green's functions \(G^{\lessgtr} = G^R [\sum_i \Sigma_i^{\lessgtr} + \Sigma_{im}^{\lessgtr} + \Sigma_{vib}^{\lessgtr}] G^A\); (iv) diagrammatic self-consistent Born approximation (SCBA) for disorder and electron-vibron scattering, where the impurity self-energy is \(\Sigma_{im}(x,y,t,t') = \gamma(x-y) G(x-y,t,t') \delta(t-t')\) with \(\gamma(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}) = V_{im}^2 e^{-\alpha(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^2}\) (impurity correlation kernel) and the vibron self-energies include the Hartree term \(\Sigma_{SCBA}^{H,r}(\sigma) = i\hbar \sum_\lambda \sum_{\sigma'} \frac{2}{\Omega_\lambda} \int \frac{d\omega'}{2\pi} M^\lambda \operatorname{Tr}[G^<(\sigma',\omega') M^\lambda]\) and the Fock term \(\Sigma_{SCBA}^{F,r}(\sigma,\omega) = i\hbar \sum_\lambda \int \frac{d\omega'}{2\pi} M^\lambda [D_0^r(\lambda,\omega-\omega') G^<(\sigma,\omega') + D_0^r(\lambda,\omega-\omega') G^r(\sigma,\omega') + D_0^<(\lambda,\omega-\omega') G^r(\sigma,\omega')] M^\lambda\), with \(D_0^r\) and \(D_0^<\) the retarded and lesser vibronic Green's functions, \(M^\lambda\) the electron-vibron coupling matrix, and \(\lambda\) the vibron mode index. The Meir-Wingreen current formula \(J_i = \frac{1}{\hbar} \int \frac{d\omega}{2\pi} \operatorname{Tr}[\Sigma_i^<(\omega) G^>(\omega) - \Sigma_i^>(\omega) G^<(\omega)]\) is used to obtain the non-equilibrium current in the left or right lead \(i\).

steps.reasoning:
State the overall modeling goal: construct a computational workflow to compute non-equilibrium transport through a finite graphene nano-ring central device coupled to semi-infinite graphene leads, including spin-orbit (Rashba) coupling, impurity scattering and electron-vibron interactions, and to obtain non-equilibrium currents; specify that the central device studied numerically is a ring of 114 carbon atoms connected to semi-infinite armchair graphene nanoribbon leads (device geometry and size used as the concrete application of the workflow).
Fig. 1

Define the single-particle tight-binding Hamiltonian of the central device $H_D$ used as the starting microscopic model: $H_D = E_0\sum_i c_i^\dagger c_i - t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} c_i^\dagger c_j + \hat{H}_R$, where $E_0$ is an on-site energy, $c_i^\dagger$ ($c_i$) creates (annihilates) an electron at site $i$, $t$ is the nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude (numerical value used as energy unit $t\approx 2.7\ \mathrm{eV}$ in calculations), and $\hat{H}_R$ is the Rashba spin-orbit interaction term.

Define the Rashba spin-orbit interaction term $\hat{H}_R$ used in the device Hamiltonian: $\hat{H}_R = i\,t_R \sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} c_i^\dagger \bigl(\mathbf{s}\times\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij}\bigr)\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{z}}\, c_j + \mathrm{h.c.}$, where $t_R$ is the Rashba coupling strength, $\mathbf{s}$ is the vector of Pauli matrices (spin operators), $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij}$ is the unit vector from site $j$ to site $i$, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to the graphene plane.

Specify the partitioning of the full system Hamiltonian into device, leads and perturbations: $\hat{H}=\hat{H}_D+\hat{H}_L+\hat{H}_P$, where $\hat{H}_L$ is the Hamiltonian of the leads and $\hat{H}_P$ denotes perturbative interactions (impurities and electron-vibron couplings) to be treated within diagrammatic perturbation theory.

State the approach to include semi-infinite leads: represent each semi-infinite lead by its surface Green's function $g_L^i$ and lead self-energy $\Sigma_i^R = V_{DL}^i\, g_L^i\, V_{LD}^i$, where $V_{LD}^i$ ($V_{DL}^i$) is the hopping from lead $i$ to device (device to lead $i$) and $g_L^i = (E + i\eta - H_L^i)^{-1}$ is the retarded Green's function of the isolated semi-infinite lead; use the Lopez-Sancho iterative scheme to compute $g_L^i$ (the surface Green's function of semi-infinite armchair graphene leads) numerically and thereby obtain $\Sigma_i^R$.
[33]

Introduce the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) basic relations used to compute device Green's functions in the presence of coupling to leads and interactions: define retarded and advanced device Green's functions $G^{R/A}(\omega) = \bigl(\omega - H_D - \sum_i \Sigma_i^{R/A}(\omega) - \Sigma_{im}^{R/A}(\omega) - \Sigma_{vib}^{R/A}(\omega)\bigr)^{-1}$, where $\Sigma_i^{R/A}$ are lead self-energies, $\Sigma_{im}^{R/A}$ are impurity self-energies, and $\Sigma_{vib}^{R/A}$ are vibron (electron-phonon) self-energies; define lesser/greater Green's functions via $G^{\lessgtr}(\omega)=G^{R}(\omega)\bigl[\sum_i\Sigma_i^{\lessgtr}(\omega)+\Sigma_{im}^{\lessgtr}(\omega)+\Sigma_{vib}^{\lessgtr}(\omega)\bigr]G^{A}(\omega)$.
[31]

Record the expressions used for noninteracting lead lesser/greater self-energies which enter the NEGF: $\Sigma_{i}^{<}(\omega)=i\,n_{F}\bigl(\omega-\mu_{i}\bigr)\,\Gamma_{i}(\omega)$ and $\Sigma_{i}^{>}(\omega)=i\{n_{F}(\omega-\mu_{i})-1\}\,\Gamma_{i}(\omega)$, where $n_F$ is the Fermi distribution, $\mu_i$ is the electrochemical potential of lead $i$, and the lead-device broadening is $\Gamma_i(\omega) = i\bigl[\Sigma_i(\omega)-\Sigma_i^\dagger(\omega)\bigr]$.

Specify the perturbative treatments of scattering used in the workflow: employ the diagrammatic self-consistent Born approximation (SCBA) to obtain impurity and electron-vibron self-energies as functionals of the interacting Green's functions, using self-consistent Dyson-equation loops where the interacting Green's function $G$ determines the SCBA self-energies and the self-energies determine $G$ in turn.
[49]

Provide the impurity model and its SCBA self-energy used in the workflow: model the impurity potential as a short-range, randomly distributed, lowly correlated scattering potential with zero mean and correlation $ \langle V(\mathbf{x},t)V(\mathbf{y},t')\rangle = \gamma(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\delta(t-t') $ where $\gamma(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}) = V_{im}^2 e^{-\alpha(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^2}$, with $V_{im}$ the impurity strength and $\alpha$ controlling correlation length; the SCBA impurity self-energy is $\Sigma_{im}(x,y,t,t') = \gamma(x-y)\,G(x-y,t,t')\,\delta(t-t')$, which yields a self-consistent relation since $G$ depends on $\Sigma_{im}$.
[31]

Provide the electron-vibron (electron-phonon) model and SCBA expressions used in the workflow: define vibron Hamiltonian $H_{vib}=\sum_\lambda \hbar\omega_\lambda a_\lambda^\dagger a_\lambda$, electron-vibron coupling $H_{e-vib}=\sum_{\alpha\beta}\sum_\lambda M_{\alpha\beta}^\lambda (a_\lambda + a_\lambda^\dagger)d_\alpha^\dagger d_\beta$ with real-space coupling matrices $M^{(\lambda)}$ (nearest-neighbor structure representing hopping modulation by vibrations); give the vibron equilibrium retarded Green's function $D_0^R(\lambda,\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega-\omega_\lambda+i0^+}-\frac{1}{\omega+\omega_\lambda+i0^+}$ and lesser $D_0^<(\lambda,\omega)=-2\pi i\bigl[(N_\lambda+1)\delta(\omega+\omega_\lambda)+N_\lambda\delta(\omega-\omega_\lambda)\bigr]$ (with $N_\lambda$ the vibron occupation); give SCBA Hartree and Fock self-energy formulas: Hartree retarded $\Sigma_{SCBA}^{H,r}(\sigma)=i\hbar\sum_\lambda\sum_{\sigma'}\frac{2}{\Omega_\lambda}\int\frac{d\omega'}{2\pi} M^\lambda\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[G^<(\sigma',\omega')M^\lambda\bigr]$ (Hartree lesser/greater vanish), and Fock retarded/lesser expressions $\Sigma_{SCBA}^{F,r}$ and $\Sigma_{SCBA}^{F,\lessgtr}$ given as frequency integrals that couple $D_0^{r/<}$ and $G^{r/<}$ (explicit integral formulas are used in the numerical SCBA loops); finally the SCBA dressed Green's functions are obtained via $G_{SCBA}^{r(a)}(\sigma,\omega) = \bigl[\,(G_0^{r(a)}(\sigma,\omega))^{-1}-\Sigma_{SCBA}^{r(a)}(\sigma,\omega)\,\bigr]^{-1}$ and $G_{SCBA}^{\lessgtr}=G_{SCBA}^r\,\Sigma_{SCBA}^{\lessgtr}\,G_{SCBA}^a$.
[51]
[52]

State the formula used to obtain non-equilibrium currents from the computed Green's functions and self-energies: use the Meir–Wingreen current expression $J_i = \frac{1}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\Sigma_i^{<}(\omega)G^{>}(\omega)-\Sigma_i^{>}(\omega)G^{<}(\omega)\bigr]$, where $\Sigma_i^{\lessgtr}$ are the lead lesser/greater self-energies and $G^{\lessgtr}$ are the device lesser/greater Green's functions including SCBA self-energies.
[55]

Summarize the numerical implementation choices that instantiate the workflow: adopt the tight-binding device Hamiltonian with Rashba term as above, compute semi-infinite armchair lead surface Green's functions via the Lopez-Sancho iterative scheme to obtain $\Sigma_i^R$, solve the Dyson/Keldysh NEGF equations self-consistently with SCBA impurity and vibron self-energies to obtain $G^{R/A/\lessgtr}$, and evaluate current via the Meir–Wingreen integral; apply this pipeline to the concrete device geometry of a 114-atom graphene nano-ring connected to semi-infinite armchair leads and present results (conductance maps and I–V curves).

motivating_questions.content: Transport predictions for mesoscopic Rashba‑coupled graphene rings require three technical capabilities that were not simultaneously present in prior studies: a microscopic tight‑binding Rashba Hamiltonian on the finite ring, an accurate real‑space treatment of semi‑infinite graphene leads (to obtain correct lead self‑energies and broadenings for armchair contacts), and a controlled diagrammatic treatment of elastic (impurity) and inelastic (electron‑vibron) scattering in the nonequilibrium steady state. Earlier calculations either used simplified lead models, phenomenological dephasing, or elastic‑only scattering approximations; thus they could not self‑consistently compute how impurity and vibron self‑energies modify G^{R/A} and G^{\lessgtr} and consequently the bias‑dependent current. To make quantitative statements about AC oscillations in experimentally relevant device geometries (finite ring connected to semi‑infinite leads) one needs an approach that (a) yields surface Green's functions of the leads without explicit diagonalization of the infinite lead, (b) embeds SCBA self‑energies for both impurities and vibrons into NEGF, and (c) evaluates the Meir–Wingreen current using those self‑consistent Green's functions. The implemented workflow directly addresses this methodological gap.

A computational quantum transport framework was implemented to simulate graphene $p$-$n$ junction TMF devices: the device Hamiltonian is the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model
$$
\hat{H}=\sum_{i}^{N}\epsilon_i\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_i+\sum_{i,j}^{N}t_{i,j}\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_j,
$$
with the magnetic field included via the Peierls substitution $t_{i,j}=t_s\exp\!\left[i\frac{e}{\hbar}\int_{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\mathbf{r}_j}\mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{r}\right]$, combined with Landauer-Büttiker multiterminal transport
$$
I_p=\frac{2e^2}{h}\sum_q\left[T_{qp}V_p-T_{pq}V_q\right],
$$
transmission function
$$
T_{qp}(E)=\sum_{n\in p,m\in q}|S_{nm}(E)|^2,
$$
and a local particle current density operator
$$
J_{\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_j}(E)=-2\sum_{n\in p}\mathrm{Im}\!\left[\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)^\dagger\hat{H}_{i,j}\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_j,E)\right].
$$
The implementation (in KWANT) includes linearly varying on-site energies across a junction width $D_W$, scaled lattice parameters for computational efficiency, and two large floating/dephasing edge contacts that absorb and re-inject carriers with randomized phase while drawing no net current. This framework computes mode-resolved scattering states and all inter-lead transmission coefficients for six-terminal Hall-bar geometries and yields spatially resolved current density and nonlocal resistance $R_{15,24}=(V_2-V_4)/(I_1-I_5)$ without empirical fitting parameters.

conclusion.content:
A computational quantum transport framework is implemented to simulate graphene \(p\)-\(n\) junction transverse magnetic focusing (TMF) devices. The device Hamiltonian is the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model on a graphene lattice:
      $$
      \hat{H}=\sum_{i}^{N}\epsilon_i\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_i+\sum_{i,j}^{N}t_{i,j}\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_j,
      $$
      where \(N\) is the number of lattice sites, \(\epsilon_i\) is the on-site energy at site \(i\), \(\hat{c}_i^\dagger\) and \(\hat{c}_i\) are fermionic creation and annihilation operators, the second sum runs over first-nearest neighbor pairs, and \(t_{i,j}\) is the hopping energy between sites \(i\) and \(j\). The magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) is included via the Peierls substitution: \(t_{i,j}=t_s\exp\!\left[i\frac{e}{\hbar}\int_{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\mathbf{r}_j}\mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{r}\right]\), where \(t_s\) is the scaled hopping energy, \(e\) is the electron charge, \(\hbar\) is the reduced Planck constant, \(\mathbf{A}\) is the vector potential, and \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is the position of lattice site \(i\). Transport is described by the Landauer-Büttiker multiterminal formula for current \(I_p\) in lead \(p\):
      $$
      I_p=\frac{2e^2}{h}\sum_q\left[T_{qp}V_p-T_{pq}V_q\right],
      $$
      where \(h\) is Planck's constant, \(V_p\) is the voltage in lead \(p\), \(T_{qp}\) is the transmission function from lead \(p\) to lead \(q\). The transmission function at energy \(E\) is
      $$
      T_{qp}(E)=\sum_{n\in p,m\in q}|S_{nm}(E)|^2,
      $$
      with \(S_{nm}\) being the scattering matrix element between mode \(n\) in lead \(p\) and mode \(m\) in lead \(q\). The local particle current density between lattice sites \(\mathbf{r}_i\) and \(\mathbf{r}_j\) at energy \(E\) is
      $$
      J_{\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_j}(E)=-2\sum_{n\in p}\mathrm{Im}\!\left[\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)^\dagger\hat{H}_{i,j}\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_j,E)\right],
      $$
      where \(\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)\) is the wavefunction of the \(n\)th conducting mode in lead \(p\) at site \(\mathbf{r}_i\) and energy \(E\), and \(\hat{H}_{i,j}\) is the Hamiltonian matrix element between sites \(i\) and \(j\). The implementation (in the KWANT package) uses a scaled tight-binding model with lattice constant \(a = s_f a_0\) (scaling factor \(s_f=10\)) and hopping energy \(t_s = t_0/s_f\), where \(a_0\) is the graphene lattice constant and \(t_0 \approx 2.7\) eV is the atomistic hopping energy. It includes linearly varying on-site energies across a junction of width \(D_W\), and two large floating/dephasing edge contacts (labeled contacts 0 and 3) that absorb and re-inject carriers with randomized phase while drawing no net current (their voltages are solved self-consistently). This framework computes mode-resolved scattering states and all inter-lead transmission coefficients for a six-terminal Hall-bar geometry (contacts 0–5) and yields spatially resolved current density and the nonlocal resistance \(R_{15,24}=(V_2-V_4)/(I_1-I_5)\) without empirical fitting parameters.
