steps.reasoning: Adopt a nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian for low-energy electrons in graphene, defined as $\hat{H}=\sum_{i}^{N}\epsilon_i\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_i+\sum_{i,j}^{N}t_{i,j}\hat{c}_i^\dagger\hat{c}_j$, where $N$ is the number of lattice sites, $\hat{c}_i^\dagger$ and $\hat{c}_i$ are Fermionic creation and annihilation operators at site $i$, $\epsilon_i$ is the on-site energy at site $i$, and the second summation is taken only over first-nearest neighbors.

Include a perpendicular magnetic field $B$ via Peierls substitution in the hopping element, $t_{i,j}=t_s\exp\!\left[i\frac{e}{\hbar}\int_{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\mathbf{r}_j}\mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{r}\right]$, where $e$ is the electron charge, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck's constant, $\mathbf{A}$ is the vector potential, and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the position of site $i$; choose a Landau gauge $\mathbf{A}=\langle -By,0\rangle$ inside the channel and a circular gauge in the leads as specified for lead orientations.

Implement lattice scaling to improve computational efficiency by setting the scaled lattice constant $a=s_f a_0$ and the scaled hopping $t_s = t_0/s_f$, where $a_0$ is the physical lattice constant, $t_0\approx 2.7\ \mathrm{eV}$ is the physical nearest-neighbor hopping energy, and the scale factor $s_f=10$ is used to reduce computational cost while preserving low-energy physics.
[36]

Form a six-terminal Hall-bar device geometry with four small leads labeled 1,2,4,5 and two large leads labeled 0 and 3 (the large leads will act as dephasing/edge contacts); set device geometric parameters used in simulations as the inter-contact spacing $D_C$, device width $W$, junction width $D_W$, and contact length $L_C$ with simulated values $D_C=W=200\ \mathrm{nm}$, $D_W=50\ \mathrm{nm}$, and $L_C=60\ \mathrm{nm}$ to match the experimentally relevant geometry for observing the first transverse magnetic focusing (TMF) resonance.
Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b), Fig. 1(c)

Create a $p$-$n$ junction by setting the on-site energy on the left side of the device to $E_1$ and on the right side to $E_2$, and interpolate the on-site energy linearly across the junction over the specified junction width $D_W$; set contact on-site energies equal to the adjacent channel on-site energies so contacts are energetically matched to their connection points.
Fig. 1(c)

Model dephasing edge contacts as large, transparent leads (contacts zero and three) that allow electrons to enter without reflection and that reinject electrons with randomized phase; these contacts draw no net current (their currents are set to zero) and their voltages are treated as floating variables solved self-consistently via the multiterminal Landauer-Büttiker formalism.
[38]

Adopt the zero-bias, zero-temperature approximation appropriate for cryogenic small-bias TMF experiments and employ the Landauer-Büttiker relation for the current in lead $p$, $I_p=\frac{2e^2}{h}\sum_q\left[T_{qp}V_p-T_{pq}V_q\right]$, where $I_p$ is the electrical current in lead $p$, $V_p$ is the electrochemical potential (voltage) of lead $p$, $T_{qp}$ is the transmission from lead $p$ to lead $q$, and the sum runs over all leads including dephasing contacts; solving the resulting linear system for the six leads yields the lead voltages when given the lead currents.
[21]

Define the quantum mechanical transmission function between leads $p$ and $q$ at energy $E$ as $T_{q p}(E)=\sum_{n\in p,m\in q}|S_{nm}(E)|^2$, where $S_{nm}(E)$ is the scattering-matrix element between the $n$th transverse mode in lead $p$ and the $m$th transverse mode in lead $q$, and the summation runs over all propagating transverse modes in the respective leads at energy $E$.

Define the local particle current density between neighboring lattice sites at energy $E$ by $J_{\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_j}(E)=-2\sum_{n\in p}\mathrm{Im}\!\left[\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)^\dagger\hat{H}_{i,j}\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_j,E)\right]$, where $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the position of site $i$, $\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)$ is the wave function amplitude of the $n$th conducting mode (in injecting lead $p$) at site $i$ and energy $E$, $\hat{H}_{i,j}$ is the matrix element of the Hamiltonian between sites $i$ and $j$, and the prefactor $-2$ accounts for spin degeneracy and conversion from wavefunction amplitudes to current density.
[43]

Compute mode-resolved scattering states by solving the scattering problem for each transverse mode separately in the KWANT quantum transport package (thus obtaining $\psi_n(\mathbf{r}_i,E)$ and $S_{nm}(E)$ for each mode), enabling extraction of mode-resolved contributions to both $T_{qp}(E)$ and the local particle current density maps.
[18]

Define the four-terminal nonlocal resistance relevant to the TMF measurement geometry as $R_{15,24}=(V_2-V_4)/(I_1-I_5)$, where contacts one and five form the driven current pair with $I_1=-I_5$ and contacts 0,2,3,4 have zero net current; note algebraic reduction of this quantity to Landauer-Büttiker matrix elements is achieved by solving $\mathbf{I}=\frac{2e^2}{h}\mathbf{T}\mathbf{V}$ and using $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ to write $R_{15,24}=\frac{h}{2e^2}\frac{1}{2}(R_{45}-R_{25})$, where $R_{ij}$ are elements of the inverse transmission matrix $\mathbf{R}$.

Implement all of the above in KWANT for the six-terminal Hall-bar geometry with the specified scaled parameters, junction profile, dephasing edge contacts (floating voltages solved self-consistently), and calculation of mode-resolved scattering states; this computational framework yields inter-lead transmission coefficients $T_{qp}(E)$ for all lead pairs, spatially resolved current-density maps $J_{\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_j}(E)$, and the nonlocal resistance $R_{15,24}$ without empirical fitting parameters.
[18]

motivating_questions.content: In TMF experiments, interpreting multiterminal nonlocal resistance requires a transport model that simultaneously captures quantum interference, angle-dependent tunneling across a smooth $p$-$n$ junction, and the effect of floating contacts that provide dephasing and reinjection. Prior tools either treated transport semiclassically (omitting interference and mode structure) or considered idealized quantum setups without multiterminal Landauer-Büttiker analysis and without explicit dephasing contacts. Consequently, there was no single operational computational scheme that could produce both mode-resolved spatial current densities and the full set of transmission coefficients between all leads needed to compute experimentally measured nonlocal resistances for realistic device geometries and junction smoothness. This gap prevented direct, parameter-free comparison between quantum transport theory and multiterminal TMF measurements.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A device-level quantum-transport modeling framework for monolayer h-BN FET gas sensors is formulated by (i) representing the full device plus semi-infinite leads with the total Hamiltonian $ \mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{R}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{LD}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{DR}} $; (ii) describing the device region by a gas-functionalized tight-binding Hamiltonian $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} = \sum_i \epsilon_i c_i^\dagger c_i + \sum_{i\neq j} t_{ij} c_i^\dagger c_j $, where $ \epsilon_i $ are on-site energies and $ t_{ij} $ are hopping matrix elements; (iii) modeling each unit cell with two h-BN atoms plus one adsorbate giving the $3\times3$ momentum-space Hamiltonian $ h(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{bmatrix} E_0 & t f(\mathbf{k}) & 0 \\ t f^*(\mathbf{k}) & E_1 & t' \\ 0 & t' & E_0' \end{bmatrix} $ with $ f(\mathbf{k}) = 1 + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_1} + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_2} $, $t'$ the boron–adsorbate hopping, and $E_0,E_1,E_0'$ the N, B and adsorbate on-site energies; (iv) computing lead surface Green's functions with the Sancho iterative renormalization scheme and lead self-energies $ \Sigma_{L(R)}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}^\dagger(\mathbf{k}) \, \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) \, \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}(\mathbf{k}) $; and (v) obtaining the device retarded Green's function $ \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = [(\mathcal{E}+i\delta)\hat{I} - \mathcal{H}_D(\mathbf{k}) - \Sigma_L(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) - \Sigma_R(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) ]^{-1} $, Brillouin-zone averaging $ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E}) = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) $, and observable formulas: DOS $ \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) = -\frac{1}{N_c\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathrm{Im}[\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E})] $, carrier concentration $ n = \int \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) f(\mathcal{E}) \, d\mathcal{E} $, quantum capacitance $ C_Q = e^2 \frac{\partial n}{\partial \mathcal{E}} $, transmission $ T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds}) = \mathrm{Tr}[\Gamma_L \mathcal{G} \Gamma_R \mathcal{G}^\dagger] $, and current $ I(V_{ds}) = \frac{2e}{h} \int T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds})[f_L(\mathcal{E})-f_R(\mathcal{E})]\,d\mathcal{E} $. The model uses a single adsorbate per unit cell and employs the empirical distance-scaling relation $ t_{xy} = t\left(\frac{a_0}{d_{xy}}\right) $ to obtain adsorbate-modified hoppings.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Device-level NEGF quantum-transport framework for gas-functionalized h-BN FETs

conclusion.content: A device-level quantum-transport modeling framework for monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) field-effect transistor (FET) gas sensors based on the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism is formulated by (i) representing the full device plus semi-infinite left and right leads with the total Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{R}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{LD}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{DR}}$; (ii) describing the device region by a gas-functionalized tight-binding Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} = \sum_i \epsilon_i c_i^\dagger c_i + \sum_{i\neq j} t_{ij} c_i^\dagger c_j$, where $\epsilon_i$ are on-site energies and $t_{ij}$ are hopping matrix elements; (iii) modeling each unit cell with two h-BN atoms plus one adsorbate giving the $3\times3$ momentum-space Hamiltonian $ h(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{bmatrix} E_0 & t f(\mathbf{k}) & 0 \\ t f^*(\mathbf{k}) & E_1 & t' \\ 0 & t' & E_0' \end{bmatrix} $ with $ f(\mathbf{k}) = 1 + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_1} + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_2} $, $t'$ the boron–adsorbate hopping, and $E_0,E_1,E_0'$ the nitrogen, boron and adsorbate on-site energies; (iv) computing lead surface Green's functions with the Sancho iterative renormalization scheme (a recursive Green's function method based on Dyson's equation for semi-infinite leads) and lead self-energies $ \Sigma_{L(R)}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}^\dagger(\mathbf{k}) \, \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) \, \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}(\mathbf{k}) $; and (v) obtaining the device retarded Green's function $ \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = [(\mathcal{E}+i\delta)\hat{I} - \mathcal{H}_D(\mathbf{k}) - \Sigma_L(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) - \Sigma_R(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) ]^{-1} $, Brillouin-zone averaging $ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E}) = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) $, and observable formulas: density of states (DOS) $ \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) = -\frac{1}{N_c\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathrm{Im}[\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E})] $, carrier concentration $ n = \int \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) f(\mathcal{E}) \, d\mathcal{E} $ (where $f(\mathcal{E})$ is the Fermi-Dirac distribution), quantum capacitance $ C_Q = e^2 \frac{\partial n}{\partial \mathcal{E}} $, transmission $ T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds}) = \mathrm{Tr}[\Gamma_L \mathcal{G} \Gamma_R \mathcal{G}^\dagger] $, and current $ I(V_{ds}) = \frac{2e}{h} \int T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds})[f_L(\mathcal{E})-f_R(\mathcal{E})]\,d\mathcal{E} $ (where $f_{L,R}$ are the Fermi-Dirac distributions of left and right leads). The model uses a single adsorbate per unit cell and employs the empirical distance-scaling relation $ t_{xy} = t\left(\frac{a_0}{d_{xy}}\right) $ to obtain adsorbate-modified hoppings.

steps.reasoning: Define the full system Hamiltonian for the device and leads by writing the total Hamiltonian as the sum of the device-region Hamiltonian $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} $, the left lead Hamiltonian $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L}} $, the right lead Hamiltonian $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{R}} $, and the coupling Hamiltonians between device and leads $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{LD}} $ and $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{DR}} $, i.e. $ \mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{R}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{LD}} + \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{DR}} $; here $ \mathcal{H} $ is the total Hamiltonian operator for the extended device-plus-leads system, and each term denotes the Hamiltonian acting on the named subsystem or coupling between subsystems.

Specify the tight-binding form of the device-region Hamiltonian by writing $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}} = \sum_i \epsilon_i c_i^\dagger c_i + \sum_{i\neq j} t_{ij} c_i^\dagger c_j $, where $ \epsilon_i $ denotes the on-site energy of orbital/site $i$, $ t_{ij} $ denotes the hopping matrix element from site $j$ to site $i$, and $ c_i^\dagger $ and $ c_i $ are fermionic creation and annihilation operators on site $i$.

Model each unit cell of the gas-functionalized monolayer h-BN by three basis orbitals: one nitrogen orbital, one boron orbital, and one adsorbate orbital, leading to a $3\times3$ momentum-space device Hamiltonian $h(\mathbf{k})$ given explicitly as
$ h(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{bmatrix} E_0 & t f(\mathbf{k}) & 0 \\ t f^*(\mathbf{k}) & E_1 & t' \\ 0 & t' & E_0' \end{bmatrix} $,
where $E_0$ is the nitrogen on-site energy, $E_1$ is the boron on-site energy, $E_0'$ is the adsorbate on-site energy, $t$ is the boron–nitrogen hopping, $t'$ is the boron–adsorbate hopping, and the structure factor is $ f(\mathbf{k}) = 1 + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_1} + e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_2} $ with $ \mathbf{a}_1 $ and $ \mathbf{a}_2 $ the lattice vectors of the h-BN lattice.

State numerical/parameter context used in the model: the homogeneous on-site energies used in the tight-binding baseline are $E_0 = -2.55\ \mathrm{eV}$ (nitrogen) and $E_1 = 2.46\ \mathrm{eV}$ (boron); the adsorbate is represented by adding a single adsorbate site per unit cell (one adsorbate per unit cell) whose coupling to boron is $t'$; the adsorbate-modified hoppings $t_{xy}$ are obtained from the empirical distance-scaling relation $ t_{xy} = t\left(\frac{a_0}{d_{xy}}\right) $, where $a_0$ is the pristine lattice constant and $d_{xy}$ is the distance between the h-BN site and the adsorbate site.

Obtain the energy bands of the periodic gas-functionalized lattice by solving the secular equation $ \det\left[h(\mathbf{k}) - \mathcal{E}\,\hat{I}\right] = 0 $, which for the displayed $3\times3$ model yields the cubic characteristic equation
$ (E_0-\mathcal{E})\left\{(E_1-\mathcal{E})(E_0'-\mathcal{E})-{t'}^{2}\right\} - t^{2}|f(\mathbf{k})|^{2}(E_0'-\mathcal{E}) = 0 $,
where $ \mathcal{E} $ denotes the band energy and $ \hat{I} $ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix.

Describe the method to include semi-infinite leads and compute their influence on the device: treat each lead as a semi-infinite periodic array of identical unit cells with intra-cell and inter-cell matrices matching the principal-layer representation, and compute the retarded surface Green's function of a lead projected onto its surface unit cell in momentum space as
$ \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = \langle 0 | \left[(\mathcal{E}+i\delta)\hat{I} - \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L(R)}}(\mathbf{k})\right]^{-1} | 0 \rangle $,
where $|0\rangle$ denotes the surface unit-cell basis, $ \delta $ is a positive broadening, and $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{L(R)}}(\mathbf{k}) $ is the $ \mathbf{k} $-resolved lead Hamiltonian.
[52, 53]

State how the lead surface Green's functions are computed numerically: use the Sancho iterative renormalization (recursive Green's function) scheme to evaluate $ \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) $ efficiently and stably for semi-infinite leads, thereby avoiding direct inversion of infinite-dimensional matrices and producing the surface projection needed to form self-energies.
[52, 53]

Formulate the lead self-energies in momentum space from the computed surface Green's function via
$ \Sigma_{L(R)}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}^\dagger(\mathbf{k})\,\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E})\,\mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}(\mathbf{k}) $,
where $ \mathcal{H}_{L(DR)}(\mathbf{k}) $ denotes the $ \mathbf{k} $-dependent coupling matrix between the left (right) lead and the device region; these self-energies encode the open-boundary escape rates and level shifts induced by the leads.
[45]

Write the device-region retarded Green's function in the presence of lead couplings as
$ \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) = \left[(\mathcal{E}+i\delta)\hat{I} - \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}}(\mathbf{k}) - \Sigma_L(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) - \Sigma_R(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E})\right]^{-1} $,
where all symbols have their previous meanings and $ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{D}}(\mathbf{k}) $ is the $ \mathbf{k} $-space device Hamiltonian; this retarded Green's function describes the open-system spectral response of the device for each $ \mathbf{k} $ and energy $ \mathcal{E} $.
[44, 45]

Prescribe Brillouin-zone averaging to obtain the $ \mathbf{k} $-averaged device Green's function by sampling $N_k$ momentum points and forming
$ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E}) = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E}) $,
where $ \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E}) $ is the Green's function averaged over the Brillouin zone and used to compute macroscopic observables.

Provide the observable formulas expressible in terms of the Green's functions: define the total density of states (DOS) as
$ \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) = -\frac{1}{N_c\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{k}} \mathrm{Im}\left[\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},\mathcal{E})\right] $,
where $ N_c $ is the number of unit cells and $ \mathrm{Tr} $ denotes the matrix trace; define the carrier concentration as $ n = \int \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}) f(\mathcal{E}) \, d\mathcal{E} $ where $ f(\mathcal{E}) = \left[1+\exp\left(\frac{\mathcal{E}-\mathcal{E}_F}{k_B T}\right)\right]^{-1} $ is the Fermi–Dirac distribution with Fermi energy $ \mathcal{E}_F $, Boltzmann constant $ k_B $, and temperature $ T $; define the quantum capacitance as $ C_Q = e^2 \frac{\partial n}{\partial \mathcal{E}} $ where $ e $ is the elementary charge; define the transmission function as $ T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds}) = \mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma_L(\mathcal{E}) \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E}) \Gamma_R(\mathcal{E}) \mathcal{G}^\dagger(\mathcal{E})\right] $ where $ \Gamma_{L(R)}(\mathcal{E}) = i\left(\Sigma_{L(R)}(\mathcal{E}) - \Sigma_{L(R)}^\dagger(\mathcal{E})\right) $; and define the current through the device under drain-source bias $ V_{ds} $ by the Landauer–Büttiker integral
$ I(V_{ds}) = \frac{2e}{h}\int T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds})\,[f_L(\mathcal{E})-f_R(\mathcal{E})]\,d\mathcal{E} $,
where $ h $ is Planck's constant and $ f_{L(R)} $ are the lead Fermi functions shifted by the lead chemical potentials.
[45, 50]

Summarize implementation conventions used in the model: represent the adsorbate by a single extra site per unit cell (single adsorbate per unit cell assumption), obtain adsorbate-modified hoppings via the empirical distance-scaling $ t_{xy} = t\left(\frac{a_0}{d_{xy}}\right) $ where $ a_0 $ is the lattice constant and $ d_{xy} $ is the adsorbate distance (tabulated per gas), compute lead surface Green's functions using the Sancho recursive scheme, construct self-energies from the surface Green's functions, compute the device Green's function and then derive DOS, $n$, $C_Q$, $T(\mathcal{E})$, and $I(V_{ds})$ via the formulas above to produce device-level quantum-transport predictions for gas-functionalized h-BN FET sensors.

motivating_questions.content: In practical sensing, device observables such as drain current, gate-dependent capacitance and temperature-dependent sensitivity require a formalism that couples atomistic adsorption-induced electronic perturbations to open-boundary, finite-bias transport. Previously available equilibrium DFT calculations provide adsorption geometries, on-site shifts and indications of mid-gap states, but cannot by themselves produce non-equilibrium transport quantities because they lack explicit lead couplings, lead self-energies, and a Brillouin-zone-resolved device Green's function. Device engineers therefore needed a tractable computational pipeline that (a) takes adsorbate-induced local orbital shifts and boron–adsorbate hybridization as input, (b) embeds those perturbations into a momentum-resolved device Hamiltonian, (c) computes lead self-energies for semi-infinite contacts, and (d) yields DOS, $n$, $C_Q$, $T(\mathcal{E},V_{ds})$, and $I(V_{ds})$ under gate fields and temperature. Without such a framework, predictions of gate-tunable sensing performance, bias-dependent selectivity, and temperature-optimized operation remained qualitative and disconnected from measurable device currents.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
Finite, structureless probes (leads) can be included as additional self-energy terms $\Sigma^{L}$ attached to device sites to compute transmissions and bond currents. Each lead self-energy is constructed as
$$
\Sigma_{ij}^{L} \;=\; V_{is}^{L}\; g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j)\; V_{sj}^{L},
$$
where $V_{is}^{L}$ is the coupling between device site $i$ and the lead, and $g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is the surface Green's function of a model lead (a semi-infinite single-atomic chain with surface GF $g^s=(E\pm\sqrt{E^2-4\gamma^2})/(2\gamma^2)$, $\gamma=|t|$). To prevent unphysical intersite coupling via the lead, the off-diagonal lead-GF elements are given a distance dependence
$$
g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j) \;=\; \delta_{ij} g^{s} + (1-\delta_{ij}) \frac{g^{s}}{|\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j|}.
$$
Bond currents injected from a lead $L$ are computed from device Green's functions via
$$
J_{ij}^{L} \;=\; -H_{ij}\; \frac{\mathrm{Im}\big[(G^{a}\,\Gamma^{L}\,G^{r})_{ij}\big]}{\hbar},
$$
where $H_{ij}$ is the tight-binding matrix element and $\Gamma^{L}=i(\Sigma^{L}-\Sigma^{L\dagger})$. These forms allow finite, spatially localized probes and the calculation of local current patterns in the patched device.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Inclusion of finite probes and bond-current calculation via lead self-energies with distance-dependent coupling

steps.reasoning: Begin from the upstream established capabilities: the patched Green's function framework provides the device Green's function blocks (including $ \boldsymbol{G}_{1,1} $ and off-diagonal blocks) via the adaptive recursive algorithm, and the boundary self-energy $ \Sigma_B $ encapsulating the infinite host is available; use these as known inputs when adding finite probes (leads) and computing bond currents.

Introduce finite, structureless probes as additional self-energy attachments to device sites: model each lead $L$ by a self-energy matrix with elements
$$
\Sigma_{ij}^{L} \;=\; V_{is}^{L}\; g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j)\; V_{sj}^{L},
$$
where $V_{is}^{L}$ is the coupling matrix element between device site $i$ and the lead electrode site $s$, $ \boldsymbol{r}_i $ denotes the spatial position of device site $i$, and $ g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) $ is the surface Green's function of the chosen model lead evaluated at separation $ \boldsymbol{r} $.

Specify the chosen structureless lead model and its surface Green's function: use a semi-infinite single-atomic-chain lead whose surface Green's function (for energy $E$ and chain hopping parameter $\gamma$) is
$$
g^{s} \;=\; \frac{E \pm \sqrt{E^{2} - 4\gamma^{2}}}{2\gamma^{2}},
$$
and choose $ \gamma = |t| $ (with $t$ the graphene nearest-neighbor hopping) so that the lead has an approximately constant density of states within the energy range of interest. This form and parameter choice avoid energy-dependent structure in the lead density of states that would otherwise complicate interpretation. [76]

Introduce a physically motivated distance dependence for off-diagonal lead-GF elements to avoid unphysical intersite coupling mediated by a structureless lead: define
$$
g^{s}(\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j) \;=\; \delta_{ij}\, g^{s} + (1-\delta_{ij})\, \frac{g^{s}}{|\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j|},
$$
where $ \delta_{ij} $ is the Kronecker delta, so that diagonal (on-site) lead couplings use the surface GF $g^{s}$ while off-diagonal couplings decay as the inverse separation $1/|\boldsymbol{r}_i-\boldsymbol{r}_j|$ appropriate for a structureless three-dimensional free-electron-like coupling; this choice prevents unrealistic long-range intersite coherence induced by the lead.

Define the broadening matrix associated with a lead and the formula for bond currents injected from a lead: for lead $L$ define $ \Gamma^{L} = i(\Sigma^{L} - \Sigma^{L\dagger}) $, using the retarded lead self-energy $ \Sigma^{L} $. The bond current from lead $L$ between device sites $i$ and $j$ is computed from device Green's function blocks by
$$
J_{ij}^{L} \;=\; -H_{ij}\; \frac{\mathrm{Im}\big[(G^{a}\,\Gamma^{L}\,G^{r})_{ij}\big]}{\hbar},
$$
where $H_{ij}$ is the tight-binding Hamiltonian matrix element connecting sites $i$ and $j$, $G^{r}$ and $G^{a}$ are the retarded and advanced device Green's functions, respectively, and $ \hbar $ is the reduced Planck constant. This expression yields the local bond currents sourced by the lead $L$ and can be evaluated using the off-diagonal Green's function blocks obtained from the recursive algorithm.
Fig. 8

Connect the lead self-energy and bond-current implementation to transport observables: include $ \Sigma^{L} $ terms in the forward recursion for the cell containing probe-coupled sites (typically cell $n=1$), use $ \Gamma^{L} $ to compute transmission via $ \mathcal{T}_{L,L'}(E) = \operatorname{Tr}\big[\boldsymbol{G}_{L',L}\, \Gamma^{L}\, \boldsymbol{G}_{L,L'}^\dagger\, \Gamma^{L'}\big] $, and compute spatial bond-current patterns $J_{ij}^{L}$ to obtain local current maps and to identify phenomena such as vortexlike circulating currents near nanostructures.

motivating_questions.content: To study local transport (e.g., dual-STM-probe setups) one must attach probes to a finite device patch embedded in an infinite host without introducing spurious long-range intersite couplings mediated by the lead model. Simple local lead attachments can produce artificial coupling between multiple device sites. Therefore, a prescription was required to model structureless probes with a physically motivated distance-dependent intersite coupling through the lead, and a corresponding bond-current formula compatible with the patched-device Green's function. The above lead self-energy construction and the bond-current expression provide a practical and physically regularized way to include probes and compute local currents within the patched GF framework.

Define the local probe used to detect confinement: the local density of states (LDOS) at lattice site $i$ and energy $E$ is $\mathrm{LDOS}(E)=\sum_{l}\left|\langle i|l\rangle\right|^{2}\delta(E-E_{l})$, where the sum runs over all single-electron eigenstates $|l\rangle$ of $H$ with eigenenergy $E_{l}$; this quantity was evaluated to obtain spatially resolved maps of electronic localization in and around the dots.

motivating_questions.content: To make concrete device-relevant predictions one must perform numerically exact, lattice-scale simulations that include realistic finite-size ribbons, contacted leads, and the spatial profile of gate potentials. Approximate continuum results or small-cluster lattice studies leave open whether the predicted resonances and transport features survive in realistically large, contacted systems and how they appear in observable quantities (LDOS, conductance). A demonstration based on exact tight-binding numerics bridges this gap by producing device-scale, quantitative data.

Specify Module (ii) — secular-equation builder: assemble region-specific Hamiltonian blocks for (a) perfect leads $\boldsymbol{H}^L$, (b) lead–bridge matching domains $\boldsymbol{H}^{LB}$, and (c) the bridge Hamiltonian $\boldsymbol{H}^B$; choose matching-domain sizes $N_{LB}$ according to required inclusion of lead-proximal atoms; explicitly organize the composite Hamiltonian in the block-sum form $\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{H}^{L}+\boldsymbol{H}^{LB}+\boldsymbol{H}^{B}$ and build corresponding matrix entries for $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ used in the homogeneous eigenproblem.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
The open-boundary quantum problem for a device connected to semi-infinite leads can be reduced exactly to a finite-dimensional linear system for the device region by folding the effect of the left and right leads into energy-dependent self-energy matrices.  The device retarded Green's function $G(E)$ satisfies
$$
[A(E)]\,G(E)=I\qquad\text{with}\qquad A(E)\equiv EI-H_{D}-\Sigma_{lead}(E),
$$
where $H_{D}$ is the device Hamiltonian (discrete tight-binding or discretized effective-mass operator) defined on the finite device grid, and the only non-zero blocks of the contact self-energy $\Sigma_{lead}(E)$ are the surface-coupling terms
$$
\Sigma_{L}=\;T_{D,L}\;g_{L}^{surf}(E)\;T_{L,D},\qquad
\Sigma_{R}=\;T_{D,R}\;g_{R}^{surf}(E)\;T_{R,D}.
$$
Here $T_{D,L}$ ($T_{D,R}$) couples the device to the left (right) lead, and $g_{L}^{surf}(E)$ and $g_{R}^{surf}(E)$ are the surface Green's functions of the semi-infinite leads (solutions of the quadratic matrix equation $[A_{l}-T_{l}^{\dagger}g_{l}T_{l}]g_{l}=I$ when leads are periodic).  $\Sigma_{L}(E)$ and $\Sigma_{R}(E)$ generally have complex values whose imaginary parts determine contact escape rates.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Finite-device Green's-function formulation with contact self-energies (folding semi-infinite leads)

conclusion.content:
The open-boundary quantum transport problem for a finite device region coupled to two semi-infinite leads is reduced exactly to a finite linear system for the device by folding the leads into energy-dependent contact self-energy matrices: the device retarded Green's function G(E) (the matrix inverse of the device operator at energy E) satisfies
      $$
      [A(E)]\,G(E)=I,\qquad A(E)\equiv EI-H_{D}-\Sigma_{lead}(E),
      $$
      where E is the real energy parameter, I is the identity on the device Hilbert space, H_{D} is the device Hamiltonian defined on the finite device grid (discrete tight-binding or discretized effective-mass operator), and the only nonzero blocks of the contact self-energy matrix $\Sigma_{lead}(E)$ are the surface-coupling terms
      $$
      \Sigma_{L}(E)=T_{D,L}\,g_{L}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)\,T_{L,D},\qquad
      \Sigma_{R}(E)=T_{D,R}\,g_{R}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)\,T_{R,D},
      $$
      with $T_{D,L}$ ($T_{D,R}$) the device–left (device–right) coupling matrices and $g_{L}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)$, $g_{R}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)$ the surface Green's functions of the semi-infinite leads (the matrices describing the linear response of the lead edge to a perturbation at energy E under the retarded boundary condition).  The contact self-energies $\Sigma_{L,R}(E)$ are generally complex; their anti‑Hermitian parts produce level broadening and escape rates characterized by $\Gamma_{L,R}(E)=-2\,\mathrm{Im}[\Sigma_{L,R}(E)]$, which set the rates at which carriers leave the device into the leads.

For a semi-infinite lead composed of a periodic sequence of identical layer operators $A_{l}$ (the block Hamiltonian acting on a single lead layer) and identical inter-layer coupling matrices $T_{l}$ (so the lead Hamiltonian is block-periodic along the transport direction), the retarded surface Green's function $g_{l}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)$ is defined as the matrix solution of the quadratic matrix equation
      $$
      \big[A_{l}-T_{l}^{\dagger}\,g_{l}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)\,T_{l}\big]\,g_{l}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)=I,
      $$
      where $E$ is the (complexified retarded) energy parameter and $I$ is the identity on the single-layer subspace; this quadratic (matrix) equation has a well‑defined retarded solution branch (poles displaced into the lower half of the complex energy plane by an infinitesimal negative imaginary part) provided the lead is periodic, and the resulting surface Green's function $g_{l}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)$ is the correct object to fold the semi-infinite lead into the finite device via the self-energy $\Sigma_{L}=T_{D,L}\,g_{l}^{\mathrm{surf}}(E)\,T_{L,D}$.

The full Schr\"odinger / tight-binding problem on the combined device+leads domain yields an infinite-dimensional linear system because the leads are semi-infinite.

Write the retarded Green's-function equation for the full system as $[E-H+i\eta]G=I$, where $E$ is energy, $H$ is the total Hamiltonian (device plus leads), $G$ is the full Green's function, $I$ is the identity matrix, and $\eta$ is an infinitesimal positive number that enforces the causal (retarded) boundary condition.

Partition the full system into Left lead (L), Device (D), and Right lead (R) blocks and write the block matrix form of the operator $A'=[E I - H - \Sigma_{Phonon}]$ (where $\Sigma_{Phonon}$ is any phonon self-energy; set to zero for the purely contact-folding derivation). Denote the device-block equation (after eliminating lead degrees of freedom) as an $n$-dimensional matrix equation for the device-block Green's function $G_{DD}$.

Eliminate the semi-infinite leads by solving the linear equations for the lead blocks formally and substituting back into the device block equation; this produces additional terms that enter only at the device boundary layers. The resulting finite-dimensional device equation can be written as $A\,G_{D D}=I$, where $A$ is the device operator that includes the effect of the leads via self-energies (this is the finite-dimensional reduction of the open-boundary problem).

Define explicitly the device operator $A(E)$ that appears in the reduced finite-dimensional equation: $A(E)\equiv EI-H_{D}-\Sigma_{lead}(E)$, where $EI$ denotes the energy times the identity on the device grid, $H_{D}$ is the device Hamiltonian defined on the finite device grid, and $\Sigma_{lead}(E)$ is the contact self-energy matrix induced by the left and right semi-infinite leads.

Show the nonzero structure of the contact self-energy: only surface-coupling blocks connecting the device to each lead are nonzero. Denote the device–left-lead coupling matrix as $T_{D,L}$ and the device–right-lead coupling as $T_{D,R}$ (with $T_{L,D}=T_{D,L}^{\dagger}$ and $T_{R,D}=T_{D,R}^{\dagger}$). Then the left contact self-energy block on the device is $\Sigma_{L}(E)=T_{D,L}\;g_{L}^{surf}(E)\;T_{L,D}$ and the right contact self-energy block is $\Sigma_{R}(E)=T_{D,R}\;g_{R}^{surf}(E)\;T_{R,D}$, where $g_{L}^{surf}(E)$ and $g_{R}^{surf}(E)$ are the surface Green's functions of the semi-infinite leads evaluated at the device–lead boundary layers.

Define the surface Green's function of a semi-infinite lead: the surface Green's function $g_{l}^{surf}(E)$ of a lead satisfies the matrix quadratic Dyson-like equation $\big[A_{l}-T_{l}^{\dagger}\,g_{l}^{surf}(E)\,T_{l}\big]g_{l}^{surf}(E)=I$, where $A_{l}$ is the block on-site operator of one lead layer, $T_{l}$ is the inter-layer coupling within the periodic lead, and $I$ is the identity in the layer subspace. This scalar/quadratic structure arises when the lead is periodic and all layer blocks are identical.

Assemble the finite-device Green's-function equation: the device retarded Green's function $G(E)$ (i.e., $G_{DD}(E)$) satisfies
$$[A(E)]\,G(E)=I\qquad\text{with}\qquad A(E)\equiv EI-H_{D}-\Sigma_{lead}(E),$$
where the only non-zero blocks of $\Sigma_{lead}(E)$ are the two surface-coupling blocks $\Sigma_{L}(E)$ and $\Sigma_{R}(E)$ defined above.

State physical interpretation of the contact self-energies: $\Sigma_{L}(E)$ and $\Sigma_{R}(E)$ are, in general, complex-valued matrices; their imaginary parts determine contact escape rates (scattering rates into the leads) through $\Gamma_{lead}=-2\Im[\Sigma_{lead}]$, so the imaginary part of the contact self-energy gives the rate at which device states couple (decay) into lead continua.

Refer to the one-dimensional lattice derivation and the explicit elimination steps presented earlier for the tight-binding example (where the lead surface Green's function is evaluated as $g_{L-1,-1}=e^{+ik_{l}a}t_{l}^{-1}$ for a uniform lead). This explicit tight-binding example demonstrates concretely how the semi-infinite lead contributions reduce to the surface self-energy blocks shown above.

motivating_questions.content: In quantum modeling of open nanoscale devices the full Hamiltonian including semi-infinite leads is infinite-dimensional; direct solution of the full Schrodinger problem with open boundaries is not numerically feasible.  Prior to this reduction, practical simulations either treated device-lead coupling approximately or required explicitly truncating leads (incurring artificial reflections).  A self-contained finite-device formulation that exactly accounts for semi-infinite leads was needed to obtain exact open-boundary conditions, to define contact-induced level broadening and injection rates in an energy-resolved way, and to make the problem numerically tractable for self-consistent device–Poisson simulations.  Folding the leads into energy-dependent self-energies provides that finite formulation while preserving the physics of injection, absorption and level broadening by the contacts.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
The Landauer-Büttiker conductance expression
$$
G(E)=G_0\mathcal{T}(E)=\frac{2e^2}{h}\mathrm{Tr}\big[\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^a\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{R}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^r\big]
$$
is implemented in the nonorthogonal QO basis by using the conductor retarded Green's function in the generalized (nonorthogonal) form
$$
\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}=\big(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C}}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}\big)^{-1},
$$
with self-energies
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r}=(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}})\,\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}\,(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}})^{\dagger},
$$
and similarly for $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}$ [Eqs. (2), (7)--(11), (8)--(9)]. The implementation uses the QO-derived Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}$ and overlap $\mathbf{S}$, the Sancho et al. iterative surface-Green's-function method for $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0},\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{R}}^{0}$, and Löwdin orthogonalization in conductance-eigenchannel analysis; this yields an efficient, robust toolchain that computes transmission $\mathcal{T}(E)$ and energy-resolved conductor DOS from QO-based ab initio TB matrices while preserving the DFT-level electronic-structure accuracy within the chosen $E_{\mathrm{th}}$.

conclusion.content:
The Landauer-Büttiker conductance expression $G(E) = G_0 \mathcal{T}(E) = \frac{2e^2}{h} \mathrm{Tr}[\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L}} \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^a \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{R}} \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^r]$, where $G_0 = 2e^2/h$ is the conductance quantum, $\mathcal{T}(E)$ is the transmission probability, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L,R}} = i(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L,R}}^r - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L,R}}^a)$ are the coupling matrices between the conductor and the left and right leads, $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r(a)}$ are the retarded (advanced) Green's functions of the conductor, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L,R}}^{r(a)}$ are the retarded (advanced) self-energies, is implemented in the nonorthogonal quasiatomic-orbital (QO) basis. The conductor retarded Green's function in the nonorthogonal basis is given by the generalized form
      $$
      \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r} = (z \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}} - \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C}} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r})^{-1},
      $$
      where $z = E + i\eta$ with $\eta$ an infinitesimal positive number, $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C}}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}}$ are the QO-derived Hamiltonian and overlap matrices of the conductor region, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L,R}}^{r}$ are the retarded self-energies due to coupling to semi-infinite leads. The left self-energy is expressed as
      $$
      \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r} = (z \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}} - \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}}) \mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0} (z \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}} - \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}})^{\dagger},
      $$
      and similarly for $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}$, where $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}$ are the coupling Hamiltonian and overlap between the conductor and the left lead's first principal layer, and $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}$ is the surface Green's function of the left semi-infinite lead computed using the iterative method of Sancho et al. that recursively doubles the number of principal layers to obtain the surface Green's function of a semi-infinite lead. The implementation uses the QO-derived Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}$ and overlap $\mathbf{S}$, the Sancho et al. iterative surface-Green's-function method for $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{R}}^{0}$, and Löwdin orthogonalization (transformation by $\mathbf{S}^{1/2}$) in the conductance-eigenchannel analysis. This yields a toolchain that computes transmission $\mathcal{T}(E)$ and energy-resolved conductor density of states from QO-based ab initio tight-binding matrices while preserving the DFT-level electronic-structure accuracy within the chosen energy threshold $E_{\mathrm{th}}$.

A nonorthogonal quasiatomic-orbital (QO) basis $\{|\mathrm{Q}_{I i}\rangle\}$ is constructed for each atom $I$ and orbital index $i$ by projecting pseudoatomic orbitals $|\mathrm{A}_{I i}\rangle$ onto an optimized subspace $Q(\mathbf{k}) = R(\mathbf{k}) \cup C(\mathbf{k})$ of Bloch states, where $R(\mathbf{k})$ is the subspace spanned by the $R_{\mathbf{k}}$ Kohn-Sham eigenstates $\{|\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle\}$ with eigenvalues below a chosen energy threshold $E_{\mathrm{th}}$, and $C(\mathbf{k})$ is the complementary subspace of $C_{\mathbf{k}} = qN - R_{\mathbf{k}}$ orthonormal states $\{|c_{m\mathbf{k}}\rangle\}$ constructed from the perpendicular components $|\mathrm{A}_{I i,\mathbf{k}}^\perp\rangle = |\mathrm{A}_{I i,\mathbf{k}}\rangle - \sum_n \hat{P}_{\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}}|\mathrm{A}_{I i,\mathbf{k}}\rangle$ by selecting the largest eigenvalues of the Gramian matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{k}}$ with elements $(\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{k}})_{I i, J j} = \langle \mathrm{A}_{I i,\mathbf{k}}^\perp |\hat{S}| \mathrm{A}_{J j,\mathbf{k}}^\perp \rangle$, where $\hat{S}$ is the overlap operator accounting for pseudopotential augmentation. The QOs are then defined as
      $$
      |\mathrm{Q}_{I i}\rangle = \sum_{n\mathbf{k}} \hat{P}_{\phi_{n\mathbf{k}}} |\mathrm{A}_{I i}\rangle = \sum_{n\mathbf{k}} (\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}})_{n, I i} |\phi_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle,
      $$
      where $\{\phi_{n\mathbf{k}}\} = \{\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}\} \cup \{c_{m\mathbf{k}}\}$ is the orthonormal basis for $Q(\mathbf{k})$, and $(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}})_{n, I i} = \langle \phi_{n\mathbf{k}} | \hat{S} | \mathrm{A}_{I i} \rangle$ is the coefficient matrix. Using these QOs, the real-space ab initio tight-binding Hamiltonian and overlap matrices between QOs at unit cell 0 and unit cell $\mathbf{X}_L$ are obtained as Fourier sums over the Brillouin zone:
      $$
      H_{Ii,Jj}(\mathbf{X}_L) = \sum_{\mathbf{k}} e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{X}_L} (\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}}^\dagger \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{k}} \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}})_{Ii,Jj},
      \qquad
      O_{Ii,Jj}(\mathbf{X}_L) = \sum_{\mathbf{k}} e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{X}_L} (\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}}^\dagger \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{k}})_{Ii,Jj},
      $$
      where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{k}}$ is the Hamiltonian matrix in the $\{\phi_{n\mathbf{k}}\}$ basis, with diagonal elements $\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$ for $n \leq R_{\mathbf{k}}$ and off-diagonal elements between $c_{m\mathbf{k}}$ states computed explicitly. Provided a radial cutoff distance $R_{\rm cut}$ is chosen such that matrix elements with $|\mathbf{X}_L| > R_{\rm cut}$ are negligible, these $H$ and $O$ matrices reproduce the plane-wave Kohn-Sham eigenvalues and eigenstates below $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ when the generalized eigenvalue problem $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{|\mathbf{X}_L| \leq R_{\rm cut}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{X}_L} H(\mathbf{X}_L)$ is solved. The QO construction avoids explicit computation of high-energy (unoccupied) Bloch states by using the resolution-of-identity in the Bloch space and selecting the largest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{k}}$, thus reducing storage and computational cost while preserving atomiclike orbital character.

steps.reasoning: Starting point (use upstream result as known): take as given the ab initio tight-binding Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}$ and overlap $\mathbf{S}$ matrices in the nonorthogonal QO basis computed from the QO construction and real-space Fourier transforms (conclusion 1); these provide localized, sparse matrices for leads and conductor with the localization length controlled by $R_{\mathrm{cut}}$.

Adopt the Landauer-Büttiker expression for zero-temperature conductance: define conductance quantum $G_{0}\equiv 2e^{2}/h$ (factor 2 for spin degeneracy), energy-dependent transmission $\mathcal{T}(E)$, and write $G(E)=G_{0}\mathcal{T}(E)=\frac{2e^{2}}{h}\mathrm{Tr}[\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{a}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{R}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}]$, where $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{a}$ are the conductor retarded and advanced Green's functions at energy $E$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}$ describe coupling from the leads; here $\mathrm{Tr}[\cdot]$ denotes the matrix trace.

Formulate the conductor retarded Green's function in the generalized (nonorthogonal) matrix form: define complex energy $z\equiv E+i\eta$ with infinitesimal positive broadening $\eta$, and write
$$
\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}=\big(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C}}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}\big)^{-1},
$$
where $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}}$ and $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C}}$ are the conductor overlap and Hamiltonian blocks in the QO basis, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L/R}}^{r}$ are retarded self-energy matrices due to coupling to the left and right semi-infinite leads.

Express the lead self-energies in terms of conductor-lead coupling blocks and the surface Green's function of a principal layer: define conductor-left coupling matrices $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}}$ and $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}$ (matrix blocks coupling conductor orbitals to principal-layer orbitals L0), and define the principal-layer surface Green's function $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}$ as the retarded Green's function of the semi-infinite lead projected on its surface principal layer; then write
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r}=(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}})\,\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}\,(z\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{CL}}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{CL}})^{\dagger},
$$
and the analogous expression for $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}$ with right-lead blocks; all matrix products are in the QO basis restricted to the conductor/principal-layer orbital indices.

Compute the principal-layer surface Green's functions $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{R}}^{0}$ using an efficient iterative decimation technique: employ the Sancho et al. iterative surface-Green's-function method (an algorithm that recursively doubles the number of included principal layers using only the principal-layer Hamiltonian and coupling blocks), as implemented in the work; include citations for the Sancho iterative method. [85-87]  Define that $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{L}}^{0}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{R}}^{0}$ are the retarded surface Green's functions of the lead principal layer L0 and R0 respectively.

Define the coupling matrices $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}$ from the retarded and advanced self-energies via
$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}=i(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}^{r}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}^{a}),
$$
and note the relationships $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}=(\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{a})^{\dagger}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}^{r}=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}^{a})^{\dagger}$ that ensure Hermitian-conjugation consistency.

Implement conductance eigenchannel analysis in the nonorthogonal QO basis by performing Löwdin orthogonalization: define Löwdin orthogonalization of overlap matrix $\mathbf{S}$ via $\mathbf{S}^{1/2}$ and $\mathbf{S}^{-1/2}$, transform the spectral function $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{a}$ to $\overline{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathbf{S}^{1/2}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{L}}\mathbf{S}^{1/2}$, diagonalize $\overline{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{L}}$ to obtain orthogonal scattering-channel eigenvectors and eigenvalues $\lambda_{l}$, scale eigenvectors as $[\tilde{\mathbf{U}}]_{ml}=\sqrt{\lambda_l/(2\pi)}[\mathbf{U}]_{ml}$, construct the transmission matrix in this orthogonal basis $T=2\pi\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{\dagger}\overline{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_{\mathrm{R}}\tilde{\mathbf{U}}$ with $\overline{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_{\mathrm{R}}=\mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{R}}\mathbf{S}^{-1/2}$, and finally diagonalize $T$ to obtain eigenchannel transmission probabilities $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}$ and eigenchannel coefficients from which energy-normalized eigenchannel wavefunctions in the original nonorthogonal QO basis are reconstructed; this procedure follows the formulation of energy-normalized conductance eigenchannels. [88]

Realize practical computational pipeline: assemble conductor and lead Hamiltonian and overlap blocks from the QO-derived real-space TB matrices (conclusion 1), compute surface Green's functions via Sancho iterations, evaluate self-energies and $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}$, obtain $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L,R}}$ and compute transmission $\mathcal{T}(E)$ via the Landauer trace formula, and compute the conductor DOS $\rho_{\mathrm{C}}(E)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\mathrm{Im}\{\mathrm{Tr}[\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{C}}^{r}(E)\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{C}}]\}$; the method thus returns both transmission curves and energy-resolved conductor DOS while working entirely in the nonorthogonal QO basis.

Summarize accuracy and efficiency: because the QO TB matrices reproduce plane-wave DFT eigenvalues and eigenstates below $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ when $R_{\mathrm{cut}}$ is chosen appropriately (from conclusion 1), the Green's-function implementation in the QO basis yields transmission $\mathcal{T}(E)$ and conductor DOS that preserve plane-wave DFT-level electronic-structure accuracy within the chosen $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ while benefiting from reduced basis size and sparsity of QO TB matrices, producing an efficient and robust toolchain for ab initio transport.

motivating_questions.content: To compute conductance one must evaluate surface self-energies and invert the conductor Green's-function operator in a basis that may be nonorthogonal. Plane-wave representations make these operations expensive because of matrix sizes; localized bases make them feasible but must be supplied in an ab initio-consistent form (Hamiltonian and overlap matrices) that accurately represents the low-energy electronic structure. Furthermore, nonorthogonality requires careful definition of Green's functions and of coupling matrices $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\{\mathrm{L,R}\}}$; numerical surface-Green's-function methods are needed for semi-infinite leads. Therefore a practical transport algorithm must combine (i) compact, accurate H and S matrices (from a minimal ab initio basis such as QOs), (ii) correct nonorthogonal Green's-function algebra (retarded Green's function with $z\mathbf{S}-\mathbf{H}$ inversion and self-energy construction), and (iii) numerically stable surface-Green's-function evaluation. The implementation cited above integrates these elements so that inversion dimensions are those of the minimal QO conductor subspace and the costly plane-wave occupied/unoccupied space is not explicitly inverted.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A self-contained recursive algorithm in matrix notation is presented that yields the retarded/advanced and lesser Green's functions and the bond-current for two-terminal tight-binding devices. The algorithm combines: (a) surface-lead recursion by section-doubling providing surface Green's functions $g_{aa}^{[n]}$, with the basic doubling-step formula $g_{aa}^{[2]} = \left(1 - g_{aa}^{[1]} V_{ab} g_{bb}^{[1]} V_{ba}\right)^{-1} g_{aa}^{[1]}$, where $g_{aa}^{[1]}$ is the isolated-slice Green's function and $V_{ab}$ is the hopping between adjacent slices; (b) left/right sweeps that attach device slices to leads via the recurrence $G_{nn}^{L} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}\right)^{-1}$ and $G_{nn}^{R} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n+1,n}\right)^{-1}$, where $H_n$ is the Hamiltonian matrix of slice $n$ and $V_{n,n\pm1}$ are inter-slice coupling matrices; (c) assembly of the central retarded Green's function $G_{nn} = \left[(E+i\eta)I - H_n - \Sigma^{L} - \Sigma^{R}\right]^{-1}$ with $\Sigma^{L}=V_{n-1,n}^{\dagger} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}$ and $\Sigma^{R}=V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n,n+1}^{\dagger}$; and (d) recursive evaluation of lesser Green's functions using surface lesser relations $G_{00}^{L,<}=-f_{L}[G_{00}^{L}-\left(G_{00}^{L}\right)^{\dagger}]$, $\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<}=V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L,<} V_{n-1,n}$, and the central expression $G_{mn}^{<}=G_{nn}\left(\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<}+\Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}\right)G_{nn}^{\dagger}$. Local bond-current between lattice sites $i$ and $j$ is given as $I_{ij} = i_{0}\int 2\Re\!\left(t_{ij}^{*} G_{ij}^{<}\right) dE$ with $i_{0}=2e/h$, and in the low-temperature, low-bias limit the differential conductance density is $\sigma_{(n,i)\rightarrow(n,j)} = \frac{2e^{2}}{h}\left[2\Re\left(H_{n}^{*} * G_{mn}^{<}\right)_{ij}\right]$, where $H_n$ is the intra-slice Hamiltonian matrix and $*$ denotes the Hadamard product $(A*B)_{ij}=A_{ij}B_{ij}$. All symbols are defined within the algorithm: $G^{r/a}$ retarded/advanced Green's functions of the whole system, $\Gamma_{L/R}=i(\Sigma_{L/R}^r-\Sigma_{L/R}^a)$ linewidth matrices, and $g_{L/R}^r$ left/right lead surface Green's functions.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Explicit recursive matrix algorithm for two-terminal NEGF and bond-current evaluation

conclusion.content: A recursive matrix algorithm for two-terminal non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) transport and bond-current evaluation in tight-binding devices consists of the following steps. (a) Surface Green's functions of the semi-infinite leads (denoted $G_{00}^{L}$ for the left lead and $G_{m+1,m+1}^{R}$ for the right lead) are obtained by section doubling from isolated-slice Green's functions $g_{aa}^{[1]}$ with inter-slice hopping matrix $V_{ab}$. The doubling-step formula is $g_{aa}^{[2]} = \left(I - g_{aa}^{[1]} V_{ab} g_{bb}^{[1]} V_{ba}\right)^{-1} g_{aa}^{[1]}$, where $g_{aa}^{[1]}$ and $g_{bb}^{[1]}$ are the Green's functions of two initial slices and $V_{ab}$ is the hopping between them. Iteration continues until convergence, yielding $G_{00}^{L} = g_{dd}^{[n]}$ and $G_{m+1,m+1}^{R} = g_{aa}^{[n]}$. (b) Device slices are attached to leads by left and right sweeps. The left sweep recurrence is $G_{nn}^{L} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}\right)^{-1}$, where $H_n$ is the Hamiltonian matrix of device slice $n$, $V_{n,n-1}$ is the coupling matrix from slice $n$ to $n-1$, and $G_{n-1,n-1}^{L}$ is the surface Green's function after attaching slices $1$ through $n-1$. The right sweep recurrence is $G_{nn}^{R} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n+1,n}\right)^{-1}$. (c) The retarded Green's function for a selected slice $n$ is assembled as $G_{nn} = \left[(E+i\eta)I - H_n - \Sigma^{L} - \Sigma^{R}\right]^{-1}$, with self-energies $\Sigma^{L} = V_{n-1,n}^{\dagger} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}$ and $\Sigma^{R} = V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n,n+1}^{\dagger}$. (d) Lesser Green's functions are evaluated recursively starting from the surface lesser relations $G_{00}^{L,<} = -f_L\left[G_{00}^{L} - \left(G_{00}^{L}\right)^{\dagger}\right]$ and $G_{m+1,m+1}^{R,<} = -f_R\left[G_{m+1,m+1}^{R} - \left(G_{m+1,m+1}^{R}\right)^{\dagger}\right]$, where $f_{L/R}$ are Fermi-Dirac distribution functions, and the lesser self-energies $\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<} = V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L,<} V_{n-1,n}$ and $\Sigma_{nn}^{R,<} = V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R,<} V_{n+1,n}$. The lesser Green's function at the center slice is $G_{nn}^{<} = G_{nn}\left(\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<} + \Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}\right) G_{nn}^{\dagger}$. The bond-current between lattice sites $i$ and $j$ is $I_{ij} = i_{0}\int 2\Re\left(t_{ij}^{*} G_{ij}^{<}\right) dE$ with $i_{0}=2e/h$, and in the low-temperature, low-bias limit the differential conductance density is $\sigma_{(n,i)\rightarrow(n,j)} = \frac{2e^{2}}{h}\left[2\Re\left(H_{n}^{*} * G_{nn}^{<}\right)_{ij}\right]$, where $*$ denotes the Hadamard product $(A*B)_{ij}=A_{ij}B_{ij}$.
conclusion.metadata: {"narrative": "The algorithm's correctness rests on the formal derivation and its numerical implementation. P5 raises a load-bearing risk: the surface Green's function convergence criterion is not validated across energy regimes, which could cause failures in applications near band edges. However, H1 provides strong empirical credit by demonstrating successful calculations in three distinct physical regimes (wide leads, narrow leads, QPC), each probing different energy ranges and geometries. The numerical tests partially insulate the algorithm from the convergence risk because they implicitly test convergence at the energies where they run; the risk remains for untested regimes (e.g., near Van Hove singularities). premises.content: The recursive algorithm for two-terminal nonequilibrium Green's functions is validated by applying it to three distinct physical scenarios within the same code: (i) a clean 2DEG with wide leads, producing quantized conductance steps that align with band-structure thresholds; (ii) a 2DEG contacted by narrow one-dimensional leads, reproducing sharp resonant transmission peaks at the device eigenenergies, each reaching unit transmission; and (iii) a quantum point contact with a saddle-point potential, giving conductance steps whose spacing increases with confinement strength and current patterns showing jets and interference fringes. Each scenario tests a different part of the formalism (surface Green's function for wide leads, lesser Green's function recursion for bond-currents, addition of a spatially varying potential). The consistent production of physically expected results across these cases indicates that the algorithm is correctly implemented and robust for two-terminal tight-binding devices.

steps.reasoning: Define the full two-terminal tight-binding system Hamiltonian matrix $H$ as the block-tridiagonal assembly of slice Hamiltonians $H_n$ (the diagonal blocks) and inter-slice coupling matrices $V_{n,n\pm1}$ (the off-diagonal blocks), where each slice $n$ is a collection of lattice sites; define the identity matrix $I$ of appropriate block size and an infinitesimal positive scalar $\eta\to 0^{+}$ used to regularize the energy denominator. The retarded Green's function of the whole system is defined by the matrix inverse $G=\left[(E+i\eta)I-H\right]^{-1}$, where $E$ is the energy variable used for all subsequent spectral formulas.

Address the semi-infinite leads by treating each lead as a periodic sequence of identical slices and computing a convergent finite-dimensional surface Green's function for a representative lead slice: define $g_{aa}^{[1]}$ as the isolated-slice Green's function of one lead slice via $g_{aa}^{[1]}=\left[(E+i\eta)I-H_{\text{slice}}\right]^{-1}$, where $H_{\text{slice}}$ is the Hamiltonian matrix of that single lead slice; the objective is to obtain the surface Green's function $g_{aa}^{[n]}$ of an effectively semi-infinite lead by iterative section-doubling that glues slices together until convergence.

Use Dyson's equation in operator form $g = g^{(0)} + g^{(0)} V g$ (where $g^{(0)}$ is the Green's function before attaching a perturbation $V$) and sandwich it between slice basis states to derive the doubling-step recursion: beginning with two identical isolated slices $a$ and $b$ with $g_{aa}^{[1]}=g_{bb}^{[1]}$, obtain the coupled two-slice surface Green's function element
$g_{aa}^{[2]} = \left(I - g_{aa}^{[1]} V_{ab} g_{bb}^{[1]} V_{ba}\right)^{-1} g_{aa}^{[1]}$,
where $V_{ab}$ is the coupling matrix from slice $a$ to adjacent slice $b$, $V_{ba}=V_{ab}^{\dagger}$, and $I$ is the identity of slice-dimension.

Extend the doubling procedure recursively: after computing $g^{[2]}$ for a two-slice section, glue two equivalent sections and re-apply Dyson's equation between the appropriate boundary slices to form $g^{[3]}$, then repeat doubling ($g^{[4]}$, $g^{[5]}$, ...) until convergence. Convergence is monitored by the elementwise difference matrix norm $|g^{[n]}-g^{[n-1]}|$ and checking every element is below a small tolerance $\delta$ (for example, $\delta=10^{-8}$ as used in the implementation). When converged, declare the resulting $g_{aa}^{[n]}$ and its partner as the left/right lead surface Green's functions $g_{L}^r$ and $g_{R}^r$, respectively. 4,11,25

Define the lead self-energy matrices for the coupling of the semi-infinite left and right leads to the device: $\Sigma_L^r = V_L^\dagger g_L^r V_L$ and $\Sigma_R^r = V_R g_R^r V_R^\dagger$, where $V_{L}$ ($V_R$) is the coupling matrix between the device edge slice and the first lead slice on the left (right), and $g_{L}^r$ ($g_R^r$) is the corresponding converged lead surface Green's function computed in the doubling procedure; define the linewidth (broadening) matrices by $\Gamma_{L/R} = i\left(\Sigma_{L/R}^r - \Sigma_{L/R}^a\right)$ with $\Sigma^a=(\Sigma^r)^\dagger$.

Avoid full inversion of the entire device Hamiltonian by performing left and right recursive sweeps that attach device slices progressively to the respective leads: define $g_n\equiv (EI-H_n)^{-1}$ as the isolated Green's function of the $n$th device slice (with slice Hamiltonian $H_n$) and $G_{nn}^{L}$ as the Green's function of the block consisting of the left lead plus device slices up to $n$ (the "left-augmented" surface Green's function for slice $n$). Using Dyson's equation and sandwiching between slice states yields the left-sweep recurrence
$G_{nn}^{L} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}\right)^{-1}$,
where $V_{n,n-1}$ is the coupling from slice $n$ to slice $n-1$ and $G_{n-1,n-1}^{L}$ is assumed known from the previous leftward step. This recurrence is initialized with $G_{00}^{L}=g_{\text{left-surface}}$ obtained from the lead-surface doubling.

Analogously define $G_{nn}^{R}$ as the Green's function of the block consisting of the right lead plus device slices up to $n$ approached from the right, and perform the right-sweep recurrence
$G_{nn}^{R} = \left(EI - H_n - V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n+1,n}\right)^{-1}$,
where $V_{n,n+1}$ is the coupling from slice $n$ to slice $n+1$ and $G_{n+1,n+1}^{R}$ is known from the previous rightward step; initialize the right sweep with the converged right lead surface Green's function $G_{m+1,m+1}^{R}=g_{\text{right-surface}}$.

Assemble the full retarded Green's function of a target device slice $n$ after completing left and right sweeps up to the neighbors $(n-1)$ and $(n+1)$: define the left and right embedding self-energies for slice $n$ as
$\Sigma^{L}=V_{n-1,n}^{\dagger} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L} V_{n-1,n}$ and
$\Sigma^{R}=V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R} V_{n,n+1}^{\dagger}$.
Then the central (device-slice) retarded Green's function is
$G_{nn}=\left[(E+i\eta)I - H_n - \Sigma^{L} - \Sigma^{R}\right]^{-1}$,
which follows from Dyson's equation when treating the two embedding blocks as perturbations to the isolated slice.

Compute device-level transport observables from the assembled block Green's functions: define the system transmission at energy $E$ by $T(E)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(G^a \Gamma_L G^r \Gamma_R\right)$ where $G^{r/a}$ are the full system retarded/advanced Green's functions and $\Gamma_{L/R}$ were defined earlier; the two-terminal conductance at low temperature is obtained via Landauer formula $G=(2e^2/h)T(E_F)$ at Fermi energy $E_F$. All matrix traces are taken in the device Hilbert-space basis of lattice sites.

Obtain lesser Green's functions recursively to compute nonequilibrium local currents: define the Fermi-Dirac distributions $f_L(E)$ and $f_R(E)$ for the left and right leads respectively. Compute the lead-surface lesser Green's functions from the surface retarded/advanced components and occupations via
$G_{00}^{L,<} = -f_L \left[G_{00}^{L} - \left(G_{00}^{L}\right)^{\dagger}\right]$ and
$G_{m+1,m+1}^{R,<} = -f_R \left[G_{m+1,m+1}^{R} - \left(G_{m+1,m+1}^{R}\right)^{\dagger}\right]$,
where $G_{00}^{L}$ and $G_{m+1,m+1}^{R}$ are the converged surface Green's functions computed in the left/right sweep procedures.

Propagate lesser self-energies inward by recursion: define the lesser self-energy for slice $n$ induced by the left lead as $\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<}=V_{n,n-1} G_{n-1,n-1}^{L,<} V_{n-1,n}$ and similarly for the right lead $\Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}=V_{n,n+1} G_{n+1,n+1}^{R,<} V_{n+1,n}$, where $G_{n-1,n-1}^{L,<}$ and $G_{n+1,n+1}^{R,<}$ are the lesser Green's functions of the left/right augmented blocks obtained by the left/right sweeps; then obtain each block lesser Green's function on the sweep via
$G_{nn}^{L,<}=G_{nn}^{L}\,\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<}\,\left(G_{nn}^{L}\right)^{\dagger}$ and
$G_{nn}^{R,<}=G_{nn}^{R}\,\Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}\,\left(G_{nn}^{R}\right)^{\dagger}$,
treating the left- and right-augmented blocks separately until they meet at a chosen central slice $n$.

Combine retarded and lesser ingredients to obtain the device lesser Green's function for arbitrary matrix indices $m,n$ across the central slice $n$: compute
$G_{mn}^{<} = G_{nn}\left(\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<} + \Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}\right)G_{nn}^{\dagger}$,
where $G_{nn}$ is the retarded Green's function of the central slice assembled in the left/right sweep step and $\Sigma_{nn}^{L,<},\Sigma_{nn}^{R,<}$ are the lesser self-energies propagated inwards.

Express the local bond-current between two lattice sites $i$ and $j$ (which may be intra-slice or inter-slice) directly in matrix notation suitable for block-sliced computation: define the scalar prefactor $i_{0}=2e/h$ (numerically $i_{0}\approx 7.748092\ \mathrm{A}/\mathrm{eV}$). The bond-current from site $i$ to site $j$ is
$I_{ij} = i_{0} \int 2\Re\!\left(t_{ij}^{*} G_{ij}^{<}(E)\right) dE$,
where $t_{ij}$ is the hopping matrix element between sites $i$ and $j$ and $G_{ij}^{<}(E)$ the corresponding lesser Green's function element; for slice-wise matrix implementation rewrite intra-slice currents as
$I_{(n,i)\rightarrow(n,j)} = i_{0} \int 2\Re\!\left[H_{n}^{*} * G_{nn}^{<}\right]_{ij}\, dE$,
where $H_n$ is the intra-slice Hamiltonian matrix and the Hadamard product is $(A*B)_{ij}=A_{ij}B_{ij}$, and analogous expressions apply to inter-slice currents using the coupling matrices $V_{n,n\pm1}$.

Provide the low-temperature, low-bias differential conductance density per bond from the lesser Green's function integrand by viewing the integrand as constant in the linear-response limit: define the conductance density for intra-slice bond $(n,i)\rightarrow(n,j)$ as
$\sigma_{(n,i)\rightarrow(n,j)} \;=\; \frac{\partial I}{\partial V} \;=\; \frac{2e^{2}}{h}\left[2\Re\!\left(H_{n}^{*} * G_{mn}^{<}\right)_{ij}\right]$,
which follows by taking $i_{0}=2e/h$ and evaluating the integrand at the Fermi energy under linear-response assumptions.

Summarize the algorithmic assembly into an implementable recipe: (i) discretize device into slices and form $H_n$ and $V_{n,n\pm1}$; (ii) compute isolated-slice Green's functions $g_n$ and lead-surface Green's functions $g_{L}^r,g_{R}^r$ via iterative doubling until convergence; (iii) perform left and right sweeps using the recurrences for $G_{nn}^{L}$ and $G_{nn}^{R}$ to obtain embedding self-energies; (iv) compute central retarded $G_{nn}$ and full retarded/advanced $G^{r/a}$ as needed for transmission; (v) compute surface lesser $G_{00}^{L,<},G_{m+1,m+1}^{R,<}$ and sweep inward lesser self-energies $\Sigma^{L,<},\Sigma^{R,<}$ to obtain $G_{mn}^{<}$; (vi) evaluate bond-currents via $I_{ij}=i_{0}\int 2\Re(t_{ij}^{*} G_{ij}^{<})\,dE$ or conductance densities via the linear-response expression above. This completes the self-contained, slice-wise recursive matrix algorithm for two-terminal NEGF and bond-current evaluation.

motivating_questions.content: In the context of tight-binding two-terminal transport calculations, practitioners needed an implementable, slice-based recursion that resolves two intertwined numerical issues: (1) how to replace inversion of an infinite lead-plus-device Hamiltonian by a convergent surface-lead recursion that yields finite-dimensional surface Green's functions, and (2) how to avoid full-device inversion for large center regions by computing slice-resolved retarded and lesser Green's functions via left/right sweeps and local Dyson relations. Prior literature supplied transmission formulas and some lesser/retarded expressions but lacked a unified, matrix-level, stepwise recursive recipe implementing surface doubling, left/right sweep recursions, explicit self-energy assembly, and a concrete procedure to obtain slice-to-slice lesser Green's functions required to compute intra-slice and inter-slice bond-currents. Without an explicit algorithm, reproducible computation of spatially resolved bond-current maps and efficient coding for larger device geometries was difficult.

$\Sigma_{1;1}^{R B}=t_{1;0} F_-^{-1}$,
where $F_-=U_- \Lambda_z^{-1} U_-^{-1}$, $U_-$ contains the left-traveling bulk-mode eigenvectors in the local orbital basis, and $\Lambda_z$ is the diagonal propagation matrix with elements $e^{i k_{z}\Delta}$ for the lead Bloch modes. The corresponding lesser/greater boundary self-energies follow from the contact broadening $\Gamma^{B}$ and the contact Fermi distribution $f_{\mu}$ via $\Sigma^{<B}=i f_\mu \Gamma^{B}$ and $\Sigma^{>B}=-i(1-f_\mu)\Gamma^{B}$ with $\Gamma^{B}=i(\Sigma^{RB}-\Sigma^{RB\dagger})$.

premises.content: For a multiband nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian with a diatomic basis in the planar-orbital representation, the retarded boundary self-energy of a semi-infinite bulk lead is derived step by step from the transfer-matrix formulation of the Schrödinger equation. The derivation (Appendix B) yields the expression $\Sigma_{1;1}^{RB}(k,E) = t_{1;0}(k) [U_-(k,E) \Lambda_z^{-1}(k,E) U_-^{-1}(k,E)]^{-1}$, where $U_-$ contains the left-traveling (or decaying) bulk Bloch eigenvectors in the orbital basis, $\Lambda_z = \operatorname{diag}(e^{ik_z^{1}\Delta}, \ldots, e^{ik_z^{N_b/2}\Delta})$ is the propagation matrix, and $t_{1;0}$ is the device-to-lead interlayer coupling. The lesser and greater boundary self-energies are then obtained from the broadening function $\Gamma^B$ and the contact Fermi distribution via $\Sigma^{<B}=i f_\mu \Gamma^B$ and $\Sigma^{>B}=-i(1-f_\mu)\Gamma^B$ (Eqs. (25)–(27)). No additional approximations beyond the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model are introduced.

premises.content:
A steady-state microscopic transport theory for illuminated bipolar quantum well heterostructures is formulated by combining a multiband tight-binding (planar orbital) Hamiltonian with the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism and self-consistent electrostatics. The total Hamiltonian is written as $\hat{H}=\hat{H}_0+\hat{H}_i$ with $\hat{H}_0$ containing the single-particle tight-binding kinetic terms, on-site energies, interlayer couplings, and the Hartree potential $U(z)$ from Poisson's equation, and $\hat{H}_i=\hat{H}_{ep}+\hat{H}_{e\gamma}$ containing carrier–phonon and carrier–photon interactions. The steady-state Green's functions satisfy Dyson and Keldysh equations
      $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)=\{[G_0^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)]^{-1}-\Sigma^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)-\Sigma^{RB}(\mathbf{k},E)\}^{-1}$,
      $G^{\lessgtr}(\mathbf{k},E)=G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)[\Sigma^{\lessgtr}(\mathbf{k},E)+\Sigma^{\lessgtr B}(\mathbf{k},E)]G^{A}(\mathbf{k},E)$,
      with $G_0^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)=[(E+i\eta)\mathbb{1}-H_0(\mathbf{k})]^{-1}$, and the Hartree potential obtained from Poisson's equation $\epsilon_0 \frac{d}{dz}[\epsilon(z)\frac{d}{dz}U(z)]=n(z)-p(z)-N_{dop}(z)$. This formulation defines electron and hole densities via $G^{\lessgtr}$ and provides expressions for LDOS, layer currents, and absorption within the same microscopic framework.

motivating_questions.content: In open quantum-device calculations the coupling to semi-infinite crystalline contacts sets injection and escape boundary conditions and determines contact-induced broadening. Prior simple implementations used either single-band boundary conditions or numerical matching without an explicit multiband tight-binding construction. For realistic multiband tight-binding descriptions (planar orbital basis) of layered heterostructures, an explicit formula for the retarded and correlation boundary self-energies in terms of the lead bulk modes is required to properly match device orbitals to left- and right-traveling Bloch states, to obtain physically correct level broadening and contact-injection spectra, and to allow numerically stable inclusion of contacts in the NEGF equations. Without these boundary self-energies, computed LDOS, escape lifetimes, and current spectra would not correctly reflect the influence of bulk contacts in multiband heterostructures.

The non-interacting nearest-neighbor tight-binding model with on-site potential $\epsilon_i=0$ and nearest-neighbor hopping integral $t$ (taken as the energy unit), described by the Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}=\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{i}-t\sum_{\langle i,jangle}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{j}$, yields metallic behavior for both pure $
u_{1/5}$ (also denoted $\chi_3$) and $
u_{1/6}$ (also denoted $ eta_{12}$) borophene nanoribbons (BNRs). Here $
u_{1/5}$ and $
u_{1/6}$ are boron sheet polymorphs composed, respectively, of $(2,2)$ chains (two atoms in the narrow row and two in the wide row) and $(2,3)$ chains (two atoms in the narrow row and three in the wide row). For $
u_{1/5}$ BNRs, the transmission spectrum exhibits multiple conductance plateaus quantized at integer multiples of the conductance quantum $G_{0}=2e^{2}/h$. For $
u_{1/6}$ BNRs, the conductance is metallic but with reduced magnitude and shows oscillatory (non-plateau) structure, attributed to scattering at the interfaces between the central scattering region (comprising the $
u_{1/6}$ ribbon) and the semi-infinite $
u_{1/5}$ lead ribbons.
