steps.reasoning: Define the non-interacting nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian used for all transport calculations as $\mathcal{H}=\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{i}-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{j}$, where $a_{i}^{\dagger}$ ($a_{i}$) creates (annihilates) an electron at site $i$, $\epsilon_{i}$ is the on-site potential energy at site $i$, $t$ is the nearest-neighbor hopping integral and $\langle i,j\rangle$ denotes nearest-neighbor pairs; in numerical work the authors set $\epsilon_{i}=0$ and $t=1$ (energy unit).

State the Landauer–Büttiker expression for two-terminal conductance used to compute transmission spectra as $G = G_{0}\operatorname{Tr}[\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{L}}\mathbf{G}^{r}\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{G}^{a}]$, where the conductance quantum is $G_{0}=2e^{2}/h$, the retarded Green's function is $\mathbf{G}^{r}(E) = [E\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{c}}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}}^{r}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{R}}^{r}]^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{c}}$ the central scattering region (CSR) Hamiltonian and $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{R}}^{r}$ the retarded self-energies due to the left/right semi-infinite leads, and the linewidth functions are $\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{R}} = i(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{R}}^{r}-\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{L}/\mathrm{R}}^{a})$.

Specify the numerical setup used to obtain the pure-boron-nanoribbon results: the authors consider semi-infinite $
u_{1/5}$ BNR leads coupled to a CSR that is either a pure $
u_{1/5}$ BNR (all (2,2) chains) or a pure $
u_{1/6}$ BNR (all (2,3) chains), and compute the energy-dependent conductance $G(E)$ using the Hamiltonian and Landauer formula above; parameters are $\epsilon_{i}=0$ and $t=1$ as energy unit.

Report the computed conductance behavior of the pure $
u_{1/5}$ BNR: the transmission spectrum for the pure $
u_{1/5}$ BNR exhibits multiple conductance plateaus quantized at integer multiples of $G_{0}$, which the authors attribute to translational symmetry of the $
u_{1/5}$ lattice leading to quantized channel contributions across energy ranges; this feature is shown by the computed $G(E)$ curve for the pure $
u_{1/5}$ CSR. 
Fig. 1(b)

Report the computed conductance behavior of the pure $
u_{1/6}$ BNR: the computed $G(E)$ for the pure $
u_{1/6}$ CSR also indicates metallic behavior (nonzero conductance at energies near the Fermi level), but the conductance magnitude is reduced relative to the $
u_{1/5}$ case and the spectrum shows pronounced oscillatory, non-plateau structure rather than quantized plateaus; the authors attribute this to scattering induced by the (2,3)-chain geometry at the CSR–lead interfaces which breaks the translational symmetry responsible for plateaus.
Fig. 1(c)

Cite experimental agreement and summarize the combined conclusion: the authors note that both $
u_{1/5}$ and $
u_{1/6}$ BNRs exhibit metallic behavior in the absence of line defects, consistent with experimental reports, and therefore conclude that the tight-binding Hamiltonian and transport calculation described yield metallic behavior for both pure $
u_{1/5}$ and pure $
u_{1/6}$ BNRs, with (i) $
u_{1/5}$ showing conductance plateaus at integer multiples of $G_{0}$ and (ii) $
u_{1/6}$ showing reduced, oscillatory conductance due to (2,3)-chain-induced scattering at interfaces.
[21–23,50,58]
Fig. 1(b); Fig. 1(c)

motivating_questions.content: In the study of borophene electronic transport it was necessary to establish baseline transport behavior of ideal, translationally invariant BNRs before introducing LD disorder. Previous experimental reports and some calculations indicated metallic bands in borophene polymorphs, but transport signatures (quantized plateaus versus oscillatory transmission) depend sensitively on chain arrangement and interface scattering. Without confirming how the simple tight-binding model reproduces metallic transport for the two prototypical polymorphs, one cannot attribute subsequent changes uniquely to LD-induced disorder or to intrinsic band-structure differences between $\nu_{1/5}$ and $\nu_{1/6}$ geometries.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
The tight-binding non-equilibrium Green's-function framework is extended to produce mode-resolved transmission amplitudes $t_{j\alpha,l\beta}$, reflection amplitudes $r_{j\beta,l\beta}$, and the full scattering-state matrix $\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)$ for an incident Bloch mode $l$ in lead $\beta$ in a general multi-terminal scattering geometry even when a lead's primitive-cell inter-cell hopping matrix $H_1$ is non-invertible because the primitive cell contains multiple sub-layers. The extension proceeds by (a) partitioning a primitive cell into $n$ layers with invertible intra-layer and nearest-layer hopping blocks $h_{ij}$, constructing layerwise transition matrices $t_i$ and a cell transition matrix $T_i$ whose eigenvalues yield $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$ and eigenvectors yield the layer-resolved Bloch functions $\phi_i^{(m)}$ [Eqs.$\;(7)$--$(12)$], (b) computing lead surface Green's functions $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}$ from the left- and right-going Bloch-mode bases via Eqs.$\;(13)$--$(14)$, and (c) relating the system Green's function $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$ to mode-resolved amplitudes by the identities
$$
t_{\alpha,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{L\alpha}}\;\chi_{L i\alpha}^{\,z'-z}\;\Phi_{L i\alpha}^{-1}\;G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\;V_{i'\beta}\;\Phi_{L i'\beta}\;\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
$$
r_{\beta,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{R\beta}}\;\Phi_{R i\beta}^{-1}\left(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z,i)-V_{i\beta}^{-1}\right)V_{i\beta}\Phi_{L i\beta}\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
and
$$
\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)=G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\,V_{i'\beta}\,\Phi_{L i'\beta},
$$
where $v_{L/R}$ are diagonal velocity matrices (evanescent-mode entries set to zero), $\Phi_{L/R,i}$ are matrices of left/right Bloch-layer eigenvectors, $\chi_{L/R}$ are diagonal matrices of $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$, and $V_i$ are layer-dependent coupling matrices defined in Eqs.$\;(13)$--$(14)$. These relations yield mode-to-mode transmission and reflection coefficients $T_{\alpha j,\beta l}=|t_{\alpha j,\beta l}|^2$ and $R_{\beta j,\beta l}=|r_{\beta j,\beta l}|^2$ and provide scattering wavefunctions and current densities in real space for each incident mode.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Extension of mode-resolved Green's-function formalism to multi-terminal leads with multi-layer primitive cells

conclusion.content:
The tight-binding non-equilibrium Green's-function framework is extended to produce mode-resolved transmission amplitudes $t_{j\alpha,l\beta}$, reflection amplitudes $r_{j\beta,l\beta}$, and the full scattering-state matrix $\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)$ for an incident Bloch mode $l$ in lead $\beta$ in a general multi-terminal scattering geometry even when a lead's primitive-cell inter-cell hopping matrix $H_1$ is non-invertible because the primitive cell contains multiple sub-layers ($H_1$ is the hopping matrix between adjacent primitive cells). The extension proceeds by (a) partitioning a primitive cell into $n$ layers with invertible intra-layer Hamiltonians $h_{ii}$ and nearest-layer hopping Hamiltonians $h_{i,i+1}$, constructing layerwise transition matrices $t_i = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & I \\ -h_{i,i+1}^{-1} h_{i-1,i}^\dagger & -h_{i,i+1}^{-1}(h_{ii} - E) \end{bmatrix}$ and a cell transition matrix $T_i = t_{i-1}\cdots t_1 t_n \cdots t_i$; the eigenvalue equation $T_i [\phi_{i-1}(z); \phi_i(z)]^\mathrm{T} = e^{\mathrm{i}k} [\phi_{i-1}(z); \phi_i(z)]^\mathrm{T}$ yields Bloch wavevectors $k$ and layer-resolved Bloch functions $\phi_i^{(m)}$ (the $\phi_i$ are the eigenvectors), (b) computing the lead surface Green's function $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}$ from the left- and right-going Bloch-mode bases via $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r} = (1 - \Phi_{R n} \chi_R^{-1} \Phi_{R1}^{-1} \Phi_{L1} \chi_L \Phi_{Ln}^{-1}) / V_n$ for truncation at the first layer and $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r} = (1 - \Phi_{R,i-1} \Phi_{Ri}^{-1} \Phi_{Li} \Phi_{L,i-1}^{-1}) / V_{i-1}$ for truncation at the $i$-th layer ($i=2\cdots n$), where the coupling matrices $V_i$ are $V_1 = h_{n1}^\dagger (\Phi_{Ln} \chi_L^{-1} \Phi_{L1}^{-1} - \Phi_{Rn} \chi_R^{-1} \Phi_{R1}^{-1})$ and $V_i = h_{i-1,i}^\dagger (\Phi_{L,i-1} \Phi_{Li}^{-1} - \Phi_{R,i-1} \Phi_{Ri}^{-1})$ for $i=2\cdots n$, and (c) relating the system Green's function $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$ to mode-resolved amplitudes by the identities
      $$
      t_{\alpha,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{L\alpha}}\;\chi_{L i\alpha}^{\,z'-z}\;\Phi_{L i\alpha}^{-1}\;G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\;V_{i'\beta}\;\Phi_{L i'\beta}\;\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
      $$
      $$
      r_{\beta,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{R\beta}}\;\Phi_{R i\beta}^{-1}\left(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z,i)-V_{i\beta}^{-1}\right)V_{i\beta}\Phi_{L i\beta}\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
      $$
      and
      $$
      \Psi_{\beta}(z,i)=G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\,V_{i'\beta}\,\Phi_{L i'\beta},
      $$
      where $v_{L/R}$ are diagonal velocity matrices (evanescent-mode entries set to zero), $\Phi_{L/R,i}$ are matrices of left/right Bloch-layer eigenvectors, $\chi_{L/R}$ are diagonal matrices of $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$, and $V_i$ are the coupling matrices defined above. These relations yield mode-to-mode transmission and reflection coefficients $T_{\alpha j,\beta l}=|t_{\alpha j,\beta l}|^2$ and $R_{\beta j,\beta l}=|r_{\beta j,\beta l}|^2$ and provide scattering wavefunctions and current densities in real space for each incident mode.

No load-bearing weak points were identified because the derivation is self-contained and the assumptions (existence of a layer partition with invertible inter-layer hoppings) are explicit conditions rather than uncertain bridges. The conclusion's credibility is high: the method is valid whenever the lead satisfies the partitioning condition, which holds for all leads used in this paper (graphene nanoribbons with multi-layer primitive cells). premises.content: For a generic multi-terminal scattering device whose leads have primitive cells composed of multiple atomic layers (such that the inter-cell hopping matrix H_1 is non-invertible as a single block), the paper constructs a layerwise transition matrix formalism: each primitive cell is partitioned into n layers with invertible intra-layer and nearest-layer hopping matrices h_{ii} and h_{i,i+1}. From these, transition matrices t_i are defined for each layer boundary (Eq.7) and composed into a cell transition matrix T_i (Eq.9-10) whose eigenvalues are e^{ik} and eigenvectors give the layer-resolved Bloch wavefunctions φ_i^{(m)}. This construction is mathematically derived from the tight-binding Schrödinger equation (Eq.3-5) without additional approximations, and the eigenvalue problem is solved numerically to obtain all Bloch modes (propagating and evanescent). Subsequently, the surface Green's function formulas (Eq.13-14) and the transmission/reflection/scattering-state formulas (Eq.17-19) are derived in closed form from the mode bases and the system Green's function.
premises.metadata: {"role": "highlight", "conclusion_id": "1", "strength_types": ["formal", "model"], "credit": "This derivation provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for the entire subsequent transport analysis. Without this formal extension, the standard Sanvito-Lambert method would be inapplicable to leads with multi-layer primitive cells (such as those used for the armchair and zigzag graphene nanoribbons in this paper), and the mode-resolved transmission/reflection matrices and scattering wavefunctions could not be computed. The self-contained algebraic construction (transition matrices \u2192 Bloch modes \u2192 surface Green's function \u2192 mode amplitudes) is a substantive formal achievement that underwrites all eight conclusions of the paper by enabling the numerical calculations that support them. The derivation's rigor means that the method is provably correct under the stated layer-invertibility assumptions, making the methodology a reliable tool for the subsequent physics conclusions."}
premises.title: Formal derivation of layerwise Bloch solution

steps.reasoning: Begin from the tight-binding Hamiltonian of the multi-terminal scattering device, where the Hamiltonian operator $H$ is expressed as $H = \sum_{i} \epsilon_{i} a_{i}^{\dagger} a_{i} + \sum_{i,j} t_{ij} a_{i}^{\dagger} a_{j}$. Here $a_{i}$ ($a_{i}^{\dagger}$) is the annihilation (creation) operator on site $i$, $\epsilon_i$ are on-site energies, and $t_{ij}$ are hopping matrix elements between sites $i$ and $j$. This provides the tight-binding basis for all subsequent derivations. [43]

Represent a lead as a periodic chain of primitive cells indexed by integer coordinate $z$ so that the lead Hamiltonian in block form (blocks labeled by cell index) leads to the discrete Schrödinger equation for cell wavefunctions $\phi(z)$:
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\ddots & & & \\
& H_1^\dagger & H_0 - E & H_1 & \\
& & H_1^\dagger & H_0 - E & H_1 \\
& & & & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\vdots\\
\phi(z)\\
\phi(z+1)\\
\vdots
\end{bmatrix}=0,
$$
where $H_0$ is the intra-cell Hamiltonian of a primitive cell, $H_1$ is the inter-cell hopping matrix between adjacent primitive cells, $E$ is the eigenenergy, and $\phi(z)$ denotes the column vector of amplitudes within cell $z$. Define the Bloch form $\phi(z)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kz}\phi$ to reduce the problem to an eigenproblem for $k$ and intra-cell amplitudes $\phi$. Fig. 1(b)

Address the case where the primitive cell contains multiple sub-layers so that the inter-cell hopping matrix $H_1$ may be non-invertible. Partition each primitive cell into $n$ internal layers and denote the intra-layer and nearest-layer hopping blocks by $h_{ij}$ (with $h_{ii}$ the Hamiltonian of the $i$-th layer and $h_{i,i+1}$ the hopping between layer $i$ and $i+1$). The cell-level matrices then take the block forms
$$
H_0=\begin{bmatrix}
h_{11} & h_{12} & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & & & & \vdots\\
\cdots & h_{i-1,i}^\dagger & h_{ii} & h_{i,i+1} & \cdots\\
\vdots & & & & \vdots\\
0 & \cdots & 0 & h_{n-1,n}^\dagger & h_{nn}
\end{bmatrix},
$$
$$
H_1=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
h_{n1} & \cdots & 0
\end{bmatrix},
$$
and the intra-cell wavefunction is $\phi(z)=[\phi_1(z),\ldots,\phi_n(z)]^\mathrm{T}$, where all $h_{ij}$ connecting adjacent layers are assumed invertible even if $H_1$ as a whole is not. This explicit layer partition makes it possible to avoid requiring $H_1$ invertible. Fig. 1(b)

Substitute the layer-partitioned matrices and the Bloch ansatz $\phi(z)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kz}\phi$ into the Schrödinger equation to obtain a block matrix eigen-equation for the intra-cell layer amplitudes:
$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}
h_{11}-E & h_{12} & 0 & \cdots & \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}k} h_{n1}^\dagger\\
\vdots & & & & \vdots\\
\cdots & h_{i-1,i}^\dagger & h_{ii}-E & h_{i,i+1} & \cdots\\
\vdots & & & & \vdots\\
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k} h_{n1} & \cdots & 0 & h_{n-1,n}^\dagger & h_{nn}-E
\end{array}\right]
\begin{bmatrix}
\phi_1\\
\vdots\\
\phi_i\\
\vdots\\
\phi_n
\end{bmatrix}=0.
$$
Form the characteristic (determinant) equation in the complex variable $x=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$, which is a rational polynomial in $x$ with highest order $N$ and lowest order $-N$, yielding $2N$ roots in total (counting multiplicity), where $N$ is the number of atomic orbitals per layer (dimension of each block). The hermiticity of the Hamiltonian implies complex-conjugate pairing of $k$ roots. This establishes the full set of leftgoing and rightgoing (including evanescent) modes for a given energy $E$.

Construct layerwise $2N\times 2N$ transition matrices $t_i$ (one for each layer index $i$) that map between adjacent layer-amplitude pairs. Define
$$
t_i=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1\\[4pt]
-h_{i,i+1}^{-1} h_{i-1,i}^\dagger & -h_{i,i+1}^{-1}(h_{ii}-E)
\end{bmatrix},
$$
with the convention that indices are cyclic within a primitive cell. These transition matrices satisfy the relations that connect pairs of neighboring layer amplitudes:
$$
t_1\begin{bmatrix}\phi_n(z-1)\\\phi_1(z)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_1(z)\\\phi_2(z)\end{bmatrix},\quad
t_i\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{i-1}(z)\\\phi_i(z)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_i(z)\\\phi_{i+1}(z)\end{bmatrix},\quad
t_n\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{n-1}(z)\\\phi_n(z)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_n(z)\\\phi_1(z+1)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
Each $t_i$ is therefore constructed from invertible nearest-layer blocks $h_{i,i+1}$ and $h_{i-1,i}^\dagger$, avoiding the need to invert the whole $H_1$.

Form the cell transition matrix $T_i$ as the ordered product of layer transition matrices,
$$
T_i=t_{i-1}\cdots t_1 t_n\cdots t_i,
$$
so that $T_i$ maps the pair $\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{i-1}(z)\\\phi_i(z)\end{bmatrix}$ to the pair one cell forward $\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{i-1}(z+1)\\\phi_i(z+1)\end{bmatrix}$. This yields the eigenvalue equation
$$
T_i\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{i-1}(z)\\\phi_i(z)\end{bmatrix}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}\begin{bmatrix}\phi_{i-1}(z)\\\phi_i(z)\end{bmatrix},
$$
so that eigenvalues of $T_i$ are $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$ and eigenvectors give the layer-resolved Bloch functions. This provides a numerically stable route to all Bloch factors $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$ and eigenvectors even when $H_1$ is non-invertible.

Partition the set of $2N$ eigenpairs of $T_i$ into leftgoing and rightgoing classes. Collect the eigenvectors corresponding to leftgoing modes into block columns $\Phi_{L,i-1}$ and $\Phi_{L,i}$ and those corresponding to rightgoing modes into $\Phi_{R,i-1}$ and $\Phi_{R,i}$. Collect the corresponding diagonal matrices of eigenvalues $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$ into $\chi_L$ and $\chi_R$, arranged by ascending modulus $|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}|$. Then $T_i$ satisfies:
$$
T_i\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{L,i-1} & \Phi_{R,i-1}\\ \Phi_{L,i} & \Phi_{R,i}\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{L,i-1} & \Phi_{R,i-1}\\ \Phi_{L,i} & \Phi_{R,i}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\chi_L & 0\\ 0 & \chi_R\end{bmatrix},
$$
with definitions
$$
\chi_L=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_1},\ldots,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_N}),\quad
\chi_R=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\bar{k}_1},\ldots,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\bar{k}_N}),
$$
$$
\Phi_{L,i}=[\phi^{(1)}_i,\ldots,\phi^{(N)}_i],\quad
\Phi_{R,i}=[\bar{\phi}^{(1)}_i,\ldots,\bar{\phi}^{(N)}_i].
$$
Here $\phi^{(m)}_i$ denotes the layer-$i$ component of the $m$-th leftgoing Bloch eigenvector, and $\bar{\phi}^{(m)}_i$ denotes the layer-$i$ component of the corresponding rightgoing eigenvector.

Define layer-dependent coupling matrices $V_i$ that appear in surface Green's functions, choosing for $i=1$:
$$
V_1=h_{n1}^\dagger\left(\Phi_{L n}\chi_L^{-1}\Phi_{L1}^{-1}-\Phi_{R n}\chi_R^{-1}\Phi_{R1}^{-1}\right),
$$
and for $i=2,\ldots,n$:
$$
V_i=h_{i-1,i}^\dagger\left(\Phi_{L,i-1}\Phi_{L i}^{-1}-\Phi_{R,i-1}\Phi_{R i}^{-1}\right).
$$
These $V_i$ are constructed from the layer-projected Bloch eigenvector matrices and encode the effective coupling at the truncated lead surface for each choice of truncation layer $i$. The $V_i$ appear naturally when expressing surface Green's functions in terms of Bloch bases.

Express the retarded surface Green's function $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}$ of a semi-infinite lead truncated at layer index $i$ in terms of the left- and right-going Bloch-mode bases and $V_i$. For truncation at layer $i=1$ (first layer of cell 0) the surface Green's function is
$$
G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}=\left(1-\Phi_{R n}\chi_R^{-1}\Phi_{R1}^{-1}\Phi_{L1}\chi_L\Phi_{L n}^{-1}\right)/V_n,
$$
and for truncation at layer $i=2,\ldots,n$:
$$
G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}=\left(1-\Phi_{R,i-1}\Phi_{R i}^{-1}\Phi_{L i}\Phi_{L,i-1}^{-1}\right)/V_{i-1}.
$$
These expressions yield the surface Green's function directly from the Bloch-mode eigenvectors and eigenvalues computed from the transition matrices, thereby avoiding any inversion of a non-invertible $H_1$. [45]

Relate the full system retarded Green's function $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$, defined by $(E-H)G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')=\delta_{zz'}\delta_{ii'}\mathbf{1}$ (where $(z,i)$ denotes layer $i$ of cell $z$), to scattering states produced by an incident Bloch mode $l$ in lead $\beta$. Use the scattering-state ansatz for an incident Bloch wave $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{l\beta} z}\phi^{(l\beta)}$ so that the scattering state $\psi^{(l\beta)}(z,i)$ takes the form of outgoing (transmitted) and reflected Bloch-mode superpositions normalized by mode velocities. Then express $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')$ in terms of mode-basis matrices and the unknown transmission matrix $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ and reflection matrix $r_{\beta,\beta}$, obtaining the blockwise representation (for appropriate relations between $z$ and $z'$ and lead indices) that contains terms proportional to $\Phi_{L i\alpha}\chi_{L\alpha}^{z-z'}\sqrt{v_{L\alpha}}^{-1} t_{\alpha,\beta}\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}\,\Phi_{L i'\beta}^{-1}V_{i'\beta}^{-1}$ and analogous reflection-sector terms. In these expressions define velocity matrices $v_{L}$ and $v_{R}$ as diagonal matrices whose diagonal entries are group velocities $v_{k_l}$ of the transporting modes (evanescent-mode entries set to zero); the group velocity for mode with Bloch factor $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_l}$ can be evaluated as
$$
v_{k_l}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar}\langle\phi_l|H_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_l}-H_1^\dagger \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}k_l}|\phi_l\rangle.
$$
This step treats the scattering-state expansion and the Green's-function definition together to place $t$ and $r$ inside $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$.

Solve algebraically for the transmission amplitude matrix $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ by evaluating the system Green's function at field coordinate $z$ located in lead $\alpha$ (with source coordinate $z'$ in lead $\beta$). The inversion of the pre-factors in the $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$ expansion yields:
$$
t_{\alpha,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{L\alpha}}\;\chi_{L i\alpha}^{\,z'-z}\;\Phi_{L i\alpha}^{-1}\;G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\;V_{i'\beta}\;\Phi_{L i'\beta}\;\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
where $\Phi_{L i\alpha}$ and $\chi_{L i\alpha}$ are the left-going Bloch-eigenvector and eigenvalue matrices at layer $i$ in lead $\alpha$, $V_{i'\beta}$ is the coupling matrix at the source truncation layer $i'$ in lead $\beta$, and the velocity matrices remove normalization ambiguities so that $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ is the matrix of amplitudes from modes in lead $\beta$ to modes in lead $\alpha$.

Similarly obtain the reflection amplitude matrix $r_{\beta,\beta}$ by evaluating $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$ at coincident cell and layer coordinates in the incident lead ($z=z'$ and appropriate layer ordering). This yields
$$
r_{\beta,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{R\beta}}\;\Phi_{R i\beta}^{-1}\Big(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z,i)-V_{i\beta}^{-1}\Big)\;V_{i\beta}\;\Phi_{L i\beta}\;\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
where $\Phi_{R i\beta}$ is the right-going Bloch-eigenvector matrix at layer $i$ of lead $\beta$, and $V_{i\beta}$ is the layer coupling matrix at that truncation. In these formulas entries corresponding to evanescent modes should be set so that their contribution is removed (practically, evanescent-mode velocities in $v_{L/R}$ are set to zero).

Express the full scattering-state matrix $\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)$ (whose columns are the scattering wavefunctions $\psi^{(l\beta)}(z,i)$ for each incident mode $l$ in lead $\beta$) directly from the system Green's function and the left-going Bloch basis at the source truncation layer:
$$
\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)=G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\,V_{i'\beta}\,\Phi_{L i'\beta},
$$
with the matrix $\Psi_{\beta}$ collecting columns $\psi^{(l\beta)}$ for $l=1,\ldots,N_\beta$. Once $\Psi_{\beta}$ is known, compute real-space scattering-state amplitudes and current densities for each incident mode by the usual tight-binding expressions for local current (the paper states these can be solved straightforwardly from $\psi^{(l\beta)}$). Fig. 1(a)

Obtain scalar mode-to-mode transmission and reflection coefficients by taking squares of the amplitude-matrix entries: for transmission from incident mode $l$ in lead $\beta$ to outgoing mode $j$ in lead $\alpha$ define $T_{\alpha j,\beta l}=|t_{\alpha j,\beta l}|^2$, and for reflections within lead $\beta$ define $R_{\beta j,\beta l}=|r_{\beta j,\beta l}|^2$. In practical calculations, set entries corresponding to evanescent modes to zero in the velocity matrices so that only transporting modes contribute to these probabilities. These quantities allow computation of total transmission $T_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j,l}T_{\alpha j,\beta l}$ and, via the Landauer-Büttiker relation, two-terminal conductance. [44]

Summarize the extension: starting from the layer partition of primitive cells and using layerwise transition matrices $t_i$ and cell transition $T_i$ (steps above) one obtains Bloch eigenvalues $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$ and layer-resolved eigenvectors $\phi_i^{(m)}$; from these build $\Phi_{L/R,i}$, $\chi_{L/R}$ and $V_i$ (steps above) and compute surface Green's functions $G_{\mathrm{surf}}^{r}$ (step 9); insert these into the full-system Green's function $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}$ and algebraically extract mode-resolved transmission amplitudes $t_{\alpha,\beta}$, reflection amplitudes $r_{\beta,\beta}$, and the scattering-state matrix $\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)$ via the displayed matrix identities:
$$
t_{\alpha,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{L\alpha}}\;\chi_{L i\alpha}^{\,z'-z}\;\Phi_{L i\alpha}^{-1}\;G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\;V_{i'\beta}\;\Phi_{L i'\beta}\;\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
$$
r_{\beta,\beta}=\sqrt{v_{R\beta}}\;\Phi_{R i\beta}^{-1}\left(G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z,i)-V_{i\beta}^{-1}\right)V_{i\beta}\Phi_{L i\beta}\sqrt{v_{L\beta}}^{-1},
$$
$$
\Psi_{\beta}(z,i)=G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{r}(z,i;z',i')\,V_{i'\beta}\,\Phi_{L i'\beta},
$$
with $v_{L/R}$ diagonal velocity matrices (evanescent-mode entries set to zero), $\Phi_{L/R,i}$ left/right Bloch-layer eigenvector matrices, $\chi_{L/R}$ diagonal matrices of $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k}$, and $V_i$ the layer-dependent coupling matrices defined earlier. These relations produce mode-to-mode probabilities $T_{\alpha j,\beta l}=|t_{\alpha j,\beta l}|^2$ and $R_{\beta j,\beta l}=|r_{\beta j,\beta l}|^2$ and enable computation of scattering wavefunctions and local current densities in real space for each incident mode, thereby completing the claimed extension of the Green's-function formalism to multi-terminal leads with multi-layer primitive cells.

motivating_questions.content: Transport calculations that resolve scattering between individual propagating modes and provide the corresponding real-space scattering-state densities are crucial to diagnose whether and how modes mix in mesoscopic devices. The previously used Green's-function procedure (Sanvito–Lambert) required that the inter-cell hopping matrix $H_1$ be invertible, which restricts its applicability to leads whose primitive cell contains a single layer or whose $H_1$ happens to be invertible. Realistic graphene nanoribbons and other materials often have primitive cells composed of multiple atomic layers (noninvertible $H_1$ when taken as a single block), preventing direct application of the original method. Without a formalism that handles multi-layer primitive cells and returns mode-resolved $t$, $r$, and real-space scattering states, one cannot obtain the transmission/reflection matrices or spatial wavefunctions needed to test hypotheses about disorder-induced mode mixing or to identify which microscopic channels are coupled by disorder. The presented extension fills this methodological gap by rewriting the Bloch problem in layer form, computing the mode bases and surface Green's functions layerwise, and relating the full system Green's function to mode amplitudes and wavefunctions for arbitrary multi-terminal geometries.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
Closed analytic expressions are derived, within the tight-binding representation and the Keldysh nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism, for the spectral (energy-resolved) bond currents between nearest-neighbor orbitals in a two-terminal device. The bond current unit is $i_0=2e/h$. For example, for a longitudinal bond between site $0n$ (in the left lead border) and site $1n$ (first device column) the finite-temperature decomposition (case $\mu_L \lt \mu_R$) is written as
$$
I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{persist})}+I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{transp})},
$$
with
$$
I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{persist})}=i_0\int dE\, f_L(E)\;2\Re\left[\,G_{11}^R(E)\,\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}(E)-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}(E)\,G_{11}^R(E)\right]_{nn},
$$
$$
I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{transp})}=i_0\int dE\,[f_R(E)-f_L(E)]\;2\Re\left[-i\,G_{11}^R(E)\,\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{right})}(E)\,G_{11}^A(E)\,\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}(E)\right]_{nn},
$$
where $G^{R/A}$ are the retarded/advanced Green's functions of the central device projected on column indices, $\Sigma^{R/A(\mathrm{left/right})}$ are the retarded/advanced lead self-energies acting on the border columns, $\Gamma=i(\Sigma^R-\Sigma^A)$, and $f_{L,R}(E)=[\exp((E-\mu_{L,R})/k_BT)+1]^{-1}$ are the lead Fermi functions. Equivalent expressions for transverse bonds and for the reversed bias case are reported and summarized in the zero- and finite-temperature Tables (Table 1 and Table 3 in the text).
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Closed analytic NEGF expressions for energy-resolved site-to-site (bond) currents in tight-binding two-terminal devices at arbitrary temperature and bias

conclusion.content:
Closed analytic expressions are derived, within the tight-binding representation and the Keldysh nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism, for the spectral (energy-resolved) bond currents between nearest-neighbor orbitals in a two-terminal device. The bond current unit is $i_0=2e/h$. For example, for a longitudinal bond between site $0n$ (in the left lead border) and site $1n$ (first device column) the finite-temperature decomposition (case $\mu_L \lt \mu_R$) is written as
      $$
      I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{persist})}+I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{transp})},
      $$
      with
      $$
      I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{persist})}=i_0\int dE\, f_L(E)\;2\Re\left[\,G_{11}^R(E)\,\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}(E)-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}(E)\,G_{11}^R(E)\right]_{nn},
      $$
      $$
      I_{0n,1n}^{(\mathrm{transp})}=i_0\int dE\,[f_R(E)-f_L(E)]\;2\Re\left[-i\,G_{11}^R(E)\,\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{right})}(E)\,G_{11}^A(E)\,\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}(E)\right]_{nn},
      $$
      where $G^{R/A}$ are the retarded/advanced Green's functions of the central device projected on column indices, $\Sigma^{R/A(\mathrm{left/right})}$ are the retarded/advanced lead self-energies acting on the border columns, $\Gamma=i(\Sigma^R-\Sigma^A)$, and $f_{L,R}(E)=[\exp((E-\mu_{L,R})/k_BT)+1]^{-1}$ are the lead Fermi functions. The zero-temperature expressions for the four cases (longitudinal and transverse currents for both bias orderings) are:
      
      **Longitudinal current for $\mu_L < \mu_R$:** $I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(a1)}+I_{0n,1n}^{(a2)}$ with $I_{0n,1n}^{(a1)}=i_{0}\int_{0}^{\mu_{L}}dE\,2\Re\left[G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}G_{11}^{R}\right]_{nn}$ and $I_{0n,1n}^{(a2)}=i_{0}\int_{\mu_{L}}^{\mu_{R}}dE\,2\Re\left[-iG_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})}G_{11}^{A}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\text{left})}\right]_{nn}$.
      
      **Longitudinal current for $\mu_R < \mu_L$:** $I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(b1)}+I_{0n,1n}^{(b2)}$ with $I_{0n,1n}^{(b1)}=i_{0}\int_{-\infty}^{\mu_{R}}dE\,2\Re\left[G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}G_{11}^{R}\right]_{nn}$ and $I_{0n,1n}^{(b2)}=i_{0}\int_{\mu_{R}}^{\mu_{L}}dE\,2\Re\left[G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})}G_{11}^{R}+iG_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})}G_{11}^{A}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\text{left})}\right]_{nn}$.
      
      **Transverse current for $\mu_L < \mu_R$:** $I_{1n,1n+1}=I_{1n,1n+1}^{(a1)}+I_{1n,1n+1}^{(a2)}$ with $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(a1)}=i_{0}\int_{-\infty}^{\mu_{L}}dE\,2\Re\left\{t_{1n,1n+1}\left[G_{1n+1,1n}^{R}-G_{1n+1,1n}^{A}\right]\right\}$ and $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(a2)}=i_{0}\int_{\mu_{L}}^{\mu_{R}}dE\,2\Re\left\{t_{1n,1n+1}\left[-iG_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})}G_{11}^{A}\right]_{n+1,n}\right\}$.
      
      **Transverse current for $\mu_R < \mu_L$:** $I_{1n,1n+1}=I_{1n,1n+1}^{(b1)}+I_{1n,1n+1}^{(b2)}$ with $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(b1)}=i_{0}\int_{-\infty}^{\mu_{R}}dE\,2\Re\left\{t_{1n,1n+1}\left[G_{1n+1,1n}^{R}-G_{1n+1,1n}^{A}\right]\right\}$ and $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(b2)}=i_{0}\int_{\mu_{R}}^{\mu_{L}}dE\,2\Re\left\{t_{1n,1n+1}\left[-iG_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\text{left})}G_{11}^{A}\right]_{n+1,n}\right\}$.
      
      The finite-temperature expressions for the same four cases are:
      
      **Longitudinal current for $\mu_L < \mu_R$:** $I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{persist})}+I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{transp})}$ with $I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{persist})}=i_0 \int dE f_L 2\Re \left[ G_{11}^R \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} - \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} G_{11}^R \right]_{nn}$ and $I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{transp})}=i_0 \int dE (f_R - f_L) 2\Re \left[ -i G_{11}^R \Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})} G_{11}^A \Sigma_{11}^{A(\text{left})} \right]_{nn}$.
      
      **Longitudinal current for $\mu_R < \mu_L$:** $I_{0n,1n}=I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{persist})}+I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{transp})}$ with $I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{persist})}=i_0 \int dE f_R 2\Re \left[ G_{11}^R \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} - \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} G_{11}^R \right]_{nn}$ and $I_{0n,1n}^{(\text{transp})}=i_0 \int dE (f_L - f_R) 2\Re \left[ G_{11}^R \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} - \Sigma_{11}^{R(\text{left})} G_{11}^R +i G_{11}^R \Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})} G_{11}^A \Sigma_{11}^{A(\text{left})} \right]_{nn}$.
      
      **Transverse current for $\mu_L < \mu_R$:** $I_{1n,1n+1}=I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{persist})}+I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{transp})}$ with $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{persist})}=i_0 \int dE f_L 2\Re \left\{ t_{1n,1n+1} \left[ G_{1n+1,1n}^R - G_{1n+1,1n}^A \right] \right\}$ and $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{transp})}=i_0 \int dE (f_R - f_L) 2\Re \left\{ t_{1n,1n+1} \left[ -i G_{11}^R \Gamma_{11}^{(\text{right})} G_{11}^A \right]_{n+1,n} \right\}$.
      
      **Transverse current for $\mu_R < \mu_L$:** $I_{1n,1n+1}=I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{persist})}+I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{transp})}$ with $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{persist})}=i_0 \int dE f_L 2\Re \left\{ t_{1n,1n+1} \left[ G_{1n+1,1n}^R - G_{1n+1,1n}^A \right] \right\}$ and $I_{1n,1n+1}^{(\text{transp})}=i_0 \int dE (f_L - f_R) 2\Re \left\{ t_{1n,1n+1} \left[ -i G_{11}^R \Gamma_{11}^{(\text{left})} G_{11}^A \right]_{n+1,n} \right\}$.
      
      In these expressions, $t_{1n,1n+1}$ is the nearest-neighbor hopping along the transverse direction in column 1, $G_{1n+1,1n}^{R/A}$ are the retarded/advanced Green's functions between sites $1n$ and $1n+1$, and all other symbols are as defined above.

steps.reasoning: Define the tight-binding one-body Hamiltonian of the complete device, partitioned into three uncoupled parts plus the coupling perturbation: $H=H_{0}+W_{pert}$, where $H_{0}=H_{0}^{(\mathrm{left})}+H_{0}^{(\mathrm{center})}+H_{0}^{(\mathrm{right})}$. Here $H_{0}^{(\mathrm{left})}$, $H_{0}^{(\mathrm{center})}$ and $H_{0}^{(\mathrm{right})}$ are the Hamiltonians of the left lead, the central device, and the right lead respectively, each written in the single-orbital-per-site tight-binding basis with site indices $(m,n)$ ($m$ = column index, $n$ = chain index). The perturbation $W_{pert}=W_{pert}^{(\mathrm{left})}+W_{pert}^{(\mathrm{right})}$ contains the nearest-neighbour hoppings that connect Col. $0$ to Col. $1$ and Col. $M$ to Col. $M+1$, explicitly $W_{pert}^{(\mathrm{left})}=\sum_n t_{0n,1n} c_{0n}^\dagger c_{1n}+\mathrm{h.c.}$ and analogously for the right contact.

Introduce the retarded ($G^{R}$), advanced ($G^{A}$) and lesser ($G^{<}$) Green's function operators of the full open system, and the disconnected-region Green's functions $g^{R},g^{A},g^{<}$. Use the abridged column-block notation: for retarded propagators $[G_{mm'}^{R}]_{nn'}=G_{mn,m'n'}^{R}=\langle\phi_{mn}|G^{R}|\phi_{m'n'}\rangle$, where $\phi_{mn}$ denotes the orbital at site $(m,n)$. Define the lead self-energies on a border column (e.g. Col. 1) as $\Sigma_{11}^{R,A(\mathrm{left})}$ and on Col. $M$ as $\Sigma_{MM}^{R,A(\mathrm{right})}$, with the coupling matrices $\Gamma \equiv i(\Sigma^{R}-\Sigma^{A})$ so that $\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{left})}=i\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}-i\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}$ and analogously for the right lead.

State the microscopic expression for the steady-state longitudinal bond current flowing from site $0n$ to site $1n$: $I_{0n,1n}=\dfrac{2(-e)}{\hbar}\int \dfrac{dE}{2\pi}2\Re\left[t_{0n,1n}\,G_{1n,0n}^{<}(E)\right]$. Define the natural unit of spectral current $i_0\equiv 2e/h$, so that $I_{0n,1n}=-i_0\int dE\,2\Re\left[t_{0n,1n}\,G_{1n,0n}^{<}(E)\right]$; here $e$ is the elementary charge and $h$ is Planck's constant.

Use the general relation connecting full and uncoupled lesser Green's functions: $G^{<}=g^{<}+G^{R}W_{pert}g^{<}+G^{<}W_{pert}g^{A}$. Projecting this relation on the matrix element $G_{1n,0n}^{<}$ and using the explicit form of $W_{pert}^{(\mathrm{left})}$ yields
$G_{1n,0n}^{<}=\sum_{n'}G_{1n,1n'}^{R}t_{1n',0n'}g_{0n',0n}^{<}+\sum_{n'}G_{1n,1n'}^{<}t_{1n',0n'}g_{0n',0n}^{A}$,
where $g_{0n',0n}^{<,A}$ are uncoupled lead Green's functions.

Define the lesser and advanced left-lead self-energy matrix elements by $\Sigma_{1n',1n}^{<(\mathrm{left})}=t_{1n',0n'}\,g_{0n',0n}^{<}\,t_{0n,1n}$ and $\Sigma_{1n',1n}^{A(\mathrm{left})}=t_{1n',0n'}\,g_{0n',0n}^{A}\,t_{0n,1n}$. Using these definitions the factor $t_{0n,1n}G_{1n,0n}^{<}$ appearing in the current integrand becomes $[\,G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{<(\mathrm{left})}+G_{11}^{<}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}\,]_{nn}$, so that the bond current is
$I_{0n,1n}=-i_0\int dE\,2\Re\left[\,G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{<(\mathrm{left})}+G_{11}^{<}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}\,\right]_{nn}$.

Introduce the Keldysh kinetic relation for the lesser Green's function projected on the central device: $G^{<}=G^{R}\Sigma^{<(\mathrm{leads})}G^{A}$. Here $\Sigma^{<(\mathrm{leads})}$ is the sum of the lead lesser self-energies. Using Fermi-Dirac distributions $f_L(E)$ and $f_R(E)$ of the left and right reservoirs, this gives $G^{<}=i f_L G^{R}\Gamma^{(\mathrm{left})}G^{A}+i f_R G^{R}\Gamma^{(\mathrm{right})}G^{A}$ when the leads are described by equilibrium reservoirs at their respective chemical potentials $\mu_L$ and $\mu_R$; define $f_{L,R}(E)=[\exp((E-\mu_{L,R})/k_BT)+1]^{-1}$ where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant and $T$ is temperature.

Project the kinetic relation on Col. 1 to obtain $G_{11}^{<}=i f_L G_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{left})}G_{11}^{A}+i f_R G_{1M}^{R}\Gamma_{MM}^{(\mathrm{right})}G_{M1}^{A}$. Insert this expression and the explicit form of $\Sigma_{11}^{<(\mathrm{left})}=i f_L \Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{left})}$ into the current formula of the previous step to obtain the spectral integrand form
$i_{0n,1n}(E)=i_0\big\{ f_L 2\Re[\,G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}-G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}-i G_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{left})}G_{11}^{A}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}\,]_{nn} + f_R 2\Re[ -i G_{1M}^{R}\Gamma_{MM}^{(\mathrm{right})}G_{M1}^{A}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}]_{nn}\big\}$,
which is valid at arbitrary temperature.

Specialize to zero temperature where $f_{L}(E)=\Theta(\mu_L-E)$ and $f_{R}(E)=\Theta(\mu_R-E)$ (Heaviside step functions). The spectral current then acquires a piecewise form depending on the ordering of $\mu_L$ and $\mu_R$ and on the energy intervals $E<\min(\mu_L,\mu_R)$, $\min(\mu_L,\mu_R)<E<\max(\mu_L,\mu_R)$, and $E>\max(\mu_L,\mu_R)$. For instance, in the case $\mu_L<\mu_R$ the longitudinal spectral current is
$i_{0n,1n}^{(a)}(E)=i_0\,2\Re\begin{cases}
[\,G_{11}^{R}\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}-\Sigma_{11}^{R(\mathrm{left})}G_{11}^{R}\,]_{nn}, & E<\mu_L,\\[4pt]
[ -i G_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{right})}G_{11}^{A}\Sigma_{11}^{A(\mathrm{left})}\,]_{nn}, & \mu_L<E<\mu_R,\\[4pt]
0, & E>\mu_R.
\end{cases}$
This piecewise structure follows directly from inserting the step-function occupations into the general spectral integrand.

Derive the transverse bond spectral current analogously starting from $I_{1n,1\,n+1}=-i_0\int dE\,2\Re\left[t_{1n,1\,n+1}\,G_{1\,n+1,1n}^{<}\right]$ and using the projected kinetic relation for $G_{11}^{<}$. At zero temperature and for $\mu_L<\mu_R$ the transverse spectral current pieces become
$i_{1n,1\,n+1}^{(a)}(E)=i_0\,2\Re\begin{cases}
t_{1n,1\,n+1}[\,G_{1\,n+1,1n}^{R}-G_{1\,n+1,1n}^{A}\,], & E<\mu_L,\\[4pt]
t_{1n,1\,n+1}[ -i G_{11}^{R}\Gamma_{11}^{(\mathrm{right})}G_{11}^{A}]_{n+1,n}, & \mu_L<E<\mu_R,\\[4pt]
0, & E>\mu_R.
\end{cases}$
Hence both longitudinal and transverse spectral currents admit closed analytic expressions resolved in energy and space within the tight-binding NEGF framework.

Note that the finite-temperature expressions are obtained from the zero-temperature piecewise forms by replacing step functions with the smooth Fermi factors $f_{L,R}(E)$; equivalently the general finite-temperature spectral integrand given above is the starting point. The authors summarize the zero-temperature formulas in a compact table (Table 1) and the finite-temperature versions in a corresponding table (Table 3), showing that all branch currents can be written in closed analytic NEGF form in terms of $G^{R/A}$, $\Sigma^{R/A}$, $\Gamma$ and $f_{L,R}(E)$.

motivating_questions.content: In two-terminal tight-binding devices, practical imaging requires bond currents expressed in terms of the few device quantities that are computed in NEGF workflows (retarded/advanced Green's functions of the device and lead self-energies) and that remain well defined at finite bias and temperature. Prior methods produced either total transmissions or ad hoc site projections with limited scope. What was needed is a set of self-contained, general formulas that (a) give the spectral (energy-resolved) bond current for any nearest-neighbor bond, (b) are valid at arbitrary nonequilibrium bias and temperature, and (c) use only standard NEGF objects ($G^{R/A}$, $\Sigma^{R/A}$, $\Gamma$, $f_{L,R}$) so they can be implemented directly and compared across device geometries and external fields.

steps.reasoning: The system under consideration is a quasi-one-dimensional quantum wire of width W and length L, with a central scattering region connected to left and right leads. The first-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian is defined as H = sum_i epsilon_i a_i^† a_i + sum_{⟨i,j⟩} V_{ij} a_i^† a_j, where all hopping energies are fixed at V_{ij} = -t, with t taken as the energy unit. On each lead site, the on-site energy is 0. In the scattering region of size L × W, the on-site energies vary randomly and independently.

In model I (the all-impurity model), the on-site energy at each scattering site is randomly selected from the interval [−w_dis/2, w_dis/2] with a uniform distribution. The disorder strength w_dis is set to 4, giving the interval [−2, 2]. The system size initially studied is 3 × 3, so there are 9 sites in the scattering region.

The descriptor chosen for each sample is the set of on-site energies of all sites in the scattering region. For a 3 × 3 system, this is a 9-dimensional vector. The label for each sample is the zero-temperature conductance at the Fermi energy E_F=0, calculated via the Landauer-Büttiker formula G = G_0 T_RL(E_F), where G_0 = 2e^2/h is the conductance quantum and T_RL(E) is the total transmission probability from left lead to right lead. A fully connected deep neural network (DNN) is constructed with three hidden layers, each containing 20 neurons. The input layer accepts the 9 descriptor values; the output layer has a single neuron yielding the predicted conductance. The activation function for all hidden neurons is the rectified linear unit σ(x) = max(0,x). Training minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) between predicted and true conductance, using the Adam optimization algorithm at a learning rate of 0.001.

A training data set of 40,000 statistically independent samples (each consisting of a descriptor of 9 random on-site energies and the corresponding computed conductance) is generated. A separate testing data set of 20,000 independent samples is also created.

In a $3\times 3$ tight-binding lattice with random on-site energies drawn from $[-2,2]$, there are only 9 independent parameters. Prior machine learning studies (e.g., ridge regression with five parameters) had shown promise for small systems, but it was unknown whether a DNN could accurately capture the conductance values for such a disordered configuration without assuming a peak structure. Without a quantitative baseline for a simple case, the feasibility of using neural networks for larger disordered systems could not be assessed. Form the Landauer-Büttiker transmission matrix for chiral plus non-chiral edges using the chiral+non-chiral parametrization $T_{i,i+1}=1+k$, $T_{i,i-1}=k$ (with the geometry-adjusted modification described below), producing a transmission (or conductance) matrix describing edge-only contributions; denote this matrix $G^{\mathrm{edge}}(k)$ when converted to the same conductance-like representation.

Combine bulk and edge contributions in a pragmatic element-wise additive manner to form the device conductance matrix
\[

\]
i.e., add corresponding matrix elements computed separately from the finite-element bulk runs and the Landauer-Büttiker edge model to obtain conductance predictions for each measurement configuration.

Account for device geometry in the edge model when forming $G^{\mathrm{edge}}(k)$: note that there are two different inter-lead spacings on the device perimeter with a spacing ratio of $1.8$, and modify the non-chiral inter-lead transmission probabilities to be inversely proportional to the inter-lead distance so that for more closely-spaced leads $T_{i,j}=k$ and for less-closely-spaced leads $T_{i,j}=k/1.8$; this geometric adjustment is implemented when computing $G^{\mathrm{edge}}(k)$.

Justify why the combined model gives a conservative (lower-bound) estimate: argue that including edge–bulk coupling would generally open additional conduction pathways (additional scattering channels that connect edge and bulk), which would increase the total device conductivity for a given $k$; therefore neglecting such coupling yields a model prediction that is a lower bound on device conductivity as a function of $k$.

motivating_questions.content: Real devices can have coupling between edge-localized states and bulk states: scattering processes that transfer carriers between these subsystems can modify measured resistances relative to naive sums of independent-channel conductances. A rigorous microscopic theory would include such coupling and possibly nonlocal self-consistent boundary conditions, but such a treatment is computationally and conceptually more complex. In order to compare bulk-dominated and edge-dominated hypotheses using tractable numerical workflows on a realistic device geometry, a simpler operational combination (sum of a bulk-conductivity-derived conductance matrix and an edge-transmission matrix) is desirable. However, the assumption of no coupling must be recognized as an approximation that biases inferred conductivities low; quantifying the effect of neglected coupling is necessary to make definitive statements about the absolute strength of edge conduction from fits that use this approximate combination.

Prior work on electrons in fractals gives information on eigenvalue distributions and localization properties but does not predict concrete measurable two-terminal conductances for realistic lead geometries. reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
An atomistic tight-binding simulation scheme was implemented to model graphene QPCs and SGM using a finite computational box for the device region together with explicit semi-infinite leads that reproduce an effectively infinite graphene half plane: horizontal semi-infinite leads are attached along the upper and lower edges of the output side of the computational box to simulate the in-plane graphene sheet, and additional semi-infinite leads attached at the top-right and bottom-right corners act as vertical current sinks that absorb current not entering the horizontal leads, thereby eliminating artificial corner backscattering. The atomistic Hamiltonian is the $p_z$-orbital nearest-neighbor tight-binding model
$$
H=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\left(t_{ij}c_i^{\dagger}c_j+\mathrm{H.c.}\right)+\sum_i V(\mathbf{r}_i)c_i^{\dagger}c_i,
$$
with the nearest-neighbor intralayer hopping taken as $t_{ij}=-3.12\ \mathrm{eV}$ and with bilayer interlayer hoppings and impurity parametrizations described within the same atomistic framework; the tip potential is modeled as a Lorentzian
$$
V(x,y)=\frac{V_t}{1+\left[(x-x_t)^2+(y-y_t)^2\right]/d^2}.
$$
This setup preserves the graphene crystal structure at the lead interfaces and allows Landauer-conductance calculations via wave-function matching on a finite atomistic grid while suppressing spurious finite-box corner scattering.

Include dilute-fluorination impurity parametrization within the same atomistic framework by using for the hopping between a fluorine adatom and a carbon atom the parameter $T=5.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ and an on-site energy on the fluorine ion $\varepsilon_F=-2.2\ \mathrm{eV}$; these impurity parameters are applied as additional terms in the same tight-binding Hamiltonian for sites occupied by adatoms.
[40]

Model the scanning-probe tip potential as a Lorentzian scalar potential in the plane: $V(x,y)=\frac{V_t}{1+\left[(x-x_t)^2+(y-y_t)^2\right]/d^2}$, where $V(x,y)$ is the potential energy at Cartesian coordinates $(x,y)$, $V_t$ is the maximal tip potential value, $(x_t,y_t)$ are the instantaneous tip coordinates, and $d$ is the effective lateral width of the tip potential; the paper uses this Lorentzian form for all SGM simulations and sets $V_t=1.25\ \mathrm{eV}$ as a typical value unless stated otherwise.
[42]

Introduce open-boundary simulation geometry by attaching explicit semi-infinite atomistic leads to the finite computational box: attach horizontal semi-infinite leads that extend along the upper and lower edges of the output side of the computational box to simulate the in-plane graphene half plane (these horizontal leads connect to the atomic edge cells and preserve the graphene crystal structure at the lead interfaces), and attach additional semi-infinite leads at the top-right and bottom-right corners that act as vertical current sinks absorbing current that does not enter the horizontal leads; the horizontal leads are semi-infinite in the $y$ direction and the corner sink leads are semi-infinite in the vertical (out-of-plane) direction as described in the text and depicted schematically.
Fig. 1(c)
Fig. 3

Explain the purpose of the extra leads and sinks: the horizontal semi-infinite leads eliminate the effects of backscattering from the finite nanoribbon vertical edges and the subband quantization that would otherwise produce multiple transverse Fermi wavelengths, while the corner vertical-sink leads absorb current that would be backscattered at the corners of the finite computational box, thereby suppressing artificial corner reflections and producing an effectively infinite graphene half plane to the right of the QPC.
Fig. 1(c)

Describe the numerical transport evaluation method used on this finite atomistic grid with attached semi-infinite leads: use the wave-function-matching (WFM) technique to compute scattering amplitudes $t^{mn}$ from incoming mode $n$ in the input lead to outgoing mode $m$ in the output lead, where the transmission probability to mode $m$ is $T^{m}=\sum_n|t^{mn}|^2$, and compute the two-terminal conductance $G$ via the Landauer formula $G=G_0\sum_m T^{m}=G_0\sum_{m,n}|t^{mn}|^2$, with $G_0=2e^2/h$; this WFM/Landauer procedure is applied to the atomistic Hamiltonian on the finite computational box with the explicit semi-infinite leads attached.
[43]

Conclude that the combined setup—an atomistic $p_z$-orbital nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian with bilayer and impurity parametrizations, a Lorentzian tip potential, horizontal semi-infinite in-plane leads to emulate an infinite graphene half plane, and corner vertical-sink semi-infinite leads to absorb nonin-plane currents—preserves the graphene crystal structure at the lead interfaces, enables Landauer-conductance calculations via wave-function matching on a finite atomistic grid, and suppresses spurious finite-box corner scattering to produce realistic open-boundary transport simulations for SGM of graphene QPCs.
Fig. 3

motivating_questions.content: Numerical studies of SGM and QPCs require simulation domains large enough to avoid reflections from device edges that would mix many transverse modes and produce spurious interference. Prior atomistic tight-binding studies either used large finite flakes with uncontrolled corner scattering or imposed boundary conditions that left edge reflections and subband quantization in the output region, which convoluted the SGM signal and prevented isolation of tip-induced backscattering. There was therefore a need for a finite-box atomistic method that reproduces an effectively infinite graphene half plane and that absorbs outgoing currents without introducing artificial scattering centers at the computational-box corners, so that calculated conductance maps reflect only the QPC, tip-induced scattering, and intentionally included defects.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A working simulation framework is established that computes ballistic quantum transport in atomistically resolved graphene nanoribbon devices by (a) representing the device Hamiltonian $H_{D}$ in a nearest-neighbor $\pi$-orbital tight-binding form $H_{D}=\sum_{ij}\bigl(t|i\rangle\langle j|-q\phi_{D}\delta_{ij}\bigr)$ with coupling parameter $t=-3\ \mathrm{eV}$ and self-consistent electrostatic potential $\phi_{D}$, (b) evaluating the retarded Green's function $G(E)=\bigl[(E+i0^{+})I-H_{D}-\Sigma_{S}-\Sigma_{D}\bigr]^{-1}$ with source/drain self-energies $\Sigma_{S,D}$ computed by the Sancho–Rubio recursive surface Green's function method for semi-infinite reservoirs, (c) obtaining contact broadening $\Gamma_{S(D)}=i(\Sigma_{S(D)}-\Sigma_{S(D)}^{+})$, the electron correlation function $G^{n}(E)=G\,\Sigma^{in}\,G^{+}$ with ballistic in-scattering $\Sigma^{in}_{S(D)}=\Gamma_{S(D)}f(E,E_{F_{S(D)}})$, and currents via $I_{j\rightarrow j+1}=\frac{ie}{h}\int dE\,[H_{j,j+1}G^{n}_{j+1,j}(E)-H_{j+1,j}G^{n}_{j,j+1}(E)]$, and (d) coupling these quantities self-consistently to a three-dimensional Poisson solver implemented with the method of moments (boundary element method) treating device grid points on every carbon atom and boundary grid points on gate/source/drain surfaces. The simulator is applied under the ballistic transport assumption to double-gate GNR MOSFET geometries with SiO2 insulators (thickness 1 nm), source/drain regions doped to 0.08 electrons per carbon atom, and channel lengths of 12.5 nm; it thereby provides atomistic predictions of local density of states, transmission, spatially resolved current spectrum, and terminal I–V characteristics for specified device geometries and contact models.

premises.content: In the method-of-moments Poisson solver used for the double-gate graphene nanoribbon metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (GNR MOSFET) geometry (oxide thickness 1 nm, gate width twice the ribbon width), the charge on each carbon atom is represented as a point charge located at the center of a circle of radius R_eff = 0.2 nm, and the on-site potential is computed as Phi_ii = (rho_si sqrt(Delta S_i))/(2 pi epsilon), where rho_si is the surface charge density, Delta S_i is the area of the differential element, and epsilon is the permittivity. The accuracy of this point-charge representation for computing the electrostatic potential on an atomically thin (single-layer) graphene ribbon between two planar gate electrodes is not compared to an analytical solution (e.g., a parallel-plate capacitor with a charge sheet) or to a more accurate fine-grid finite-element calculation. The error introduced by the approximation and the choice of R_eff may affect the potential profile, especially near the edges of the ribbon and at the source/drain contacts.

The quantitative numbers reported in conclusions 5 and 6 would be unreliable, and the qualitative trends in conclusions 4 and 7 might also be affected."}

premises.content: For an infinite 2D graphene sheet described by the same π-orbital nearest-neighbor tight-binding model (coupling t = -3 eV), the surface Green's function computed with the Sancho–Rubio recursive method reproduces the known density of states and transmission from Saito et al., including the van Hove singularities and the transmission plateau (Fig. 1). The agreement is quantitative across the full energy range of interest.

premises.content: The electrostatic problem for the double-gate GNR MOSFET (oxide thickness 1 nm, source/drain and gate electrode surfaces) is solved in full three dimensions using the method of moments (boundary-element method). Grid points are placed on every carbon atom for the device charge, and rectangular elements are used on the electrode surfaces. The potential accounts for on-site terms via an effective radius and dielectric imaging effects. This approach avoids any reduction to 1D or 2D electrostatics and captures the three-dimensional fringing fields from the finite-width ribbon and gates.
premises.metadata: {"role": "highlight", "conclusion_id": "1", "strength_types": ["model", "computational"], "credit": "This preempts the failure mode that a reduced-dimensionality electrostatic model (e.g., a 1D vertical Poisson or a 2D cross-section) would omit fringing effects and in-plane potential variations that are critical for narrow, finite-length ribbons. It underwrites the electrostatic layer of all device metrics: the computed SS, DIBL, and I_ON in conclusions 5 and 6 rely on the accuracy of the potential profile. The atomistic resolution (grid on every carbon atom) ensures that the potential couples correctly to the tight-binding Hamiltonian, which is essential for the NEGF charge density calculation."}

steps.reasoning: Define the device Hamiltonian $H_{D}$ by the nearest-neighbor $\pi$-orbital tight-binding approximation: $H_{D}=\sum_{ij}\left(t|i\rangle\langle j|-q\phi_{D}\delta_{ij}\right)$, where $t$ is the nearest-neighbor coupling energy, $|i\rangle$ denotes the atomic $\pi$ orbital at site $i$, $q$ is the electronic charge, $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta, and $\phi_{D}$ is the self-consistent electrostatic potential on the device. The coupling parameter is taken to be $t=-3\ \mathrm{eV}$ to reproduce graphene band structure. This tight-binding form is the electronic-structure basis of the transport simulator. [18]

Express the retarded Green's function $G(E)$ for the open device using the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism: $G(E)=\left[\left(E+i0^{+}\right)I-H_{D}-\Sigma_{S}-\Sigma_{D}\right]^{-1}$, where $E$ is energy, $i0^{+}$ enforces causal boundary conditions, $I$ is the identity matrix, and $\Sigma_{S}$ and $\Sigma_{D}$ are the self-energies describing coupling to the source (left) and drain (right) reservoirs. This is the central propagator from which densities and currents are computed. [16]

Compute the self-energies for semi-infinite reservoirs using the Sancho–Rubio recursive surface Green's function method: the iterative algorithm yields $\Sigma_{S}$ and $\Sigma_{D}$ that represent the effect of infinite-length contacts on the finite device region. These self-energies enter $G(E)$ and thereby incorporate contact coupling and open-boundary conditions into the simulation. [21]

Define contact broadening matrices $\Gamma_{S(D)}$ from the self-energies as $\Gamma_{S(D)}=i\left(\Sigma_{S(D)}-\Sigma_{S(D)}^{+}\right)$, where the superscript $+$ denotes Hermitian conjugation; these matrices quantify the energy-dependent level broadening induced by coupling to the reservoirs and are used in DOS and in-scattering calculations.

Compute the electron correlation function (lesser Green's function) in the ballistic approximation as $G^{n}(E)=G(E)\,\Sigma^{in}(E)\,G^{+}(E)$, where the in-scattering from contacts in the ballistic case is $\Sigma^{in}_{S(D)}(E)=\Gamma_{S(D)}(E)\,f\bigl(E,E_{F_{S(D)}}\bigr)$, and $f(E,E_F)$ denotes the Fermi-Dirac distribution with reservoir Fermi level $E_{F_{S(D)}}$. This yields the energy-resolved occupancy of device states injected from the contacts. [16]

Obtain the contact-resolved local density of states (DOS) contribution by $DOS_{S(D)}(E)=(1/2\pi)\,G(E)\,\Gamma_{S(D)}(E)\,G^{+}(E)$, which follows from the Green's function and broadening definitions and identifies how contact coupling contributes to available states at each energy. This quantity enables plotting device DOS and transmission for validation.

Compute the spatial charge density from the electron correlation function by integrating over energy: $\rho_{j}=e\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dE}{2\pi}G^{n}_{j}(E)$, where $\rho_{j}$ is the electronic charge at device site $j$ (site $j$ corresponds to a carbon atom), and $e$ is the elementary charge; this yields the real-space charge distribution used in electrostatics. [16]

Compute the bond current between neighboring device sites from the energy-resolved electron correlation function via $I_{j\rightarrow j+1}=\frac{ie}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dE}{2\pi}\left[H_{j,j+1}G^{n}_{j+1,j}(E)-H_{j+1,j}G^{n}_{j,j+1}(E)\right]$, where $H_{j,j+1}$ is the tight-binding coupling between sites $j$ and $j+1$, $h$ is Planck's constant, and the integration yields the total current through that bond. This expression provides spatially resolved current and, upon summation, terminal currents. [16]

Implement a three-dimensional Poisson solver using the method of moments (boundary element method) to obtain the self-consistent electrostatic potential $\phi_{D}$: discretize the device charge into point charges placed at carbon-atom positions (device grid points) and discretize gate/source/drain surfaces into rectangular boundary elements (boundary grid points); the electrostatic kernel $K(r,r')$ relating potentials to charges is assembled and used to compute device potentials from device charge and fixed boundary potentials via $\Phi_{D}=(A-BD^{-1}C)\,n_{D}+BD^{-1}\Phi_{B}$, where $A,B,C,D$ are subblocks of $K$ partitioned into device/boundary contributions, $n_{D}$ and $n_{B}$ are device and boundary charge vectors, and $\Phi_{D}$ and $\Phi_{B}$ are device and boundary potentials. The on-site self-potential of an element is taken as $\Phi_{ii}=\frac{\rho_{si}\sqrt{\Delta S_i}}{2\pi\varepsilon}$ under the point-charge approximation with effective device-element radius $R_{\text{eff}}$ (taken as $0.2\ \mathrm{nm}$ in this work). This couples the NEGF charge to 3D electrostatics. [17]

Combine NEGF and Poisson self-consistently: iterate (a) solve Green's function $G(E)$ and $G^{n}(E)$ for a given potential $\phi_{D}$, (b) compute charge density $\rho$ from $G^{n}(E)$, (c) solve the 3D Poisson problem to update $\phi_{D}$, and (d) repeat until convergence. This self-consistent loop yields physically consistent electrostatics and quantum transport in the atomistic device representation. [16]

Validate and calibrate the implementation by computing DOS and transmission $T(E)$ for an infinite 2D graphite (graphene) sheet and comparing with established results: the computed DOS and $T(E)$ for the infinite 2D sheet show the expected features for the $\pi$-orbital tight-binding model, thereby confirming accurate calculation of reservoir self-energies and spectral properties. (This is illustrated by the density-of-states and transmission data presented for the infinite sheet.) Fig. 1

Specify the device geometries and operating assumptions used in the simulations reported: double-gate GNR MOSFET geometry with SiO2 insulators of thickness $t_{\text{ins}}=1\ \mathrm{nm}$, channel length $L=12.5\ \mathrm{nm}$, source/drain regions doped to $0.08$ electrons per carbon atom (corresponding in the paper to $1.37\times10^{8}$ electrons/m), and ballistic transport assumption (no scattering inside channel). The device grid places a device grid point on every carbon atom and boundary grid points on gate/source/drain surfaces. Fig. 3

State the simulator outputs that follow from the above formalism and setup: spatially and energy-resolved local density of states $\text{LDOS}(x,E)$ (averaged per atom in a unit cell for plotting), transmission $T(E)$, energy- and position-resolved current density spectrum $J(x,E)$, real-space charge density $\rho(x)$, and terminal current–voltage ($I$–$V$) characteristics as functions of bias. These quantities are produced for specified device geometries and contact models under the ballistic-transport assumption. Fig. 4

motivating_questions.content: Device-level predictions for sub-10–20 nm GNR MOSFETs require an atomistic treatment that simultaneously captures (i) quantum mechanical transmission and tunneling, (ii) contact self-energies for different contact dimensionalities, and (iii) realistic three-dimensional electrostatics of an atomically thin channel. Before this work, available models either used semiclassical transport approximations that omitted coherent tunneling and contact-specific induced states, or used lower-dimensional electrostatics approximations that could not capture the full boundary-element coupling between carbon-atom-resolved charge and gate/source/drain electrodes. Without a combined real-space NEGF and 3D Poisson capability, it was not possible to compute, self-consistently and at atomistic resolution, the energy- and position-resolved local density of states, the partitioning of current into thermionic and tunneling components, or the quantitative device metrics (SS, DIBL, $I_{\\mathrm{ON}}$, $I_{\\mathrm{OFF}}$) for specified GNR geometries and contact types; hence predictions about the impact of contact engineering or the feasibility of BTBT operation lacked rigorous microscopic support.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A practical computational workflow is established: compute $G^{R,A}$ for the central tight-binding region with SCB dephasing using the continued-fraction / renormalization-decimation expansion (convergent matrix continued fractions), compute $P$ and invert $1-\gamma^{2}P$ to obtain $Q$, form $K^{(\mathrm{left/right})}$ from Eq. (11), then obtain $G^{<,>}$ from $G^{R}\Sigma^{<,>}G^{A}$ and evaluate $I_{\mathrm{coh}}$, $I_{\mathrm{inc}}$, $T_{\mathrm{tot}}$, and $S(0)$ using the derived formulas. This procedure was implemented within a single-orbital-per-site square-lattice tight-binding description and applied to central-device sizes corresponding to $M=1,2,5$ columns and width $N=150$ chains, with parameter choices (examples) $\gamma=0,100,200,400\ \mathrm{meV}$, lattice spacing $a\approx1.342\ \mathrm{nm}$, hopping $t\approx-424\ \mathrm{meV}$, and magnetic flux parameter $\alpha=\Phi_p/\Phi_0$ to represent $B=0$ and $B=10\ \mathrm{T}$ cases. The scheme attains the numerical accuracy necessary to resolve quantized conductance plateaus and extremely small shot-noise values.

premises.metadata: {"weak_types": ["computational"], "weakness_reason": "In computational quantum transport, the accuracy of continued-fraction methods depends on the truncation order and the stopping criterion; matrix inversions require a tolerance for the linear solver. Without reporting these settings, the claim that the scheme achieves \"high accuracy\" is unquantified. The absence of error bars or convergence studies is particularly relevant for the quantitative claims about extreme shot-noise suppression (by at least seven orders of magnitude), as such small values are sensitive to numerical artifacts. The field standard for papers that make quantitative accuracy claims typically includes a convergence test, a residual estimate, or a comparison with an independent method.", "failure_mode": "Without convergence and error quantification, the computed values of conductance and Fano factor are not demonstrably accurate. For instance, the Fano factor suppression to 10^{-7} could be an artifact of the numerical scheme not resolving a slightly larger value due to accumulated errors from the continued fraction truncation or the matrix inversion, rather than the true model output. The qualitative trends (existence of plateau regions) might survive, but the quantitative precision needed to support the claim of at least seven orders of magnitude suppression (conclusion 10) would be unsupported. Similarly, exact conductance quantization (conclusion 9) could be an artifact of insufficient resolution of small deviations from integer values."}

premises.content:
The coupled self-consistent Born (SCB) equations for the retarded Green's function \(G^{R}(E)\) of the central device (size \(M\) columns \(\times\) \(N\) transverse chains) are
      $$
      G^{R}(E)=\frac{1}{E-H^{(C)}-\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{leads})}(E)-\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{scatt})}(E)},
      $$
      where \(H^{(C)}\) is the electronic Hamiltonian of the central device, \(\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{leads})}(E)\) is the retarded self-energy due to the left and right open leads, and \(\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{scatt})}(E)=\gamma^{2}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sup}}\,G^{R}(E)\) with \(\gamma\) the dephasing coupling strength and \(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sup}}\) the superoperator that preserves diagonal elements. These equations admit an explicit computational representation as a matrix continued fraction
      $$
      G^{R}(E)=\frac{1}{E-H^{(C)}-\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{leads})}-\gamma^{2}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sup}}\frac{1}{E-H^{(C)}-\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{leads})}-\gamma^{2}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sup}}\frac{1}{E-\cdots}}}
      $$
      which can be evaluated numerically using renormalization-decimation or continued-fraction techniques to obtain \(G^{R}\) for the central region with high convergence speed.

The lesser scattering self-energy and the effective scattering-mediated couplings to reservoirs are obtained by solving linear matrix equations. For the central device of size \(MN\) (with \(M\) columns and \(N\) transverse chains), define the matrix
      $$
      P_{j\nu}\equiv G_{j\nu}^{R}G_{\nu j}^{A}=\left|G_{j\nu}^{R}\right|^{2},

      $$
      Q\equiv\left(1-\gamma^{2}P\right)^{-1},
      $$
      where \(G^{R}\) (\(G^{A}\)) is the retarded (advanced) Green's function of the central device and \(\gamma\) is the dephasing coupling strength. The diagonal elements of the effective coupling matrices \(K^{(\mathrm{left/right})}\) (which enter \(\Sigma^{<(\mathrm{scatt})}=i f_L K^{(\mathrm{left})}+i f_R K^{(\mathrm{right})}\)) are
      $$
      K_{jj}^{(\mathrm{left})}(E)=\gamma^{2}\sum_{\nu} Q_{j\nu}\left[\,G^{R}\Gamma^{(\mathrm{left})}G^{A}\right]_{\nu\nu},
      $$
      $$
      K_{jj}^{(\mathrm{right})}(E)=\gamma^{2}\sum_{\nu} Q_{j\nu}\left[\,G^{R}\Gamma^{(\mathrm{right})}G^{A}\right]_{\nu\nu},
      $$
      where \(\Gamma^{(\mathrm{left/right})}=i\Sigma^{R(\mathrm{left/right})}-i\Sigma^{A(\mathrm{left/right})}\) are the lead linewidth matrices (with \(\Sigma^{R/A(\mathrm{left/right})}\) the retarded/advanced self-energies due to left/right leads) and \(f_{L,R}(E)\) are the Fermi-Dirac distribution functions of the left and right reservoirs. The \(K\) matrices are diagonal on central-device sites and represent the effective, scattering-mediated coupling of the central region to the left and right reservoirs.

motivating_questions.content: To test and demonstrate the theoretical identities and to explore the noisy-to-noiseless crossover one needs a concrete, end-to-end numerical implementation that is both accurate and scalable to physically relevant tight-binding discretizations. Prior implementations either neglected full SCB dephasing, used heuristic probes, or lacked the numerical convergence required to separate tiny shot-noise signals (many orders of magnitude smaller than the Poisson value) from numerical noise. A computational scheme that integrates the continued-fraction solution of $G^{R}$ with the exact linear algebra solution for $\Sigma^{<(\mathrm{scatt})}$ (via $P,Q,K$) and then computes currents and noise was not previously demonstrated for the tight-binding quantum-wire geometries studied here; providing and applying that workflow was necessary to produce the quantitative numerical results reported.
